T0.title: The language-model training loop
T0.definition: Training changes a language model's parameters using examples. A batch supplies input tokens and known targets; the model predicts, a loss measures mistakes, backpropagation computes gradients and an optimizer updates the parameters. Validation and generation use the model differently: they do not apply these training updates.
T0.example: A sequence [3,7,2,9] supplies inputs [3,7,2] and next-token targets [7,2,9]. One supplied target probability illustrates loss, while a separate scalar gradient illustrates an update. They explain the stages but are not one fully differentiated numerical model.
T0.connection: The foundations and DL course introduced loss, gradients and updates. This lesson assembles them for token sequences, keeping the repeated training path separate from periodic validation, checkpoint selection and fixed-weight use.

steps.title: Prepare inputs, targets and masks
steps.prose: Use training-only text and a compatible tokenizer to construct a batch. Shift tokens once so each input position predicts its successor. Define visibility and target masks before the forward pass; document and conversation boundaries affect what can be learned.
steps.terms: B counts batch examples and T prediction positions. A causal mask controls access to future positions; a loss mask selects targets that contribute to the objective.
steps.next: Run the current model on these permitted inputs without changing its parameters yet.

steps.title: Calculate predictions with current parameters
steps.prose: The forward pass maps input IDs through embeddings and model layers to vocabulary logits. Softmax defines a distribution for each scored position. The supplied probability 0.5 is an illustration, not the measured output of the scalar update below.
steps.terms: A logit is an unnormalized vocabulary score. Parameters define the predictor; computing predictions is not itself an optimizer update.
steps.next: Compare the assigned target probabilities with the known labels to obtain a scalar loss.

steps.title: Calculate loss over valid targets
steps.prose: Take the negative log-probability of each included correct token, then reduce under the intended convention. Here one target with probability 0.5 gives log two. Padding and unscored prompt positions must not enter the denominator accidentally.
steps.terms: In the equation m_t selects targets, p_t(y_t) is the correct-token probability and the mask sum counts valid targets. Natural logs give nats.
steps.next: Differentiate the declared loss through the recorded computation to obtain parameter gradients.

steps.title: Compute gradients by backpropagation
steps.prose: Backpropagation follows the chain rule to measure how changing each trainable parameter would change the loss locally. It writes gradients, not new weights. The next stage's scalar gradient 2 is supplied separately to explain an optimizer.
steps.terms: Theta denotes trainable parameters; nabla L is their gradient. A gradient's sign and magnitude are not a certainty estimate about an answer.
steps.next: Pass the gradients to an optimizer under the chosen accumulation and clipping rules.

steps.title: Apply one optimizer update and repeat
steps.prose: The scalar illustration changes weight 1 using gradient 2 and the selected learning rate. A real AdamW update also uses optimizer history and decay rules. Clear gradients at the correct boundary, fetch another batch and repeat under the budget.
steps.terms: Eta is learning rate and g a gradient. An optimizer step can combine several microbatches; it is not necessarily one pass over the dataset.
steps.next: Continue with the next batch; at scheduled intervals, evaluate separate validation text without updates.

steps.title: Evaluate periodically on validation text
steps.prose: Pause updates, use the intended evaluation mode and disable derivative recording. The hypothetical losses [1.2,1.0,1.1] select checkpoint two. Validation supports selection; feeding its gradients into the optimizer would change the experiment.
steps.terms: Evaluation mode controls behaviors such as dropout. No-grad controls derivative recording. Development evidence is not the untouched final test.
steps.next: Save selected weights or complete restart state according to the checkpoint's purpose.

steps.title: Save state for selection, resumption or use
steps.prose: A weights export supports inference only with compatible configuration and tokenizer. Exact continuation additionally needs optimizer, scheduler, random and sampler state as appropriate. Generation loads fixed parameters and appends chosen tokens instead of receiving known future targets.
steps.terms: A checkpoint's contents determine its supported use. Selecting a checkpoint, resuming training and generating from it are different actions.
steps.next: The next lesson examines how changing prediction targets and available context changes the training objective.

T1.title: Language-model training objectives
T1.definition: A training objective defines what the model predicts, which information it may use and how mistakes are scored. Causal language modelling predicts successors from prefixes; masked modelling reconstructs selected tokens from permitted surrounding text; encoder–decoder learning predicts a target sequence conditioned on a source. These are different prediction problems, not interchangeable names for pretraining.
T1.example: Choose an objective to compare visibility and targets. A separate fixed set of three correct-target probabilities [0.5,0.25,0.5] illustrates mean negative log-likelihood. The numbers do not establish which objective trains a better model.
T1.connection: The complete training loop can optimize different objectives. Define their information access before comparing losses or downstream behavior; a language-model objective alone does not establish instruction following or safe deployment.

steps.title: Define the prediction target
steps.prose: The selected objective determines whether an answer is the next token, a withheld original token or a token of a conditional target sequence. Observed text supplies these labels. Self-supervision therefore does not mean training without any targets.
steps.terms: Theta denotes learned parameters. The expectation in the loss describes averaging over examples; y is the target under the selected task.
steps.next: Specify what the model may read when predicting that target.

steps.title: Specify permitted context and visibility
steps.prose: Causal prediction uses a permitted prefix; masked prediction uses corrupted surrounding input; conditional decoding uses a source plus earlier target tokens. Attention visibility must enforce this access even when many positions are computed together.
steps.terms: An attention mask limits information flow. A loss mask chooses which positions are scored; excluding a loss does not hide its input token.
steps.next: Score only the declared targets with their correct normalization.

steps.title: Calculate mean target prediction loss
steps.prose: For the supplied probabilities [0.5,0.25,0.5], add three negative natural logarithms and divide by three. This demonstrates the scoring operation separately from the visibility examples. A different target set changes the loss's interpretation.
steps.terms: NLL is negative log-likelihood. The mean is per included target, not per padded slot or necessarily per input sentence.
steps.next: Keep the distinction between this training score and the behavior required when using the model.

steps.title: Separate pretraining, adaptation and inference
steps.prose: Pretraining learns statistical structure; continued pretraining changes exposure; supervised adaptation learns demonstrations; preference methods use feedback. These are optional recipe choices, not mandatory stages for every application. Inference normally leaves weights fixed.
steps.terms: Teacher forcing supplies known earlier target tokens during training. Generation instead conditions on earlier chosen outputs, so errors can compound.
steps.next: The data lesson next traces how source documents become compatible, auditable training examples.

T2.title: LLM training data, tokenization and packing
T2.definition: A language-model data pipeline converts permitted source material into the exact token inputs and prediction targets seen during training. It includes extraction, duplicate grouping, splits, tokenization, packing and masks. Corpus descriptions alone are insufficient: the resulting batches must preserve the intended information and evaluation boundaries.
T2.example: Four source records with one exact duplicate illustrate identity and grouping. A separate supplied token sequence [3,7,2,9] shows how window length changes the aligned input and target slices. Neither example downloads or prepares an external corpus.
T2.connection: An objective defines the intended prediction problem. The data pipeline must implement that problem without leaking evaluation examples, changing tokenizer meanings or introducing unintended cross-document targets.

steps.title: Record source provenance and identity
steps.prose: Keep source/version, permissions and content identity before deriving examples. A hash detects byte identity under its defined serialization; it does not grant rights or prove truth. Group duplicates and related records rather than treating file formats as independent sources.
steps.terms: Provenance records origin and processing. Exact duplicate detection differs from near-duplicate grouping; both require a declared comparison policy.
steps.next: Assign independent source groups to splits before learning corpus-dependent statistics.

steps.title: Reserve evaluation groups before fitting
steps.prose: Keep related documents, translations or near duplicates together under the evaluation design. Fit new tokenizer/statistical processing only on permitted training data. Reusing a pretrained tokenizer requires compatibility rather than refitting vocabulary IDs independently.
steps.terms: A group is the unit kept together in a split. Contamination includes prohibited evaluation information entering fitting or selection.
steps.next: Encode each split with the selected compatible saved tokenizer and boundary policy.

steps.title: Encode text with a compatible tokenizer
steps.prose: The example supplies token IDs [3,7,2,9]. Their values identify vocabulary entries, not semantic magnitudes. Save normalization, special tokens and tokenizer revision so new batches retain the same interpretation expected by model embeddings.
steps.terms: An end-of-sequence marker defines a boundary under a recipe; it does not alone block every cross-document attention connection.
steps.next: Build windows and score masks from these fixed IDs, checking shifts exactly once.

steps.title: Construct windows and inspect masks
steps.prose: Slice inputs and their successors under the selected prediction-window length. Real packing also decides whether documents can attend across boundaries and whether artificial boundary transitions are scored. Position resets alone do not enforce isolation.
steps.terms: T counts prediction positions in this example. Attention masks restrict reading; target masks restrict scoring, and both need independent tests.
steps.next: The Transformer walkthrough next follows the permitted input IDs through the model's actual forward calculations.

T5.title: Gradient accumulation and stable LLM training
T5.definition: Gradient accumulation combines several small forward/backward calculations before one optimizer update. The loss weighting must match the intended objective, especially when microbatches contain different numbers of valid targets. Numerical stability, clipping, scheduling and diagnostics are additional training choices, not substitutes for correctly aligned data and targets.
T5.example: Microbatch A has two scored tokens with mean loss one; B has a selectable token count with mean loss three. At six B tokens the combined token mean is 2.5, while averaging the two microbatch means gives 2.0. The control changes this accounting, not a live run.
T5.connection: The training loop identified where gradients are accumulated and applied. This lesson derives their weighting on one worker; the distributed lesson later adds the separate convention used to combine workers.

steps.title: Count the scored targets in this update
steps.prose: Count valid labels after shifting and loss masking, not padded tensor slots. The two supplied microbatch means may summarize different amounts of evidence. Plan the total denominator before backward or use a specified equivalent normalization procedure.
steps.terms: A microbatch is one forward/backward unit. An optimizer update can aggregate several such units; valid targets are the included token labels.
steps.next: Recover each microbatch's summed loss using its mean and valid-target count.

steps.title: Recover loss sums from the means
steps.prose: Multiply each mean loss by the number of included targets it summarizes. A contributes two; B contributes three times its count. These fixed losses demonstrate reduction weights, not observations from a trained checkpoint.
steps.terms: A mean times its count recovers the corresponding sum. Comparing only means can conceal the unequal evidence weights.
steps.next: Add the sums and divide by the intended total target count.

steps.title: Normalize the intended token-average objective
steps.prose: Use the combined target count so each scored token has equal influence. With equal counts this agrees with a mean of microbatch means; with unequal counts it does not. Other objectives are allowed if declared rather than silently conflated.
steps.terms: N is total valid targets; n_b counts targets in microbatch b. Loss reduction defines the statistical weighting, not just a logging choice.
steps.next: Differentiate correctly weighted contributions, accumulate their gradients and update once.

steps.title: Accumulate gradients and update once
steps.prose: Backpropagate each appropriately scaled contribution, retaining parameter gradients rather than all forward graphs. At the boundary unscale if needed, check finite gradients, clip if configured and apply one optimizer step. Then clear gradients for the next update.
steps.terms: Clipping limits gradient norm; loss scaling protects numerical computation in some precision recipes. Neither repairs incorrect target weighting.
steps.next: The deeper notes cover instability, diagnostics and schedule units; the next topic accounts for the memory those operations require.

links: Combine each target count with its supplied microbatch mean.

T6.title: LLM parameter counts, memory and compute
T6.definition: A model's parameter count, raw weight storage, training-state memory and compute budget measure different things. Training can require gradients, optimizer history, activations and temporary workspaces beyond the weights. Resource estimates are conditional accounting tools; measured peak memory and throughput must establish whether a real configuration fits and runs usefully.
T6.example: Select one, ten or one hundred million hypothetical parameters. The simple convention stores FP32 weights, FP32 gradients and two FP32 Adam moments. Its static state uses sixteen bytes per parameter before activations or runtime overhead; other recipes need different accounting.
T6.connection: The training loop explains what values exist and when. This lesson counts their storage and work before scaling, while keeping the detailed prepared-model count, scaling laws and hardware bottlenecks in the deeper explanations.

steps.title: Count actual parameter entries
steps.prose: Add the entries of the model's unique parameter tensors. Tied weights are one shared parameter storage, not two independent learned matrices. The control declares a hypothetical count; it does not inspect an unknown model or infer a count from a product name.
steps.terms: A parameter is one learned scalar. Token exposure, layer count and hidden width affect resources but are not themselves parameter counts.
steps.next: Use the parameter count with an explicit numerical format to calculate raw weight bytes.

steps.title: Calculate raw weight storage
steps.prose: Under this example's FP32 convention each weight value needs four bytes. Multiply the parameter count accordingly and distinguish decimal MB from binary MiB. Metadata, temporary copies and allocations are outside this value-only estimate.
steps.terms: Precision defines a value representation. Raw storage is not a peak device-memory estimate or a guarantee that a model will fit.
steps.next: Add the state required by the selected training recipe separately from the weights.

steps.title: Account for gradients and optimizer history
steps.prose: This FP32 Adam illustration adds four bytes per gradient and eight bytes for two moment arrays to four-byte weights. Its sixteen-byte subtotal is not a universal constant. Mixed precision, freezing, sharding and optimizer variants change the terms.
steps.terms: Optimizer state contains update history. Frozen parameters need different trainable-state accounting but still require their participating base computation.
steps.next: Include activations, workspaces and implementation overhead before interpreting the total.
steps.node: Account for gradients and optimizer history

steps.title: Measure peaks and budget the full experiment
steps.prose: Activations vary with context, batch, architecture and checkpointing. Profile a representative safe pilot rather than multiplying by an invented constant. Compute/time estimates also need achieved throughput and evaluation/checkpoint costs, not just advertised hardware peaks.
steps.terms: Peak memory is the maximum live allocation under a run. FLOPs count arithmetic, while wall-clock time also includes data movement and orchestration.

T7.title: Distributed LLM training and gradient reduction
T7.definition: Distributed training divides data, arithmetic or stored state across cooperating processes. Data parallelism uses model replicas on different examples and combines gradients; tensor, pipeline and state-sharding schemes divide other objects. Correct loss normalization and communication are required before more devices can be treated as a performance improvement.
T7.example: Two data-parallel workers have unequal valid-token counts and supplied scalar mean gradients one and three. We calculate the intended global token-weighted gradient, then the local scaling needed when a reducer averages across the two workers. This is not an executed cluster job.
T7.connection: Microbatch accumulation combined evidence on one worker. This lesson adds communication and a reducer convention across workers; multiplying device counts alone does not establish either a correct gradient or a speedup.

steps.title: Define replica ownership and local evidence
steps.prose: Each worker holds matching model parameters and receives different permitted examples. The example uses two valid tokens on A and a selectable count on B. Model replication is not layer sharding or multiplying the hidden width.
steps.terms: Data-parallel workers compute local gradients for a common objective. W is the number of participating replicas, here two.
steps.next: Use these counts both to define the desired global mean and to scale the executed local contributions.

steps.title: Calculate the reference global gradient
steps.prose: The desired gradient weights local mean gradients by their valid-token counts. This independent reference checks the distributed calculation; it is not a gradient magically fed back into each worker. The scalar values stand in for full parameter-gradient tensors.
steps.terms: n_A and n_B count valid targets, and g_A and g_B are supplied local means. A mean of local means weights workers rather than tokens.
steps.next: Compare this reference with the reducer result after applying its correct local scaling.

steps.title: Scale local losses for the reducer
steps.prose: Ordinary averaging reduction divides summed gradients by W. To recover the intended global token mean, scale each local mean loss by W times its local count divided by the global count. A sum reducer would require a different factor.
steps.terms: The global denominator must be known consistently. Reducer semantics and loss normalization are part of the algorithm, not interchangeable implementation trivia.
steps.next: Average the scaled local gradients and verify agreement with the reference objective.

steps.title: Synchronize and apply matching updates
steps.prose: Combining the two scaled contributions with the stated average reproduces the target gradient. Replicas then need the same optimizer update and consistent state. Communication failures, unequal participation and stale state can break that equivalence.
steps.terms: All-reduce aggregates values across workers. It does not pool model opinions or create another reasoning stage.
steps.next: The deeper notes compare sharding, kernels, cluster workflow and profiling before evaluation of the resulting model.

T8.title: LLM evaluation and interpretability evidence
T8.definition: LLM evaluation tests a specified claim, such as better token prediction, task accuracy, source support, robustness or efficiency. Interpretability asks different questions about computation and mechanism. A score gain, an attention picture and a controlled intervention provide different evidence; none alone establishes every claim about useful or reliable behavior.
T8.example: Two hypothetical task scores, 0.76 and 0.79, illustrate a difference of 0.03. A separate scalar intervention starts from 0.8 and subtracts a selected amount. These are interpretation exercises, not measured causal effects from a trained model.
T8.connection: After fitting and resource accounting, evaluate the artifact against its intended use. Shared metrics supply the formulas; this lesson connects matched protocols, uncertainty and mechanism claims without treating one as a substitute for another.

steps.title: Define the comparison before interpreting a gain
steps.prose: Specify the task, input access, model revision, training data and resource budget. The hypothetical 0.03 difference isolates a factor only if relevant alternatives are controlled. A different template or extra evidence can explain an apparent method gain.
steps.terms: A matched comparison holds declared conditions fixed except the intended factor. Held-out results concern a specified sample and protocol.
steps.next: Save per-case outcomes and use appropriate uncertainty and error analysis.
steps.node: Define the comparison before interpreting a gain

steps.title: Inspect disagreements and uncertainty
steps.prose: Use the same evaluation cases for a paired comparison and preserve document/group dependencies. Resampling fixed predictions estimates a conditional test-sample uncertainty; repeated training seeds measure another source of variation. Neither creates universal generalization.
steps.terms: Paired resampling keeps aligned cases for both systems. Malformed outputs, abstentions and failures need declared denominator rules.
steps.next: Distinguish these outcome measurements from inspecting or intervening on internal computations.

steps.title: Separate observation from intervention
steps.prose: An attention map or probe can motivate a hypothesis without proving a mechanism. The separate scalar intervention illustrates an effect calculation only. Real interventions need matched controls and preservation checks because unusual internal states can create broad disruption.
steps.terms: Inspection observes; an intervention changes a selected quantity. Decodability of a feature is not proof the model uses it for the task.
steps.next: State the narrow conclusion supported by the actual evidence and its controls.

steps.title: Report limitations and release evidence
steps.prose: Report which outcomes changed, what was held fixed and which alternatives remain plausible. Package compatible artifacts and reproducible settings only when permitted. Model cards document scope but do not certify truthfulness, causal explanation or safe deployment.
steps.terms: A causal claim needs a meaningful intervention design. Reproducibility requires the data/interface and selection protocol as well as final weights.
steps.next: Post-training begins by deciding whether a task needs changed weights, better evidence or a different system operation.

T4.title: Language-model architecture families
T4.definition: An architecture defines which representations interact and what state is carried through a model. Encoders, causal decoders and encoder–decoders differ in information access and output interface; expert layers and state-space operations change other parts of the computation. These categories can overlap within one model, so architecture names are not an ordered quality ranking.
T4.example: Select a family to inspect its structure. The encoder–decoder example has three source positions and two target-prefix positions. Separate supplied examples illustrate two weighted experts or a scalar recurrent state; none is a trained comparison between model families.
T4.connection: The detailed decoder provided one concrete architecture. This lesson varies the structure while keeping visibility, shape, state, active computation and cache costs distinct, with positional and multimodal extensions in the deeper notes.

steps.title: Identify source and target streams
steps.prose: Conditional generation reads an available source while predicting a separate target sequence. The target prefix must not contain unknown future target answers. Here source and current target lengths are three and two, not matching axes by default.
steps.terms: B is batch size, D hidden width, T_s source length and T_t target-prefix length. These axes have different roles.
steps.next: Encode the source and represent the permitted target prefix as separate branches.

steps.title: Encode the source
steps.prose: A source encoder can use bidirectional context within the supplied source. It creates three source-position vectors for the example. That permission does not extend to future target answers, which belong to a different sequence.
steps.terms: Encoder self-attention relates source positions. A source mask still distinguishes valid input from padding.
steps.next: Use source states as keys and values when a decoder later reads this memory.

steps.title: Represent the permitted target prefix
steps.prose: The target side reads earlier permitted target tokens under a causal rule. Its two-position hidden representation supplies decoder-side queries. Source length and target-prefix length are independent and need separate masks.
steps.terms: Target self-attention relates allowed target positions. It is not the same attention operation as reading source representations.
steps.next: Cross-attend from these target queries to the source keys and values.

steps.title: Connect target queries to source memory
steps.prose: Each target position compares with the three source positions, giving a two-by-three score matrix per head. Normalize over source keys and mix their values. Cross-attention changes available information, not which sequence is being predicted.
steps.terms: In the equation Q_t contains target queries while K_s contains source keys. The head width controls dot-product scaling, not source length.
steps.next: Project the resulting target features to scores for the next target token.

steps.title: Predict the next target token
steps.prose: The vocabulary head maps conditioned decoder features to output scores. A generation process can then extend the target prefix while reusing compatible source computation. The source stream need not grow with every generated target token.
steps.terms: Conditional generation models p(y_t | x,y_<t). Weight updates and a complete numerical encoder–decoder execution are not performed here.
steps.next: The optimization lesson next returns to training arithmetic shared across architectures.

steps.title: Calculate routing weights for a shared input
steps.prose: A router assigns gate scores to expert subnetworks. The example uses logits [1,0] and softmax to form two weights. Both experts read the same token features; the router does not split the input into different examples.
steps.terms: MoE means mixture of experts. An expert is a parameterized subnetwork, not a verified semantic specialist.
steps.next: Evaluate the declared expert branches and retain gate weights for their later combination.

steps.title: Evaluate expert A
steps.prose: The first expert is supplied to return scalar two for this input. Its own parameters define the transformation. This value illustrates combination arithmetic, not evidence that it has learned a particular topic or skill.
steps.terms: Expert outputs must have compatible feature shapes before weighted addition. Distinct expert parameters need not imply interpretable specialization.
steps.next: Combine this branch with the other selected expert under the router weights.

steps.title: Evaluate expert B
steps.prose: The second expert is supplied to return minus one for the same input. Evaluating both is deliberate in this tiny example. A sparse top-k implementation might activate a subset and specify another gate normalization policy.
steps.terms: Total expert count and active experts per token measure different things. Both stored capacity and executed work matter.
steps.next: Send this branch and the other selected output to the weighted merge.

steps.title: Merge weighted expert outputs
steps.prose: Multiply each supplied expert output by its gate weight and add matching features. The root's gate values determine the mixture. This example activates both experts; a top-one choice would be a different calculation rather than the same result for free.
steps.terms: A weighted sum combines compatible outputs without concatenation. Router weights describe this computation, not answer correctness probabilities.
steps.next: Assess load balance, storage and communication as separate system-level questions.

steps.title: Evaluate capacity, routing and cost
steps.prose: Sparse activation can avoid executing every expert for each token, but total weights still need storage or a loading design. Routing imbalance, capacity limits and inter-device communication affect actual speed and quality.
steps.terms: Active parameters are those used for a token. System-level selection of a whole classifier is not automatically token-level MoE.
steps.next: The deeper notes distinguish head sharing, sparsity, kernels and modalities without treating them as one mechanism.

steps.title: Define a carried state and transition
steps.prose: The illustrative recurrence starts at h zero and reads [1,0,1] with input coefficient 0.5 and state coefficient 0.8. It compresses earlier information into a fixed-width state instead of storing one key/value pair per earlier token.
steps.terms: A state-space recurrence updates h using a transition A and input map B; a readout C maps state to an output. This scalar case is deliberately simple.
steps.next: Apply the transition to the first input and zero boundary state.

steps.title: Update state for the first input
steps.prose: The first input contributes 0.5 while the zero prior state contributes nothing. The new scalar state is 0.5. A later transition will reuse the same coefficients, not introduce a separate learned parameter set for each position.
steps.terms: Shared recurrence parameters are distinct from carried state values. A state value changes with input even during fixed-weight inference.
steps.next: Carry this state to the second position along with its current input.

steps.title: Carry state through a zero input
steps.prose: At the second position, multiplying 0.5 by 0.8 yields 0.4, and zero input adds no new contribution. Persistence here is a numeric state transition, not a claim about remembering arbitrary exact earlier text.
steps.terms: A transition can retain or attenuate state information. A compressed state is different from a full list of token-specific attention values.
steps.next: Combine the retained state with the third input.

steps.title: Incorporate the final input
steps.prose: The third position adds 0.5 to 0.8 times the prior 0.4, yielding 0.82. The state now depends on the sequence history under the chosen recurrence. It remains one scalar rather than growing by one vector per token.
steps.terms: Modern selective state-space models use richer, often input-dependent operations. This example is not a Mamba implementation.
steps.next: Map the resulting state to an output using the separate readout coefficient.

steps.title: Read out an output
steps.prose: The fixed readout doubles 0.82 to produce 1.64. This demonstrates a state-to-output map only. Comparing with attention requires matched quality and resources, not applying attention's ordinary cache formula to a different state mechanism.
steps.terms: The readout produces output features from state. State width, exact recall and long-context quality are separate design/evaluation questions.
steps.next: The deeper notes compare recurrent/state-space and other alternatives under their own information and cost assumptions.

links: Apply the shared transition to the first input and initial state.
Carry state 0.5 into the update for the second input.
Carry state 0.4 into the update for the final input.
Project the final state with the fixed readout coefficient.

T3.title: Decoder Transformer architecture
T3.definition: A decoder Transformer predicts a token from a permitted prefix by repeatedly transforming one vector per input position. Attention mixes information between allowed positions, while feed-forward layers transform features within each position. Residual connections preserve direct paths around these transformations. Training compares predictions with known targets; generation instead chooses and appends tokens with fixed parameters.
T3.example: The walkthrough uses a small supplied vocabulary and fixed weights: hidden width four, additive positions, LayerNorm and a 4→8→4 GELU feed-forward branch. Select a head, position or block to inspect the actual arithmetic. This is not the architecture or learned competence of the locally prepared pretrained model.
T3.connection: The data lesson produced aligned token inputs. This walkthrough follows their full computation while keeping tensor axes, residual paths and attention/vocabulary normalizations distinct. The deeper notes separately explain real grouped-query dimensions and other positional methods.

steps.title: Input token IDs and tensor axes
steps.prose: The input is a sequence of vocabulary identifiers, not vectors of word meanings yet. The example's authored IDs identify pieces such as How, to and predict. Adding a token changes the sequence axis, while the feature width is chosen separately.
steps.terms: B is batch size and T input length. An integer ID names a vocabulary row; a larger ID does not mean a larger or more meaningful token.
steps.next: Look up the corresponding row of the token embedding table for each input position.
steps.node: Input token IDs and tensor axes

steps.title: Token embedding lookup
steps.prose: Replace each input ID with its saved feature vector. Two occurrences of one ID start from the same embedding row before position and context are incorporated. This lookup preserves token order and creates the hidden feature axis.
steps.terms: D denotes hidden width, here four. An embedding is a computed lookup of learned parameters, not a probability distribution over possible answers.
steps.next: Add this teaching decoder's positional vectors to make location available to later calculations.

steps.title: Additive position information
steps.prose: Add corresponding entries of the token and position vectors. The shape stays the same, but the same token at another position can now have different input features. These fixed additive vectors are one convention, not how every modern decoder represents position.
steps.terms: Position is sequence location. RoPE instead transforms query/key coordinates inside attention and must not be confused with this embedding addition.
steps.next: Pass position-aware inputs through preceding blocks, if any, to obtain the selected block's input.

steps.title: Input of the selected decoder block
steps.prose: The selector opens one block from the configured stack. Earlier blocks have still been calculated, and their output feeds the selected one. Preserve this incoming representation for the first residual addition while transforming an attention branch.
steps.terms: A block is one parameterized attention/feed-forward stage. Selecting a block changes the inspected trace slice rather than removing other blocks from the model.
steps.next: Normalize the branch input before forming queries, keys and values.
steps.node: Input of the selected decoder block

steps.title: LayerNorm before attention
steps.prose: For each token independently, subtract its feature mean and divide by the square root of feature variance plus epsilon, then apply gain/bias. The example fixes gain one and bias zero. Token count and feature width do not change.
steps.terms: Mu and sigma-squared summarize features of one token; epsilon avoids an unstable denominator. LayerNorm differs from normalizing over examples or class labels.
steps.next: Project the normalized features into separate query, key and value representations.

steps.title: Query, key and value projections
steps.prose: Apply three learned matrix maps to the normalized features. Queries and keys determine matching scores; values supply content for the weighted mixture. The familiar matching analogy does not mean literal questions or factual statements are stored in these tensors.
steps.terms: Q, K and V name three projected tensors here; V is not the vocabulary-size symbol used elsewhere. Projection means a feature-space linear map.
steps.next: Reshape the projected coordinates into the selected attention-head layout.

steps.title: Attention head dimensions
steps.prose: Split the four projected features into the selected number of heads without creating extra entries. At two heads, each head has two features per token. Each head then computes its own position-by-position mixture.
steps.terms: H is head count and d_h=D/H head width in this example. Heads are learned subspaces, not guaranteed grammar, reasoning or truth specialists.
steps.next: Compare each query with the allowed candidate keys in its own head.

steps.title: Scaled query–key scores
steps.prose: For one query, multiply corresponding query/key coordinates, sum and divide by the square root of head width. Repeat over keys to form its score row. The full tensor has separate batch, head, query-position and key-position axes.
steps.terms: In S_ij, i indexes the query and j the key. The dot product contracts feature coordinates; the scores are not probabilities yet.
steps.next: Apply the causal visibility rule before normalizing these scores.

steps.title: Causal attention mask
steps.prose: For a query at position i, retain keys at or before i and forbid later ones. The example writes negative infinity before softmax so forbidden keys receive zero weight. Parallel processing of training positions must still respect this rule.
steps.terms: Causal means no reading future sequence positions. A loss mask separately chooses which targets teach the model; it cannot enforce attention visibility.
steps.next: Normalize each permitted score row over its key positions.

steps.title: Attention softmax over key positions
steps.prose: Convert a query's permitted scores into nonnegative weights summing to one over keys. Subtracting the maximum before exponentiation preserves the result and improves numerical stability. Each query and head receives its own normalization.
steps.terms: Attention softmax's axis is source/key positions. Its weights are mixing coefficients, not confidence that the final answer is correct.
steps.next: Use the normalized row to form a weighted sum of value vectors.

steps.title: Weighted value mixture
steps.prose: Multiply each allowed value vector by its weight and add corresponding feature entries. The resulting vector has one head's feature width, not one new position for every source token. A large coefficient does not alone explain the final model answer.
steps.terms: A weighted sum mixes compatible vectors. It is different from concatenating source tokens or selecting one token as a hard evidence decision.
steps.next: Join all head outputs and apply the attention output projection.

steps.title: Head concatenation and output projection
steps.prose: Join the heads along their feature axis, then multiply by the output projection. This can combine information from their different mixtures and returns the branch to hidden width. Neither operation changes the number of token positions.
steps.terms: Concatenation appends feature coordinates; addition combines matching coordinates. W_O is the projection back into residual-compatible feature space.
steps.next: Add the preserved original block input to the attention branch output.

steps.title: First residual addition
steps.prose: The shortcut brings the selected block input unchanged around normalization and attention. Add it elementwise to the same-shaped attention output. This is a forward information path; it is not a repetition of the whole model or backpropagation.
steps.terms: The residual stream is the evolving token representation. A direct path contributes to gradients during training but does not guarantee unchanged meaning.
steps.next: Normalize this residual result before the feed-forward branch while preserving it for the next bypass.

steps.title: LayerNorm before the feed-forward branch
steps.prose: Normalize the first residual result independently at each token. The example uses the same gain/bias convention as its first norm, but a trained model can have distinct parameters for these two modules. The original embedding is not the input at this stage.
steps.terms: A feed-forward MLP transforms features within one position. Attention was the component that mixed different sequence positions.
steps.next: Expand the normalized feature vector into the intermediate MLP width.

steps.title: Feed-forward expansion
steps.prose: The first matrix map changes each token's four features into eight intermediate features. It shares its weights across token positions but not across different decoder blocks in this example. A larger intermediate width changes parameters and compute, not the context length.
steps.terms: MLP means multilayer perceptron. The intermediate width is a feature dimension, not another group of tokens or attention heads.
steps.next: Apply a nonlinear activation to these intermediate coordinates.

steps.title: GELU nonlinearity
steps.prose: Apply the displayed approximate GELU separately to each intermediate feature. Unlike ReLU it does not simply replace every negative value with zero. Without a nonlinearity, an unrestricted composition of linear maps would still be equivalent to one linear map.
steps.terms: GELU means Gaussian error linear unit. The example uses its stated tanh approximation; gated feed-forward variants are different computations.
steps.next: Project the activated intermediate vector back to hidden width.

steps.title: Feed-forward output projection
steps.prose: The second matrix maps eight activated coordinates back to four so they can be added to the residual stream. It changes feature values, not token positions. This simple branch omits biases and dropout and is not a gated Llama-style MLP.
steps.terms: The branch output must match the shortcut's shape. Feature expansion/contraction is neither generation nor a guarantee of information compression.
steps.next: Add this feed-forward correction to the preserved first residual result.

steps.title: Second residual addition
steps.prose: Carry the representation from before the feed-forward branch along its shortcut and add the branch output. Both paths have matching token and feature axes. The new representation is the selected block's output for the next block or final stage.
steps.terms: Both residual bypasses are forward connections. Full-model training differentiates through contributing operations, rather than treating attention weights as gradients.
steps.next: Continue through any later decoder blocks using their own parameters.

steps.title: Remaining decoder blocks
steps.prose: Run the configured stack in order. Each block consumes the preceding block's output and preserves the boundary shape while changing values. Inspecting an earlier block does not mean vocabulary scores are calculated from that block alone.
steps.terms: Depth counts successive parameterized transformations. Unlike a simple shared RNN recurrence, these example blocks use different matrices.
steps.next: Normalize the last block's features before mapping them to vocabulary scores.

steps.title: Final LayerNorm
steps.prose: Apply the final per-token normalization to the output of the full stack. This is separate from norms inside the inspected block. Placement is part of the declared pre-norm architecture; other Transformer recipes can differ.
steps.terms: Final hidden features have incorporated the allowed prefix through all configured blocks. Shape alone does not indicate how much useful information was learned.
steps.next: Project the final features into one raw score per vocabulary item.

steps.title: Vocabulary projection
steps.prose: Multiply each token's four final features by the separate four-by-six output matrix. Each position receives six candidate successor scores. This example keeps input and output matrices untied so its limited head-update demonstration has an unambiguous boundary.
steps.terms: A logit is an unnormalized score, not a percentage or measured accuracy. Vocabulary size controls the output score axis.
steps.next: Normalize vocabulary logits at each position to obtain next-token probabilities.

steps.title: Vocabulary softmax
steps.prose: Normalize across candidate token identities, independently for each position. This is a different axis and purpose from attention's normalization over keys. The highest score becomes the highest probability, but that probability is not verified factual confidence.
steps.terms: Vocabulary softmax predicts token identity; attention softmax mixes value information. These distributions are not interchangeable.
steps.next: At use time choose a next token; during training separately compare a known next-token target.

steps.title: Generation with fixed parameters
steps.prose: Use the final input position's distribution to choose and append a token, then predict again. The teaching button uses a bounded greedy step and recomputes earlier states. It does not train the weights or promise coherent language from fixed tiny matrices.
steps.terms: Autoregressive generation grows the input sequence. A compatible KV cache can avoid repeated projections; it is temporary inference state, not learned knowledge.
steps.next: The outer return is generation only. The training branch instead starts from a known target and a loss.

steps.title: Training loss for a known successor
steps.prose: The selected position is compared with its known next-token target, not a sampled guess treated as truth. The last position uses a supplied teaching target. The displayed loss scores one selected position rather than averaging all training positions.
steps.terms: Cross-entropy here is minus the natural log of the target probability, measured in nats. Teacher-forced training can score many permitted positions together.
steps.next: Differentiate this loss and apply an optimizer under the explicitly limited teaching update.
steps.node: Training loss for a known successor

steps.title: Head-only gradient and optimizer update
steps.prose: Freeze upstream features and calculate one exact SGD update of the output matrix at rate 0.1. This changes the illustrative head, not a saved checkpoint. Real full-model training also differentiates through embeddings and all contributing blocks.
steps.terms: The gradient measures local loss sensitivity. SGD applies it to parameters; the one-position example is not the lab's full-model AdamW training procedure.
steps.next: A real training loop takes another batch after updating; fixed-weight generation follows its separate return path.

T3.legend: The architecture shows forward feature flow and residual shortcuts. The outer return appends a generated token with fixed weights. The training branch compares a known target and illustrates only an output-head SGD update; it does not replay or modify a saved training run.

R1.title: Supervised fine-tuning and LoRA
R1.definition: Supervised fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model using demonstrations of desired outputs. Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, changes selected projections through small trainable matrix factors while keeping their base weights frozen. These choices concern the training signal and trainable parameters; they do not remove the base model or guarantee better behavior.
R1.example: A two-feature input [2,1] follows an identity base projection and a separate supplied LoRA correction. Change rank to inspect their addition and parameter count. The adapter values are fixed examples, not learned updates or a fair benchmark comparing trained ranks.
R1.connection: A trained base can be adapted rather than learned from scratch. First decide whether the failure needs changed weights, retrieved information or an external action; this lesson then explains the parameter boundary of one adaptation method.

steps.title: Send the same features to both branches
steps.prose: LoRA adds a correction beside an existing projection. Both paths read [2,1]; the input is not divided into unrelated examples. A task loss would eventually teach the adapter, but this view only computes its supplied forward values.
steps.terms: Frozen means no optimizer update to a parameter tensor. Gradient propagation through an operation is a separate question.
steps.next: Compute the frozen projection and the trainable correction as parallel branches.

steps.title: Compute the frozen base projection
steps.prose: The example uses an identity matrix, so its output remains [2,1]. Real base weights need not be identity. Keeping them frozen preserves those parameters, not necessarily the final model's behavior once a learned correction is added.
steps.terms: W_0 is the base matrix and x a row-vector input. The base still requires storage and computation when an adapter is used.
steps.next: Add this compatible base output to the independently computed adapter correction.

steps.title: Compute the low-rank correction
steps.prose: Multiply x by A, then by B, and apply alpha divided by rank. A maps two input features into rank r; B returns them to two output features. The supplied matrices change with the rank control, so score changes do not isolate a trained-rank effect.
steps.terms: In this row convention A is 2×r, B is r×2 and alpha is two. Real LoRA usually uses r much smaller than the affected matrix dimensions.
steps.next: Combine the scaled correction with the same-shaped base output.

steps.title: Add the two matching outputs
steps.prose: Add the base vector and correction elementwise. This produces adapted features for the next network operation. No optimizer has fitted the displayed adapter, and more rank is not evidence of better downstream quality from these supplied values.
steps.terms: Addition combines matching coordinates. It differs from concatenation, which would change output width and the next layer's input contract.
steps.next: Training and parameter-state savings are explained separately from this forward addition.

steps.title: Define what training updates and saves
steps.prose: A real fine-tuning objective differentiates into the declared trainable tensors. Save adapter configuration and its exact base/tokenizer contract. The tiny example has no useful low-rank compression ratio; large projections can have a much smaller adapter-state count.
steps.terms: Adapter parameter count is r(d_in+d_out) here. Parameter-state savings are not a claim that all activation, base or runtime memory disappears.
steps.next: The deeper notes cover initialization, response masks, QLoRA and selection before the preference-training lesson.

links: Apply the frozen base projection to the shared input.
Apply the low-rank adapter path to that same input.
Carry the base output unchanged into the elementwise addition.
Add the scaled adapter correction at matching output coordinates.

R2.title: Preference learning: DPO, PPO and GRPO
R2.definition: Preference and reward methods adapt which responses a language model favors. Direct preference optimization, or DPO, fits labelled response pairs relative to a reference model. Proximal policy optimization, or PPO, uses sampled behavior and an advantage-based surrogate. Group relative policy optimization, or GRPO, derives a comparison signal from responses sampled for the same prompt. Their signals and complete objectives differ.
R2.example: Choose a method. The DPO fixture calculates one pair loss; PPO illustrates a positive-advantage clipped surrogate; GRPO normalizes rewards [0,1,2]. These are separate teaching calculations, not three stages of a training run or complete trainers.
R2.connection: SFT imitates demonstrated answers. Preference training compares or scores alternatives and can still use backpropagation to change policy weights. Feedback quality, rollout/reference roles and independent evaluation matter as much as the objective name.

steps.title: Specify the preference pair and reference
steps.prose: For one prompt, label a chosen and a rejected completion. The supplied policy masses are 0.6 and 0.2; fixed-reference masses are 0.4 and 0.4. They are probabilities of those responses, not a two-class distribution that must sum to one within this pair.
steps.terms: The policy is the trainable response distribution. A reference anchors this objective; chosen/rejected describe feedback labels, not guaranteed factual correctness.
steps.next: Compare policy-relative log probabilities of the two completions.
steps.node: Specify the preference pair and reference

steps.title: Calculate the relative log-ratio margin
steps.prose: Subtract the rejected completion's policy-versus-reference log ratio from the chosen one's. Here the result is log three. Real sequence log probabilities normally sum over the declared completion tokens; changing length normalization changes the objective.
steps.terms: A log ratio compares policy and reference mass. This margin is not a learned reward score supplied by a separate model in standard offline DPO.
steps.next: Scale the margin by beta and calculate its logistic pair loss.

steps.title: Calculate the DPO pair loss
steps.prose: Multiply the margin by beta 0.1, then take negative log sigmoid. A larger relative preference margin lowers this loss. Beta is part of the stated objective, not a universal safety or quality control with the same meaning across implementations.
steps.terms: Sigmoid maps a scalar to a value between zero and one. Minimization fits the observed pair labels; it does not certify their quality.
steps.next: Differentiate through the trainable policy while keeping the reference fixed.

steps.title: Update and evaluate the policy
steps.prose: Standard offline DPO uses fixed preference pairs without requiring an online rollout loop or separate learned reward model. The fixture calculates no policy gradient. A real run still needs compatible token masks, a selection protocol and tests for reward/preference shortcuts.
steps.terms: Reference scores can be cached only under compatible data/tokenization/reference revisions. Successful preference fitting need not improve factuality or helpfulness.
steps.next: The deeper notes derive DPO and contrast its assumptions with sampled-policy methods and independent quality checks.

steps.title: Compute a new-to-rollout probability ratio
steps.prose: The supplied recorded action had probability 0.2 under the rollout policy and 0.3 under the current policy, so their ratio is 1.5. The denominator is the policy that sampled this action, not automatically the regularization reference.
steps.terms: A rollout is sampled behavior. The old sampling policy and fixed reference can serve different roles in a complete RLHF recipe.
steps.next: Combine this ratio with a separately estimated or supplied action advantage.

steps.title: Specify the advantage estimate
steps.prose: The example supplies positive advantage two rather than learning a value critic. An advantage compares return with a baseline, not reward alone. A real estimator must specify reward timing, value predictions and terminal handling.
steps.terms: G denotes return and V(s) a value estimate for state s. The external reward model and value critic are not interchangeable.
steps.next: Use the ratio and fixed advantage in PPO's clipped policy surrogate.

steps.title: Calculate the clipped surrogate to maximize
steps.prose: With clipping band [0.8,1.2], the two positive-advantage terms are three and 2.4, so their minimum is 2.4. This objective is maximized. For a negative advantage the same minimum formula has different incentives; it is not a universal ratio cap.
steps.terms: Epsilon sets the clipping band. A training implementation minimizing losses commonly negates this policy surrogate; it is not the DPO pair loss.
steps.next: Place this surrogate inside the full policy/value/reference training recipe rather than treating it as a complete optimizer.
steps.node: Calculate the clipped surrogate to maximize

steps.title: Complete and evaluate the PPO recipe
steps.prose: Real training includes sampling, advantages, optimizer steps and any declared value, entropy or reference penalties. This fixture calculates none of those model updates. Refresh rollout evidence under the specified policy rather than silently using arbitrarily stale trajectories.
steps.terms: A policy objective must declare token/sequence reduction and reference roles. Higher reward can coexist with worse independent task quality.
steps.next: The deeper notes explain policy gradients, reward learning and failure checks; other method choices use different signals.
steps.node: Complete and evaluate the PPO recipe

steps.title: Sample responses for one prompt
steps.prose: The three supplied rewards [0,1,2] belong to candidates for the same prompt. Grouping unrelated tasks would change the comparison. A real setup must specify the sampling policy, reward functions and number of responses per prompt.
steps.terms: G is group size, here three. A reward is feedback under a defined rule, not automatically verified usefulness or truth.
steps.next: Calculate the group's baseline and the stated reward-scale statistic.

steps.title: Calculate group mean and dispersion
steps.prose: The mean of [0,1,2] is one and population variance is two thirds. This fixture uses population standard deviation; another implementation may use a different estimator or normalization. Those choices change advantage magnitudes.
steps.terms: Mu is group mean and sigma its population standard deviation here. Variance uses division by G under this convention.
steps.next: Center each candidate reward and divide by the declared group scale.

steps.title: Form group-relative advantages
steps.prose: Subtract mean one from each reward and divide by the displayed standard deviation. This gives a negative, zero and positive signal relative to the group. Equal rewards provide no within-group ranking and need defined numerical handling.
steps.terms: A_i is the normalized advantage for candidate i. A stabilizing epsilon may be used, but cannot invent a quality distinction when all rewards match.
steps.next: Use advantages within a fully specified policy objective; they are not themselves gradients or an update.

steps.title: Specify the full GRPO policy objective
steps.prose: Group-relative advantages can feed a declared clipped/reference-regularized policy objective, but GRPO variants differ in reduction and other choices. The basic approach avoids a separate learned value critic; it still incurs group sampling and reward costs.
steps.terms: Reference penalties, rollout importance ratios and token weighting have distinct roles. This example implements only advantage arithmetic, not RL training.
steps.next: Independent evaluation must check reward shortcuts, unrelated behavior and compute alongside the chosen training signal.
steps.node: Specify the full GRPO policy objective

R3.title: Prompting, reasoning and output decoding
R3.definition: Prompting changes the input on which a model conditions; decoding changes how its token scores become outputs. Neither ordinarily updates learned weights. Intermediate reasoning, tool use and structured outputs add distinct procedures or constraints that must be evaluated for usefulness, source support and cost rather than assumed to make answers reliable.
R3.example: Keep logits [2,1,0] fixed while changing positive temperature. The resulting distribution becomes sharper or flatter, but the model's parameters do not change. A separate JSON example shows why valid structure does not establish a correct value.
R3.connection: Training changes the predictor; inference can instead change its input or selection procedure. This lesson separates those controls before retrieval and tool systems add external evidence, actions and permission boundaries.

steps.title: Construct the permitted prompt
steps.prose: Serialize instructions, examples, evidence and prior turns under the model's expected template. Retrieved or quoted text remains data, not an authority grant. Compare prompt conditions without silently changing several information and budget factors together.
steps.terms: Zero-shot and few-shot refer to task examples in the prompt. Conditioning on text differs from training parameter updates.
steps.next: Run the current model to produce token logits for the permitted input.

steps.title: Obtain next-token logits
steps.prose: The fixture supplies logits [2,1,0] to isolate decoding arithmetic rather than performing a real model forward pass. A trained model would produce such scores from its current prefix. A high score is not independently verified answer confidence.
steps.terms: A logit is an unnormalized candidate-token score. The next-token distribution and the truth of a whole proposition are different quantities.
steps.next: Transform the fixed scores with the selected temperature and vocabulary normalization.

steps.title: Apply temperature before softmax
steps.prose: Divide each logit by positive temperature and normalize. Lower temperature sharpens relative probabilities, while higher temperature flattens them. Greedy is a separate maximum-choice rule; it is not implemented by dividing these scores by zero.
steps.terms: Tau is positive temperature. Sampling draws from a distribution; top-k and nucleus filtering require their own selection and renormalization policies.
steps.next: A generated candidate must then be checked against its output contract and evidence, separately from the distribution calculation.

steps.title: Generate and validate a candidate
steps.prose: Selecting tokens produces a candidate, after which syntax, schema, source references and meaning require distinct checks. The illustrative JSON value can be structurally valid yet wrong. Constrained decoding cannot by itself establish a claim's truth or permission to act.
steps.terms: A schema describes fields and types. Referential validity checks actual source objects; semantic validity checks the intended meaning and support.
steps.next: The deeper notes compare reasoning budgets, structured records, abstention and focused failure diagnosis.

links: Condition the model on the permitted serialized prompt to obtain token scores.
Apply positive temperature and softmax to define the sampling distribution.

R4.title: Retrieval-augmented generation and vector indexes
R4.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, supplies external evidence to a model at use time. Ingestion builds a versioned, permission-aware source index; a query-time pipeline retrieves candidates, assembles context and generates an answer. Finding similar text and checking support are different tasks, and retrieval does not ordinarily update the generator's weights.
R4.example: Allowed passages A and B have supplied scores 0.8 and 0.3. Forbidden C scores 0.95 but must remain excluded. Select one or two eligible passages, then inspect a separate 100-token budget that reserves 20 for fixed input and 30 for output.
R4.connection: Prompting determines what context the model receives. RAG adds a source-selection system whose permissions, coverage and freshness must be evaluated separately from how the model uses the selected evidence.

steps.title: Build a versioned source index
steps.prose: Ingestion prepares approved documents as chunks and compatible vectors, carrying source identity, version and permissions. This is maintained separately from each query. A usable database needs operational controls beyond merely storing embedding arrays.
steps.terms: A chunk is a retrievable source unit. An index accelerates lookup; provenance and authoritative access checks establish other necessary contracts.
steps.next: At query time use identity and permissions to retrieve only eligible candidates.

steps.title: Retrieve only eligible passages
steps.prose: Filter the forbidden source before exposing its contents, despite its larger score. Keep the selected number of allowed candidates. Approximate nearest-vector recall, task relevance and permission filtering can each affect which evidence reaches the model.
steps.terms: Top-k ranks eligible candidates. Authorization is not established by similarity, and candidate recall is not final answer correctness.
steps.next: Fit selected permitted evidence into the actual model input budget.

steps.title: Assemble a bounded evidence prompt
steps.prose: The separate budget example leaves fifty tokens for evidence/history after fixed input and output reserve. Count the actual serialized input, deduplicate where appropriate and preserve important caveats. More retrieved text can remove useful evidence through truncation.
steps.terms: A context budget covers all required input components and any shared output allowance. Token units depend on the tokenizer and model contract.
steps.next: Generate an answer from the assembled permitted context and then inspect its support.

steps.title: Check source support and decide whether to answer
steps.prose: A model can ignore sufficient context, misread a negation or cite a real source that does not support its claim. Check claims and attached evidence; abstain or seek more permitted evidence when the task requires it. A valid citation ID alone is insufficient.
steps.terms: Source support is stronger than topical relevance. Answer correctness, faithfulness, completeness and answered coverage are distinct outcomes.
steps.next: The deeper notes trace index approximation, freshness, filtering and the evidence funnel before tool/action integration.

links: A maintained index supplies eligible records to each query-time retrieval.
Select and fit permitted candidate evidence into the token budget.
Generate from the available context, then assess source support.

R4.legend: Index ingestion is maintained separately. For each query, follow retrieval → context construction → answer/support checks. The scores and token counts are fixed examples; no external search or generator is run.

R5.title: Tool-using agents and MCP boundaries
R5.definition: A tool-using system turns a model's proposed action into a request that application code must validate, authorize and execute under limits. An agent can choose some next actions from observations; a workflow fixes more of the sequence. Model Context Protocol, or MCP, standardizes an integration boundary but does not supply planning, correctness or universal permission.
R5.example: The request is to add 2 and 3. A small typed contract accepts two numbers, while a separate allow/deny control determines whether the teaching calculation may run. Denial produces no result and leads directly to a denial report, not a fabricated successful dispatch.
R5.connection: Retrieval supplies information. Tools can also change state outside a model, so a proposed JSON call must be distinguished from authority, actual execution and a confirmed outcome. These boundaries matter even when the model sounds confident.

steps.title: Propose an action for the user's task
steps.prose: The model proposes an add operation with arguments two and three. This is intent expressed as structured data, not execution. A host application must decide what tool exists and whether this request is within the user's task.
steps.terms: A workflow has designed steps; an agent selects some actions within a policy. A model-generated instruction cannot grant itself new permissions.
steps.next: Validate the proposed tool arguments before considering dispatch.

steps.title: Validate the typed contract
steps.prose: Require the expected numeric fields and reject unsupported or malformed arguments. The two supplied numbers satisfy this example's schema. Syntactically valid JSON could still contain wrong types, nonexistent resources or semantically invalid values.
steps.terms: Validation checks the request contract. It is separate from authentication of the caller and authorization of an action.
steps.next: Check whether this caller may perform this exact action on the specified resource.

steps.title: Authorize before execution
steps.prose: Apply the selected allow or deny decision outside the model. A valid request can still be forbidden. Approval for a consequential operation must be bound to its exact arguments; changing the destination or action can require a new decision.
steps.terms: Authorization defines permitted effects. Human confirmation may be an additional policy requirement, not something inferred from a model's claim.
steps.next: If allowed, dispatch under limits; if denied, skip execution and report the denial.

steps.title: Execute only an allowed request
steps.prose: An allowed request returns the local illustrative sum five. Under denial there is no execution result. This is an in-memory teaching calculation, not a real external API/MCP invocation or evidence that a remote write succeeded.
steps.terms: Dispatch means invoking an approved implementation. A timeout after a real side effect can leave an unknown outcome rather than proving nothing happened.

steps.terms: An audit trail records what happened under retention/access rules. MCP carries contracts and results but does not replace these enforcement responsibilities.

steps.prose: Apply the selected allow or deny decision outside the model. A valid request can still be forbidden. Approval for a consequential operation must be bound to its exact arguments; changing the destination or action can require a new decision.
steps.terms: Authorization defines permitted effects. Human confirmation may be an additional policy requirement, not something inferred from a model's claim.
