R6.title: LLM inference, KV caching and serving
R6.definition: Inference uses a model's parameters to calculate outputs, while serving adds request admission, scheduling, state management and delivery. Prefill processes the known prompt; autoregressive decoding processes successive chosen tokens. A key/value cache can reuse earlier attention projections, but its memory, compatibility and privacy constraints remain separate from model-weight storage.
R6.example: The fixed cache example has two layers, four query heads, two KV heads, head width four and two-byte values. Change cached length to calculate value bytes. A separate hypothetical timing example uses first-token time 100 ms and nine later 20 ms intervals, not measured hardware performance.
R6.connection: The Transformer explained autoregressive generation with fixed parameters. Serving turns that computation into a resource-bounded service; cache accounting, throughput and user-visible latency should not be confused with the forward layers themselves.

steps.title: Admit and schedule a request
steps.prose: Check input/output limits, identity and available capacity before starting work. Requests may queue, and batching can improve throughput while adding waiting. The supplied timing example is not a latency measurement from this machine.
steps.terms: Latency measures elapsed time for a request; throughput measures completed work per time across requests. Their measurement boundaries must be declared.
steps.next: Process the admitted prompt and establish its compatible inference state.

steps.title: Prefill the prompt and build cache state
steps.prose: The known prompt can be processed across its positions under the architecture's visibility rules. Cache its keys and values for reuse. This example's grouped-query attention has four query heads sharing two KV heads, so cache counting uses two.
steps.terms: Prefill handles known prompt tokens. KV means keys and values; query-head count can differ from the number of stored key/value heads.
steps.next: Use the state for later decode steps; separately calculate its value-storage requirement.

steps.title: Calculate KV value storage as a side estimate
steps.prose: Multiply the number of K/V tensors, examples, layers, cached positions, KV heads, features per head and bytes per value. The factor two counts keys and values. Allocation metadata, padding, workspaces and other runtime storage are excluded.
steps.terms: B=1, L=2, H_kv=2, d_h=4 and b=2 bytes in this fixture. T is cached length, not the number of independent requests.
steps.next: The separate decode operation increases cached length; this estimate is not a forward layer between prefill and decoding.

steps.title: Decode successive tokens with fixed weights
steps.prose: After a token is chosen, process it with compatible cached history, append its new keys/values and predict a successor. Stop under the declared EOS or output limit. The cache grows but the model's parameters are not updated.
steps.terms: Autoregressive decoding depends on previous choices. Caching avoids some repeated projection work; it does not make all attention to history free.
steps.next: Measure the complete response separately from this repeated model computation.

steps.title: Measure latency and throughput under load
steps.prose: For the separate timing fixture, ten output tokens use one first-token interval plus nine later gaps, giving 280 ms. Real workloads vary with prompt/output lengths, queueing, concurrency and checks after generation. Include failed and timed-out requests in reporting.
steps.terms: TTFT is time to first token; ITL is inter-token latency. Tail latency and average throughput answer different service-quality questions.
steps.next: The deeper notes compare batching, prefix reuse, speculation and capacity before compression trade-offs.

links: Schedule an eligible request for prompt processing.
Use compatible prefill state while processing successive chosen tokens.
Separately account for key/value storage from the declared cache dimensions.

R6.legend: The left path is admitted request → prefill → repeated decoding. The right branch only accounts for KV value bytes; it is not a compulsory layer before decoding. The cache/latency figures are declared examples, not benchmark results.

R7.title: LLM quantization, compression and deployment
R7.definition: Compression changes a model or its representation to reduce selected storage or execution costs. Quantization approximates numerical values using a declared code range and scale; pruning and distillation use different mechanisms. Smaller values or files do not automatically produce a faster, fitting or equally capable deployed model.
R7.example: The weights [−1.2,0.4,0.8] are mapped to the full signed four-bit range [−8,7] with zero point zero. Change scale to inspect rounding, clipping and reconstruction error. The browser's ordinary arrays are not packed four-bit storage or a low-bit inference kernel.
R7.connection: Serving separated weights, cache and runtime memory. This lesson approximates stored numerical values while keeping value error, actual memory savings, hardware support and task quality as separate outcomes.

steps.title: Specify the quantization convention
steps.prose: Declare the real values, integer range, scale, rounding rule and zero point. Here the full signed range is minus eight through seven; the source also labels a distinct symmetric minus-seven-through-seven illustration. Neither convention should be assumed from bit width alone.
steps.terms: Scale s is a positive real step size and q an integer code. Zero point zero makes reconstruction s times q in this fixture.
steps.next: Divide values by scale, round under the stated rule and clip to the allowed code range.

steps.title: Round and clip to integer codes
steps.prose: Each original value divided by scale selects a rounded code, then values outside the allowed range are clamped. Small scale can improve local resolution but clip large magnitudes; large scale can preserve range while losing finer distinctions.
steps.terms: Clipping bounds the code. The fixture follows JavaScript rounding; real quantizers can use other tie, grouping or codebook conventions.
steps.next: Reconstruct approximate real values from the codes and saved scale.

steps.title: Reconstruct values and calculate numerical error
steps.prose: Multiply each code by scale and compare the result with the original weights. Mean squared error averages squared differences across these three values. Small parameter reconstruction error does not guarantee unchanged generated answers or rare-task behavior.
steps.terms: Dequantization reconstructs approximate values. Weight error, downstream loss, task quality and safety are different evaluation quantities.
steps.next: Assess storage and runtime separately rather than treating this arithmetic as a speed benchmark.

steps.title: Verify actual savings and task quality
steps.prose: One million ideally packed four-bit values require half a decimal megabyte before scales, metadata and other tensors. This is a separate accounting example. Real speed needs compatible kernels and measured workloads, including workspace, cache and output quality.
steps.terms: A low-bit value format differs from its execution precision. PTQ quantizes after training; QAT trains with quantization effects under a defined recipe.
steps.next: The deeper notes cover groupwise metadata, distillation, pruning, runtime packaging and local/cloud trade-offs.

links: Apply the declared scale, rounding and finite integer range.
Use saved scale to reconstruct and compare approximate values.

R8.title: LLM system evaluation, security and operations
R8.definition: A deployed LLM system must satisfy task-quality, access, reliability and resource requirements across its components, not just produce fluent model outputs. Release evaluation, authorization, budget enforcement, monitoring and recovery address different failure paths. They are coordinated controls rather than one model-forward chain or a certificate of complete safety.
R8.example: The budget control illustrates how many whole 0.2-unit operations fit when spending starts at zero. It is not a current API price. Other sections discuss permission checks and staged releases as separate operational decisions, with no traffic or external effects executed.
R8.connection: Generation, retrieval and tools introduced different sources of failure. This lesson joins their evaluation and operating boundaries while preserving independent enforcement outside the model and honest reporting of incomplete tasks.

steps.title: Define task success and critical failure cases
steps.prose: A useful answer with an unauthorized side effect is still a failed system task. Test representative success, missing evidence, invalid tool inputs and refusal cases. Model-only benchmarks and judge approval cannot establish the surrounding product's requirements.
steps.terms: A release suite is a versioned set of acceptance cases. A judge model is a fallible measurement component, not an independent security authority.
steps.next: Enforce trust and permission boundaries regardless of whether a model passes ordinary task tests.
steps.node: Define task success and critical failure cases

steps.title: Enforce authority outside the model
steps.prose: Retrieved content and tool output may contain hostile instructions. Keep them as data, use least privilege and enforce resource permissions in the application/service boundary. A warning prompt or text filter alone is not a dependable sandbox.
steps.terms: A trust boundary separates authority levels. Prompt injection attempts to turn untrusted content into controlling instructions or effects.
steps.next: Budget enforcement is another pre-action gate, not a replacement for permission or correctness checks.

steps.title: Check projected cost before another action
steps.prose: The illustrative operation costs 0.2 units and starts with zero spent, so only a whole number of operations may fit the selected budget. Stop before exceeding the bound. Never fabricate success or silently omit a required check to remain within budget.
steps.terms: The inequality includes already spent and proposed next cost. Token, tool, time and monetary budgets require declared accounting units.
steps.next: Monitor actual permitted behavior under controlled rollout after the system meets its release criteria.
steps.node: Check projected cost before another action

steps.title: Observe a limited rollout
steps.prose: A candidate that passes an offline suite can still fail under real traffic. Record useful outcome, latency, errors and costs with appropriate privacy limits. Shadow experiments must not duplicate real write actions, and only successful requests are a biased sample.
steps.terms: A canary exposes a limited new version. Traces connect operations; metrics aggregate behavior; logs still need access and retention controls.
steps.next: Use defined stopping and recovery rules when monitoring or release tests reveal a failure.

steps.title: Stop, recover and retest deliberately
steps.prose: Preserve confirmed state and failure evidence, contain the affected operation and restore a suitable approved version if needed. A repair requires regression tests, including legitimate use that should still work. A budget stop remains an honestly incomplete result.
steps.terms: Rollback is a controlled version restoration. Retries, status checks and incident response must respect whether external effects already occurred.
steps.next: The final lesson classifies further research interventions and the independent evidence needed to support their claims.

R9.title: LLM research methods and activation steering
R9.definition: Research methods can change data, parameters, activations, decoding or system operations, and those interventions support different claims. Activation steering changes selected runtime representations while keeping model weights fixed. A local output change demonstrates sensitivity under that intervention, not that a named concept has been isolated or reliable behavior achieved everywhere.
R9.example: The supplied hidden row vector [0.2,−0.1] is scored by a fixed projection [1,−1]. Adding alpha times direction [1,0] changes its score from 0.3 to 0.3+alpha. These authored values do not identify a real truth, safety or reasoning direction.
R9.connection: Evaluation and operations require evidence beyond plausible mechanism names. This final lesson uses one exact steering example and keeps editing, unlearning, merging, continual learning and privacy as distinct deeper branches.

steps.title: Specify the intervention location
steps.prose: Start with the supplied hidden vector and unchanged output projection. State which layer, token position and representation would be modified in a real experiment. Changing activations at use time is not the same intervention as adapting model parameters.
steps.terms: An activation is a computed representation. A steering direction lives in its feature space; a learned weight belongs to the model's parameter state.
steps.next: Apply the declared direction with a separately chosen strength.

steps.title: Add the direction with explicit strength
steps.prose: Add alpha times [1,0] to the hidden vector, changing its first coordinate while leaving the second fixed. The direction is supplied, not discovered from a trained model. Larger strength produces a larger perturbation but not necessarily a more useful one.
steps.terms: Alpha controls perturbation size. A direction's human-readable name would remain a hypothesis requiring independent tests.
steps.next: Pass the changed representation through the unchanged output projection.

steps.title: Calculate the conditional output effect
steps.prose: Use the fixed linear projection to calculate the new scalar score and compare it with 0.3. This exact arithmetic shows sensitivity for this example. It is not evidence that real LLM behavior or truthfulness changes linearly with steering strength.
steps.terms: The hidden vector is a row here; multiplying by the projection's column gives one scalar. A logit-like score is not a probability or task success rate.
steps.next: Evaluate unrelated behavior and transfer separately from this local calculation.

steps.title: Test specificity, side effects and transfer
steps.prose: A real intervention needs target prompts, unrelated capability tests and controls such as opposite or norm-matched random directions. Select settings using development evidence. Broad disruption can look like targeted control on a small hand-picked case.
steps.terms: Editing changes selected model behavior through another mechanism; unlearning has a distinct removal definition. Probe decodability and causal use are also different evidence levels.
steps.next: The deeper branches give prerequisites and falsifiable comparisons rather than promising mastery from a method catalogue.
steps.node: Test specificity, side effects and transfer

links: Apply a runtime activation perturbation at the declared feature location.
Use the unchanged linear projection to measure the example's conditional effect.

P2.title: Vectors, matrices and gradients
P2.definition: Models work with numbers arranged in lists and tables. A vector is an ordered list of features, such as a flower's length and width. A matrix holds several such lists or the weights that combine them. Calculus tells us how changing one weight would change a prediction or its error.
P2.example: Use two input features, [2, 1], to predict the number 4. We will calculate one prediction, measure its error and work backwards to find the effect of its first weight.
P2.connection: This introduces the arithmetic used by linear regression and neural networks. The gradient calculated here becomes an input to an optimizer in the next training lesson.

steps.title: Input and weight dimensions
steps.prose: Before multiplying, decide what each axis means. Here there is one example with two features. Each feature needs a matching weight; multiplying a two-feature row by a two-weight column produces one number.
steps.terms: Shape means the size of each axis. [1,2] means one row and two columns; a scalar is a single number.
steps.next: The two features and their matching weights are the inputs to the weighted sum.

steps.title: Weighted sum: the prediction
steps.prose: A weight controls how much one feature contributes. Multiply each feature by its weight, then add the contributions. In this example we omit a separate constant term, called the bias.
steps.terms: A dot product is this multiply-and-add operation. The first weight is adjustable; the second stays −1.
steps.next: The predicted number is compared with the known target 4.

steps.title: Squared prediction error
steps.prose: Subtract the target from the prediction to get a signed error. Squaring makes both positive and negative errors costly and gives larger misses more weight. This gives us a quantity that training can try to reduce.
steps.terms: Residual means prediction minus target. Loss is the numerical penalty used for training.
steps.next: The chain rule tells us how changing a weight affects this loss.

steps.title: Gradient: how the weight affects error
steps.prose: The first weight changes the prediction, and the prediction changes the loss. Multiply these two local rates of change to obtain the loss gradient for that weight. A negative gradient means a small increase in the weight would reduce loss at this point.
steps.terms: The chain rule combines derivatives along connected operations. A partial derivative varies one input while holding the others fixed.
steps.next: The loss and optimization lesson shows how an optimizer uses the gradient to choose an actual weight update.

links: Features and weights are multiplied to produce the prediction.
The prediction is compared with the known target to calculate loss.
Differentiate the loss through the prediction to the first weight.

P3.title: Probability, uncertainty and statistics
P3.definition: Probability describes how likely different outcomes are. Statistics uses a finite set of observations to estimate quantities such as a model's accuracy. These are related but different: a model's confidence in one prediction is not the same as our uncertainty about an accuracy measured on a small test set.
P3.example: Imagine a model assigns probability 0.8 to class 1 and 0.2 to class 0. We can ask whether it predicted an observed label well, how uncertain its distribution is, and how a sample-based statistic varies.
P3.connection: First distinguish probability, prediction loss and entropy. Then study resampling and confidence intervals as a separate question about the evidence in a dataset.

steps.title: A probability distribution
steps.prose: For two classes, the probabilities describe mutually exclusive possibilities and must add to one. Assigning 0.8 to class 1 leaves 0.2 for class 0. This does not mean the model must be right on this particular example.
steps.terms: A distribution lists outcomes and their probabilities. Conditional probability is a probability given stated information.
steps.next: With a known observed label, we can measure how much probability the model gave that label.

steps.title: Loss for the observed label
steps.prose: Suppose the correct class is 1. Negative log-likelihood penalizes the model for giving that class too little probability: −log(0.8) is smaller than −log(0.2). Only the probability of the label that actually occurred enters this calculation.
steps.terms: Likelihood evaluates observed data under a model. Nats are the units obtained when using natural logarithms.
steps.next: Entropy asks a different question: how spread out is the whole predicted distribution?

steps.title: Entropy of the predicted distribution
steps.prose: Entropy is largest when the two outcomes are equally likely and smaller when one dominates. Unlike the previous loss, it does not need a known correct label. A confidently wrong model can therefore have low entropy but high observed-label loss.
steps.terms: Entropy averages −log(probability) across possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities.
steps.next: The next example changes subject from one prediction to variability in a statistic estimated from observed data.

steps.title: Bootstrap: repeat a sample calculation
steps.prose: A bootstrap resample draws from the observed rows with replacement, so a row may appear more than once. Recompute the statistic on each resample. Many such repetitions approximate how sensitive the estimate is to which observed cases are included; these two tiny examples illustrate the operation, not a reliable interval.
steps.terms: A statistic is a number calculated from a sample. Sampling variability is the change caused by observing different cases.
steps.next: The confidence-interval note explains how repeated resampled scores become an interval and which uncertainty it does not include.

P4.title: Training, validation and generalization
P4.definition: A model learns from training examples, but we want it to work on new examples. That is generalization. To check it honestly, separate data used to learn weights, data used to choose settings, and data reserved for the final evaluation.
P4.example: With 100 labelled cases, we keep 10 for testing. The control changes how many of the other 90 are used for fitting and how many remain for development, also called validation.
P4.connection: This is a study plan, not a model architecture. The complete-experiment lesson later applies these boundaries to a complete experiment with saved settings, predictions and results.

steps.title: Define the task and split
steps.prose: Specify what one example is, which inputs will be available, and what the correct answer means. Then divide data into training, validation and test sets. Keep related observations together when they come from the same person, document or other shared source.
steps.terms: A label policy defines the target class. A split is an assignment of examples or independent groups to data partitions.
steps.next: Only the training partition may supply information used to fit the initial candidate models.

steps.title: Fit candidate models on training data
steps.prose: Fitting means estimating a model's learned values from examples. Preprocessing can learn values too: a feature mean or vocabulary is part of the fitted pipeline. Neither the validation nor test cases should contribute to these fitted values.
steps.terms: Parameters are learned values. A pipeline combines preprocessing with the prediction model.
steps.next: Use validation results to choose among the fitted candidates; do not choose using test results.
steps.node: Fit candidate models on training data

steps.title: Choose settings on validation data
steps.prose: Try candidate settings or checkpoints and compare their validation scores under the same metric. This is still part of developing the system. Once a candidate is chosen, fix the procedure before looking at its final test result.
steps.terms: A hyperparameter is a setting you choose, such as tree depth. Model selection means choosing a candidate using validation evidence.
steps.next: The selected system is now ready for evaluation on the reserved test cases.

steps.title: Evaluate on the reserved test set
steps.prose: The test score measures the selected system on this particular held-out sample. It does not guarantee the same score on a new hospital, language or label definition. If you use the result to revise the system, those cases are now influencing development rather than serving as an untouched final check.
steps.terms: Held out means excluded from the specified fitting or selection step. Distribution shift means the new data differs from the development setting.
steps.next: The deeper notes distinguish a change in writing style from a change in what the correct label means.
steps.node: Evaluate on the reserved test set

P5.title: How models learn: loss and optimization
P5.definition: Training adjusts a model's learned numbers so its predictions better match examples. The usual loop is: calculate a prediction, measure its error with a loss function, compute how each weight affects the loss, and use an optimizer to update the weights. A neural network repeats this idea across many connected layers.
P5.example: Our smallest model predicts y = w × x. The input is 2, the target is 4 and only one weight can change. One explicit update lets you see what happens without hiding it inside a training library.
P5.connection: The vectors and gradients lesson explains the derivative behind the gradient. This lesson uses it to update a model; DL later adds nonlinear layers and many weights without changing the basic loop.

steps.title: Forward pass: calculate a prediction
steps.prose: The current weight converts input 2 into a prediction. The target 4 is not an input to this prediction; it is kept for checking the result. Running a prediction alone does not teach the model anything.
steps.terms: The forward pass computes outputs from current weights. A parameter is a value training is allowed to learn.
steps.next: Compare this prediction with the target to obtain a loss.

steps.title: Loss: measure the error
steps.prose: The prediction can be too large or too small. Squared error measures the size of that miss without letting signs cancel. We choose this loss for the example; classification commonly uses a different loss.
steps.terms: A loss function assigns a numerical cost to a prediction and target. Here the residual is prediction minus 4.
steps.next: Differentiate this loss to find how changing the weight would affect it.

steps.title: Backward pass: calculate the gradient
steps.prose: Backpropagation applies the chain rule through the operations used in the forward pass. Here it gives one derivative. With a neural network, the same principle supplies a gradient for each trainable parameter.
steps.terms: Autograd is a library mechanism for computing derivatives from recorded operations. Backpropagation computes gradients; it does not itself change weights.
steps.next: The optimizer receives the gradient and decides the size and direction of the update.

steps.title: Optimizer step: update the weight
steps.prose: Plain stochastic gradient descent, or SGD, subtracts learning rate times gradient. The learning rate controls the attempted step size. After the update, a new forward pass uses the changed weight; more complicated optimizers also keep history from previous steps.
steps.terms: The optimizer is the update rule. The learning rate here is fixed at 0.1; the example uses one observation.
steps.next: Repeat prediction and error calculation with the updated weight. Stop or change the procedure using a separate validation rule, not this diagram's loop alone.

The backward pass differentiates the loss with respect to the weight.
SGD uses this gradient to calculate a new weight.

ML01.title: Machine learning tasks and baselines
ML01.definition: Machine learning fits a rule from examples rather than writing every decision by hand. In supervised learning, each training example has input features and a target: classification predicts a category, while regression predicts a number. Unsupervised learning instead looks for patterns without these target labels.
ML01.example: Suppose 20 of 100 cases are positive and 80 are negative. A system that always answers 'negative' gets 80% accuracy while finding none of the positive cases. This simple baseline exposes what a score can hide.
ML01.connection: Before choosing a model, decide what must be predicted and what mistakes matter. The next lesson prepares the inputs; later lessons compare methods against a baseline on the same task.

steps.title: Inputs, targets and examples
steps.prose: Start with one concrete prediction. For spam detection, one email is an example, its text supplies input features and spam/not-spam is the target. Inputs must be available when the prediction will actually be made, not created from the answer afterwards.
steps.terms: A feature is an input measurement or representation. A target is the answer the model is trained to predict.
steps.next: Count the target classes so a simple reference system has a clear interpretation.

steps.title: A majority-class baseline
steps.prose: A baseline is a simple reference, not a deliberately bad competitor. For classification, predicting the most common training class is often a useful first reference. For numerical regression, predicting a training mean or median provides a different simple baseline.
steps.terms: A majority class is the most frequent class in training data. A constant predictor gives the same answer regardless of input features.
steps.next: Check both overall correctness and whether this baseline detects the class you care about.

steps.title: Why high accuracy can be misleading
steps.prose: When negative cases dominate, an always-negative rule gets most cases right without performing positive detection. That does not make accuracy incorrect; it makes accuracy insufficient for this use. The shared metrics lesson shows the denominators behind recall and other scores.
steps.terms: Class imbalance means some target classes are much more common than others. Positive recall measures how many actual positives were found.
steps.next: A learned model should be compared against this baseline using the same split and useful metrics.
steps.node: Why high accuracy can be misleading

steps.title: Compare models on the same problem
steps.prose: A complex model earns its extra cost only if it improves something relevant: detection, numerical error, reliability or resource use. Keep the dataset, target definition and evaluation protocol clear so a change in task is not mistaken for a model improvement.
steps.terms: A controlled comparison states which factors change and which remain the same.
steps.next: The features and preprocessing lesson explains how to turn raw inputs into features without leaking information from evaluation cases.
steps.node: Compare models on the same problem

ML02.title: Features and preprocessing
ML02.definition: Most models need inputs in a consistent numerical form. Preprocessing handles missing values, represents categories and puts numerical measurements on suitable scales. Some transformations learn statistics from data, so they must be fitted on training data and reused unchanged on new cases.
ML02.example: Training values [1, 3] have mean 2 and population standard deviation 1. A new value 4 becomes (4 − 2) / 1 = 2. It is two training standard deviations above the training mean.
ML02.connection: This example focuses on standardization. The additional notes explain missing-value handling, categories and complete pipelines; distance-based and regularized methods are especially sensitive to feature units.

steps.title: Learn the training mean
steps.prose: Compute the mean from training cases only. The new query must not help determine the transformation used to evaluate it. In cross-validation, each fold needs its own training-only mean, not one mean computed before the folds were separated.
steps.terms: Fit learns transformation values. Transform applies previously fitted values to inputs.
steps.next: The same training rows also determine the standard deviation used for scaling.

steps.title: Learn the training scale
steps.prose: Standard deviation measures how far the training values typically lie from their mean. Dividing by it changes the units so a difference of one standard deviation has the same numerical size across features.
steps.terms: This calculation uses population standard deviation, dividing by n, as StandardScaler does. A constant feature needs a zero-scale convention.
steps.next: Save this scale with the mean; both are reused for new examples.

steps.title: Transform a new value
steps.prose: Subtract the saved training mean, then divide by the saved training scale. Do not recompute either statistic using the query. Changing the query changes its standardized value but not the fitted transformation.
steps.terms: A standardized value measures distance from the training mean in training-standard-deviation units.
steps.next: The transform and model need to be fitted and applied together as a pipeline.

steps.title: Keep preprocessing inside each fit
steps.prose: During validation, fit preprocessing on the fold's training rows, fit the model on their transformed values, then transform the held-out rows with those saved statistics. A pipeline helps enforce this order and preserves the same procedure for later use.
steps.terms: Data leakage is information entering fitting or selection that would not legitimately be available at that stage.
steps.next: The linear regression lesson uses numerical features in a fitted linear regression model.

ML03.title: Linear regression
ML03.definition: Linear regression predicts a number by adding weighted feature contributions and, usually, a constant intercept. Fitting chooses weights that reduce prediction errors on training examples. Ridge regression adds a cost for large weights, which can make the fit less sensitive to limited or correlated data.
ML03.example: Here one feature predicts three targets: x = [1, 2, 3], y = [1, 2, 2]. To keep the solution visible we omit the intercept. Changing the ridge penalty changes the fitted coefficient, predictions and training error.
ML03.connection: The diagram shows the small closed-form calculation, not the only way to fit regression. The loss and optimization lesson explains gradient-based fitting; the regularization lesson explains how validation chooses penalty strength.

steps.title: Training values and sums
steps.prose: With one coefficient and no intercept, every prediction is x × w. The least-squares solution can be calculated from two sums: squared inputs and input–target products. With many features these become matrix operations rather than scalar sums.
steps.terms: The design matrix X stacks input rows. Transpose, written T, swaps its axes; XᵀX and Xᵀy collect the needed products.
steps.next: Use the two training sums to solve for the fitted coefficient.

steps.title: Fit the regression coefficient
steps.prose: Choose the coefficient that minimizes summed squared error plus lambda times its square. A larger lambda shrinks this coefficient towards zero in this example. Setting lambda to zero gives ordinary least squares.
steps.terms: Ridge is linear regression with an L2 penalty. Lambda is the chosen penalty strength, not a learned feature weight.
steps.next: Use the resulting coefficient to calculate predictions; this does not fit it again.

steps.title: Predictions and training error
steps.prose: Multiply each input by the fitted coefficient, then compare these predictions with the targets used to fit it. A larger penalty can make these training errors worse while potentially helping performance on new cases. The training numbers alone cannot tell us whether it helped generalization.
steps.terms: A prediction uses a fitted model. Squared training error is not a held-out evaluation score.
steps.next: The final section explains how to judge this fitted model on separate cases.

steps.title: Evaluate on new cases
steps.prose: After selecting the fitting procedure using validation data, measure its error on held-out cases in the target's units. Compare against a simple numerical baseline and inspect where errors occur. This section is an evaluation step, not another input to the closed-form coefficient.
steps.terms: MAE and RMSE measure numerical error in different ways; their definitions are in Evaluation metrics.
steps.next: Compare this regression objective with classification in the logistic regression lesson and regularization choices in the regularization lesson.

links: The training sums and selected penalty determine the fitted coefficient.
The fitted coefficient multiplies each input to produce a prediction.

ML04.title: Logistic regression and classification
ML04.definition: Classification predicts a category rather than a numerical measurement. Binary logistic regression first calculates a weighted score, then maps it to a probability for one of two classes. A separate decision threshold turns that probability into a yes/no prediction.
ML04.example: Features [1, 2] and weights [0.2, 0.1] give score 0.4 and positive-class probability about 0.60. A threshold of 0.5 predicts positive; a threshold of 0.7 predicts negative, without changing the model.
ML04.connection: Linear regression in the linear regression lesson predicts a number directly. Logistic regression adds a probability mapping and a classification loss. The threshold controls the action, while the loss can be used to fit the probabilities.

steps.title: Calculate the raw score
steps.prose: Multiply each feature by its learned weight, add the contributions and include a bias if the model has one. The raw score can be any real number; it is not yet a probability.
steps.terms: A logit is a raw score before the logistic probability mapping. The bias is a learned constant added to the weighted sum.
steps.next: Sigmoid converts this score into a binary-class probability.

steps.title: Convert score to probability
steps.prose: The sigmoid function maps the score to a value between zero and one. A score of zero maps to 0.5; larger positive scores favour the positive class. This estimated probability is useful, but it still needs checking for calibration.
steps.terms: Sigmoid is the function 1/(1 + exp(−z)). Its input z is the score, not a class label.
steps.next: This probability has two uses: make a thresholded decision, or score it against a known label during training.

steps.title: Choose a class using a threshold
steps.prose: Predict positive if the estimated probability is at least the chosen cutoff. Moving the cutoff changes which examples are called positive, not the fitted weights or their probabilities. Different error costs can justify different cutoffs.
steps.terms: The threshold is a decision setting chosen on validation data, not a learned weight.
steps.next: The loss section uses the probability directly; it is not calculated from this thresholded label.

steps.title: Training loss for a known label
steps.prose: Binary cross-entropy measures how much probability the model assigned to the observed answer. For a positive label it is −log(p); for a negative label it is −log(1−p). Changing only the decision threshold therefore leaves this loss unchanged.
steps.terms: Cross-entropy is a probabilistic training loss. Softmax extends the probability mapping to mutually exclusive classes, as explained in the deeper notes.
steps.next: The loss and optimization lesson shows gradient updates; Evaluation metrics compares the decisions after fitting.

links: Sigmoid converts the raw score into a positive-class probability.
Compare the probability with a chosen threshold to make a class decision.
Compare the probability directly with the known label to calculate cross-entropy.

ML05.title: Regularization and model selection
ML05.definition: A model can fit its training examples closely but perform poorly on new data. Regularization discourages some kinds of overly flexible fit, for example by penalizing large coefficients. Model selection uses validation data to choose how much regularization or complexity to allow.
ML05.example: The example holds one candidate weight at 3 and its data loss at 0.4. Changing lambda shows how the L2 penalty contributes to the objective. It does not refit the candidate, so it is not evidence that one lambda trains a better model.
ML05.connection: The linear regression lesson showed a coefficient actually changing when ridge strength changes. Here we separate the data-loss term, penalty term and validation choice so they are not confused.

steps.title: Error on training examples
steps.prose: The data-loss term measures how well a candidate predicts the training answers. A very flexible model may reduce this term by capturing noise or accidental patterns, not only reusable relationships.
steps.terms: Overfitting means training performance is better than the model's performance on relevant unseen examples.
steps.next: Regularization adds a separate cost for selected properties of the fitted model.

steps.title: Cost for large coefficients
steps.prose: An L2 penalty adds lambda times the sum of squared coefficients. This makes large weights more expensive in the fitting objective. The control changes that cost while holding this demonstration's candidate weight fixed.
steps.terms: L2 means squared coefficient magnitude. L1 instead uses absolute magnitude and can produce exact zero coefficients.
steps.next: Add the penalty to the data loss to obtain the objective that fitting would minimize.

steps.title: The combined fitting objective
steps.prose: Training balances two costs: prediction error and coefficient magnitude. With a different penalty, a real fit usually chooses different coefficients. Comparing objective values across different lambdas is not itself a validation-based model comparison.
steps.terms: An objective is the quantity an optimizer minimizes; it is not necessarily the metric used to judge the final system.
steps.next: To choose lambda, actually fit candidates and compare their validation performance.

steps.title: Choose complexity using validation
steps.prose: Cross-validation repeatedly fits a full pipeline on part of the development data and scores it on the held-out part. Average these results to choose a setting, then follow the declared refitting and final-test procedure.
steps.terms: A fold is one partition in cross-validation. Regularization, tree depth and early stopping are different ways to control complexity.
steps.next: Subsequent method lessons use validation to choose their own settings; no single setting is best for every dataset.

ML06.title: Nearest neighbours, kernels and SVMs
ML06.definition: Nearest-neighbour prediction compares a new example with stored training examples and uses the answers of the closest ones. It is a local rule: the prediction depends on nearby cases rather than one fitted line. A support vector machine, or SVM, is a different method that learns a separating boundary with a margin.
ML06.example: For nearest neighbours we classify query x = 3 using labelled points at 0, 1, 2, 4 and 5. The control changes how many neighbours vote. A separate final section explains how a kernel-based SVM differs; it is not a later stage of nearest-neighbour prediction.
ML06.connection: Feature scaling from the features and preprocessing lesson affects distances. This lesson compares two uses of similarity while keeping their prediction mechanisms distinct.

steps.title: Measure distances to training cases
steps.prose: Compare the query with each training point using a chosen distance. With one numerical feature, absolute distance is enough. In several dimensions, a feature measured in large units can dominate unless scaling and distance choice are appropriate.
steps.terms: A neighbour is a nearby stored training example under the selected distance measure.
steps.next: Order the cases by distance, using a stated rule when distances tie.

steps.title: Select the k nearest cases
steps.prose: Keep the k closest training examples. Small k is very local and can react strongly to noise; larger k averages a wider neighbourhood. k is the number of neighbours, not the number of classes.
steps.terms: k is a chosen hyperparameter. A tie-breaking rule makes equal-distance choices reproducible.
steps.next: Use the selected cases' labels to form a vote.

steps.title: Vote on the class
steps.prose: Count positive labels among the selected neighbours. Their fraction is a local estimate, and a majority vote gives the class for these odd k choices. Distance-weighted voting would instead give closer cases more influence.
steps.terms: A vote fraction is not automatically a calibrated probability for the wider population.
steps.next: The next section is a comparison with another method, not a computation using this vote.

steps.title: A different method: SVM and kernels
steps.prose: An SVM learns a boundary that balances a wide margin against training violations. A kernel supplies pairwise similarities corresponding to an implicit feature space, which can support a nonlinear boundary. An RBF kernel gives high similarity to close points, but that value is not a class probability.
steps.terms: Margin is separation from the decision boundary; the RBF parameter gamma controls how quickly similarity falls with distance.
steps.next: The additional notes compare linear and kernel SVMs, scaling, regularization and prediction cost.
steps.node: A different method: SVM and kernels

ML07.title: Naive Bayes classification
ML07.definition: Naive Bayes predicts a class by combining how common the class is with how likely the observed features are within that class. For example, a word can be more common in spam than ordinary email. With several features, the model simplifies the calculation by treating them as independent once the class is known; that is the 'naive' assumption.
ML07.example: We use eight training cases: four positive and four negative. A binary feature is present in three positive cases but only one negative case. We will use this evidence to calculate a class probability for a new case with that feature.
ML07.connection: Unlike logistic regression, which directly fits a class probability from features, Naive Bayes models feature probabilities within each class. Both can classify; they make different modelling assumptions.

steps.title: Class frequencies: the priors
steps.prose: Count the classes before looking at the new case's feature. Here each class has four of eight training cases, giving equal starting probabilities. In another population, the class frequencies could be different.
steps.terms: A prior is the class probability before considering the new example's feature.
steps.next: Combine each prior with that class's feature likelihood after calculating the likelihood separately.

steps.title: Feature probabilities within classes
steps.prose: Estimate how often the observed feature occurs inside each class. Additive smoothing adds alpha to each possible feature count, reducing the chance that an unseen training combination receives probability zero. The denominator must include the added count for both feature values.
steps.terms: A likelihood is the probability of the observed feature given a class. Alpha is a smoothing setting.
steps.next: The class prior and this likelihood are separate inputs to the multiplication step.

steps.title: Multiply each prior by its likelihood
steps.prose: A class gets a larger unnormalized score when it is common and when the observed feature is likely within that class. Multiply those two factors separately for positive and negative. With several features, Naive Bayes multiplies their likelihood terms under its simplifying assumption.
steps.terms: An unnormalized score has not yet been divided so the class probabilities add to one.
steps.next: Add the two scores and divide each by their total.

steps.title: Normalize into class probabilities
steps.prose: Dividing each class score by the total produces a posterior distribution for the new case under this model. The positive probability can then be thresholded to choose a class. Correlated features can make Naive Bayes overconfident because the evidence may be counted more than once.
steps.terms: A posterior is the class probability after considering the observed evidence.
steps.next: Compare this model with logistic regression under the same data split; probability calibration needs its own evaluation.

links: The prior for each class is one factor in its class score.
The feature likelihood for each class is the other factor in its class score.
Divide each class score by the sum of all class scores.

ML08.title: Decision trees and random forests
ML08.definition: A decision tree predicts by asking feature questions, such as whether a measurement is below a cutoff. Each answer sends an example down one branch until a leaf returns a prediction. A random forest trains many varied trees and combines their predictions, making the result less dependent on one particular tree.
ML08.example: The four training examples have feature values [1, 2, 3, 4] and labels [0, 0, 1, 1]. Change the cutoff to see which groups it creates and how mixed their labels are.
ML08.connection: This diagram evaluates a candidate training split. Its two branches meet only to calculate split quality; a prediction for one new case would follow one branch, not average the two leaves. The forest note explains how multiple trees are combined.

steps.title: Class mix before the split
steps.prose: The parent group contains all four training cases, with half from each class. Gini impurity measures how mixed these labels are: it is zero for one-class groups and larger for a balanced binary group.
steps.terms: A parent is the group being split. Gini impurity is 1 minus the sum of squared class proportions.
steps.next: Apply the candidate cutoff to form two child groups.

steps.title: Split on the feature cutoff
steps.prose: Send feature values at or below the threshold to the left and larger values to the right. During real training, the algorithm compares possible feature questions and cutoffs using training data.
steps.terms: A child is one group produced by the split. A leaf is a terminal group that supplies a prediction.
steps.next: Inspect each child's labels independently; neither child feeds into the other.

steps.title: Left-group labels and impurity
steps.prose: Calculate class proportions using only the training cases sent left. A pure group contains one class and has Gini impurity zero. A leaf could use its class proportions for a class-probability estimate.
steps.terms: The left group has its own sample count and class counts.
steps.next: Its impurity and size contribute to the candidate split's weighted score.

steps.title: Right-group labels and impurity
steps.prose: Do the same calculation using only the cases sent right. A new case routed here would use this region's prediction, not the prediction from the left group.
steps.terms: A pure training group is not a guarantee of correct predictions on unseen cases.
steps.next: Combine both group impurities by their training sizes to evaluate the split.

steps.title: Training split quality
steps.prose: Weight each child's impurity by the fraction of training rows it contains. Subtract this average from the parent's impurity: a larger reduction means a cleaner training split. Tree depth and minimum leaf size limit how finely the tree can subdivide.
steps.terms: Random forests use data and feature randomness to create varied trees, then combine their predictions. They do not merge both leaves for one tree's prediction.
steps.next: The separate forest explanation compares many-tree averaging with the sequential corrections of boosting in the gradient boosting lesson.

links: The parent training cases are divided by this cutoff.
These are the cases whose feature satisfies x ≤ cutoff.
These are the cases whose feature is greater than the cutoff.
Left-group count and impurity contribute to weighted training split quality.
Right-group count and impurity contribute to weighted training split quality.

ML09.title: Gradient boosting
ML09.definition: Gradient boosting builds a predictor in stages. Each new small model tries to correct errors made by the current combined model. For squared-error regression, the correction can be trained on the remaining differences between targets and predictions. This differs from a random forest, whose trees are trained without sequentially correcting a running prediction.
ML09.example: One example has target 3 and current prediction 1, leaving residual 2. We assume a small correction model returns 2 at this point. The learning-rate control changes how much of that correction is added; this demonstration does not fit the correction model.
ML09.connection: A forest combines varied trees; boosting combines a sequence of corrections. Smaller corrections often need more stages, so learning rate and stage count should be considered together.

steps.title: Current prediction and residual
steps.prose: Start from the ensemble's current prediction. Subtract it from the known target to obtain the remaining error. Across a real training set this produces a correction target for every case, not just this one number.
steps.terms: An ensemble combines multiple models. A residual for squared-error boosting is target minus current prediction.
steps.next: Fit a new small model to these residuals, or to the appropriate loss gradients for another objective.

steps.title: A small correction model
steps.prose: For half squared error, the negative derivative with respect to a prediction equals its residual. A small model tries to predict those correction values. Here its output is assumed to be 2 so we can focus on how the ensemble update works.
steps.terms: A weak learner is the small model added at a stage. The factor one-half simplifies derivatives and does not change the squared-error minimizer.
steps.next: Scale the correction before adding it to the running prediction.

steps.title: Add a scaled correction
steps.prose: Multiply the correction by the learning rate and add it to the existing prediction. This is a change to the ensemble prediction, not a gradient update to a single linear coefficient. Later corrections must be based on the updated predictions.
steps.terms: Shrinkage is another name for scaling each new model's contribution by a learning rate.
steps.next: Compare the updated prediction with the target; recompute residuals before any later stage.

steps.title: Check the new error
steps.prose: Recalculate squared error for this same teaching point. An improvement here only shows that the assumed correction helped this point. In real boosting, validation performance and a stopping rule determine whether further stages are useful.
steps.terms: The displayed loss is ordinary squared error; the half-squared form above differs only by a constant factor.
steps.next: For another stage, start from the updated ensemble and recompute its residuals. Do not reuse a stale correction.

links: The current residuals provide correction targets for the new small model.
Scale the correction model's output and add it to the current prediction.
Compare the updated prediction with the target.

ML10.title: Probability calibration and decision costs
ML10.definition: Two models can make the same yes/no decisions but assign different probabilities. Calibration asks whether those probabilities agree with observed frequencies: among predictions made with about 80% confidence, roughly 80% should be correct in an appropriate evaluation population. Decision costs ask a separate question: how harmful are false alarms and missed cases?
ML10.example: The four positive-class probabilities are [0.9, 0.6, 0.4, 0.1]. Changing their sharpness leaves their order and 0.5-threshold decisions unchanged, but changes probability errors. A separate cost example then derives a decision threshold.
ML10.connection: The shared metrics lesson owns precision, recall and F1. Here we compare probability quality, a reliability estimate and a cost-based action rule; these are related questions, not one calculation feeding the next.

steps.title: Probabilities versus decisions
steps.prose: Convert a probability to log-odds, multiply by the selected strength, then convert back using sigmoid. Strength above one pushes probabilities towards zero or one; below one softens them. For these cases, no probability crosses 0.5, so the predicted labels stay unchanged.
steps.terms: Log-odds, also called a logit, is log(p/(1−p)). This is an illustrative confidence transformation, not fitted calibration.
steps.next: We can now measure probability errors even though accuracy and the hard decisions did not change.

steps.title: Brier score and log loss
steps.prose: Compare probabilities with the known labels. Brier score averages squared probability errors; log loss penalizes giving little probability to the observed label. Both use information discarded by a yes/no prediction.
steps.terms: For a label 1 the Brier error is (p−1)²; for label 0 it is p². Smaller matched scores are better.
steps.next: Calibration looks at whether confidence and observed frequencies agree, which is not fully described by one overall loss.

steps.title: Compare confidence with correctness
steps.prose: For each prediction, confidence is the probability of its predicted class: max(p,1−p). Group cases by confidence, then compare each group's mean confidence with its observed accuracy. Expected calibration error averages these absolute gaps using group sizes.
steps.terms: A reliability bin is a confidence range. ECE is a bin-dependent summary, not proof of calibration on a population.
steps.next: The final section changes from estimating probability quality to choosing an action from specified error costs.

steps.title: Choose a cutoff from error costs
steps.prose: If a false positive costs 3 and a false negative costs 1, a well-calibrated binary probability supports predicting positive at probability 0.75 or above under this simple cost model. Raising the cutoff reflects the greater cost of a false alarm; it is not a transformation of ECE.
steps.terms: Expected cost multiplies each possible mistake's cost by its probability. The derivation assumes no additional cost for a correct decision.
steps.next: The notes distinguish probability calibration, uncertainty in a test score, and prediction sets for new cases.
steps.node: Choose a cutoff from error costs

ML11.title: Clustering and K-means
ML11.definition: Clustering groups examples without using target class labels. K-means describes each group by a center, assigns training points to their nearest center, then moves each center to the mean of its assigned points. Repeating these two steps seeks compact groups; it does not establish that the groups are meaningful real-world categories.
ML11.example: Training points [0, 2, 8, 10] start with two centers at 0 and 10. Their assignments move the centers to 1 and 9. A separate query control lets you inspect where another point would be assigned before that update.
ML11.connection: Classification uses known labels; clustering does not. The additional notes compare K-means with Gaussian mixtures, which allow soft membership, and DBSCAN, which groups by density.

steps.title: Choose starting centers
steps.prose: Choose K, the number of groups, and initial centers. This example starts at 0 and 10. Different starting points can produce different final groupings, so real implementations often use careful initialization and repeated starts.
steps.terms: A centroid is a cluster mean. The initial center is only a starting guess, not a learned class label.
steps.next: Assign every training point to the nearest initial center.

steps.title: Assign training points to centers
steps.prose: The training points 0 and 2 go to center 0; 8 and 10 go to center 10. The selected query is only inspected: it is not added to these training groups and does not affect their means. At 5 it is tied and the first center wins by this example's rule.
steps.terms: K-means uses squared Euclidean distance. The query control inspects a distance decision, not a new training dataset.
steps.next: Use the assignments of the four training points to recompute each center.

steps.title: Move centers to group means
steps.prose: Average only the training points assigned to each group. The mean of 0 and 2 is 1, while the mean of 8 and 10 is 9. Repeat assignment with these new centers, then update again until the chosen stopping rule is satisfied.
steps.terms: For fixed assignments, the mean minimizes the within-group sum of squared distances.
steps.next: Measure that sum for the updated centers; if continuing, reassign training points before recomputing means.

steps.title: Measure within-cluster spread
steps.prose: Add the squared distances of all training points to their assigned centers. This quantity, called inertia, measures compactness. More clusters can reduce it even when the extra groups are not useful, so it is not a classification-accuracy score.
steps.terms: K-means can settle at a local solution. Group quality also depends on feature scaling, shape and the intended use.
steps.next: The dashed return means another assignment/update iteration with the new centers; it does not reset initialization.

ML12.title: PCA, dimensionality reduction and anomalies
ML12.definition: Dimensionality reduction replaces many input features with fewer coordinates. Principal component analysis, or PCA, chooses directions that preserve as much training-data variance as possible. Reconstructing an input from those fewer coordinates shows information that was lost. A large reconstruction error can be an anomaly signal, but does not prove that an example is invalid.
ML12.example: Training points lie on a diagonal line. We keep that one direction, represent the new point [2, 0] with one coordinate, then reconstruct it as [1, 1]. The control changes only the illustrative anomaly cutoff, not the fitted PCA direction.
ML12.connection: PCA compresses inputs without using class labels. Low-variance information can still matter for prediction, so preserving variance is not the same as preserving everything useful to a target task.

steps.title: Learn a principal direction
steps.prose: Center the training points by subtracting their mean, then find a direction along which they vary most. Here all variation lies along a diagonal. Dividing [1,1] by its length makes the direction a unit vector so its coordinate has a consistent scale.
steps.terms: Variance measures spread around a mean. A principal component is a fitted direction, not one of the original feature columns.
steps.next: Use this saved direction and training mean to represent a new point with fewer coordinates.

steps.title: Project onto one coordinate
steps.prose: A dot product with the unit direction measures how far the centered point lies along that direction. We retain this one number and discard its perpendicular component. The input [2,0] therefore becomes a single coordinate √2.
steps.terms: Projection expresses a point along a chosen direction. A unit vector has length one.
steps.next: Multiply the retained coordinate by the direction to reconstruct an approximation of the original point.

steps.title: Reconstruct the original features
steps.prose: Map the retained coordinate back to the original feature space and add the training mean. The reconstruction [1,1] differs from input [2,0] because one direction was discarded. This difference makes the lost information visible.
steps.terms: A reconstruction is an approximation, not necessarily the original input or a corrected ground-truth value.
steps.next: The next section optionally uses reconstruction error as an anomaly score; it is not required for PCA compression.

steps.title: Optional: score an unusual point
steps.prose: Sum the squared differences between input and reconstruction. A large value means the input lies far from this fitted subspace. A useful anomaly detector still needs a suitable reference population and a justified cutoff; low reconstruction error does not guarantee normality.
steps.terms: An anomaly score measures unusualness under a chosen model. An alarm additionally requires a decision threshold.
steps.next: The deeper notes compare PCA with other reduction and anomaly-detection methods, not just this single score.

links: Use the fitted unit direction to calculate the new point's coordinate.
Multiply the retained coordinate by the direction and restore the training mean.

ML13.title: Time-series forecasting
ML13.definition: Forecasting predicts a future value using information available when the prediction is made. A time series is a sequence of observations ordered in time, such as daily demand. A forecast origin is the prediction time; the horizon is how far ahead we predict. These boundaries determine which inputs are legitimate.
ML13.example: Our observed history is [3, 4, 5]. We predict the next value using the average of the most recent two or three values. The actual next value, 6, is kept outside that calculation and used only to score the forecast.
ML13.connection: Ordinary random row splits can be misleading when future observations help predict the past. Forecasting instead tests a procedure across appropriate time cutoffs.

steps.title: Mark when the forecast is made
steps.prose: Place a boundary after the last available observation. Anything beyond it is unknown when the prediction is made. Some future inputs, such as a calendar date or an already issued weather forecast, may be available; their later observed values are a different matter.
steps.terms: The forecast origin is the last information cutoff. Here the horizon is one time step.
steps.next: Build the input window using observations on the permitted side of the boundary.

steps.title: Select the recent history
steps.prose: Choose the last k observed values before the cutoff. A lag is an earlier time step; a window collects several lags. The control changes which already observed values enter this example, not which future value is scored.
steps.terms: The moving-average window is a chosen number of past observations. Centered windows can accidentally include the future.
steps.next: Average the selected past values to calculate the baseline forecast.

steps.title: Calculate a moving-average forecast
steps.prose: A simple baseline predicts the next value as the mean of recent observations. With the last two values, the prediction is (4+5)/2 = 4.5. This may follow gradual changes slowly, which gives more sophisticated methods a meaningful reference to beat.
steps.terms: A moving average is an average over a sliding past window; it is not the same as a fitted ARIMA moving-average component.
steps.next: Once the actual next observation becomes available, compare it with this saved forecast.

steps.title: Score after the outcome arrives
steps.prose: The next value 6 can now be used to calculate forecast error. Repeat this process over multiple origins using only information available at each origin. One forecast error alone is too little evidence to compare methods reliably.
steps.terms: Rolling-origin evaluation moves the cutoff forward. Errors from overlapping horizons or windows may be statistically dependent.
steps.next: Use the time-series notes for trend, seasonality, horizons and model alternatives.
