ML14.title: Recommendation and sequential decisions
ML14.definition: A recommender ranks items, such as films or products, for a user. A simple model scores how well learned user and item vectors match. When today's choice also affects future outcomes, we need a sequential-decision view rather than treating each recommendation as an isolated ranking problem.
ML14.example: The first example scores two items and ranks them. The second, separate example adds an immediate reward of 1 to a discounted future reward of 2. The recommendation score is not an input to the reward calculation.
ML14.connection: The common question is which action to choose. Ranking predicts relative preference; sequential methods additionally model feedback and consequences over time. These examples share a page for comparison, not because they form one pipeline.

steps.title: Example A: score user–item matches
steps.prose: Represent a user and each item with numerical vectors learned from interactions. Their dot product is one possible compatibility score. These coordinates need not have names such as 'likes comedy'; they can be useful without each coordinate having a simple interpretation.
steps.terms: An embedding is a learned vector. A compatibility score orders candidates but is not automatically a click probability.
steps.next: Rank the eligible items using these scores.

steps.title: Example A: rank eligible items
steps.prose: Sort candidates by their compatibility scores. Items a user never saw do not automatically count as disliked, because exposure affects which feedback was possible. A useful system also needs a policy for users or items with little interaction history.
steps.terms: Cold start means insufficient history for a new user or item. Exposure is whether an item was shown.
steps.next: The next example starts a different calculation about rewards over time; it does not consume these item scores.

steps.title: Example B: value rewards over time
steps.prose: An action can produce an immediate reward and influence later rewards. Discounted return adds rewards while reducing later contributions by a factor gamma per time step. Here gamma changes the value assigned to the second reward, not the recommendation ranking.
steps.terms: An action is a system choice; a reward is the feedback used to value it. Gamma is a discount factor, not a predicted probability.
steps.next: Evaluating an action rule requires many appropriate observations, not this one assumed reward sequence.
steps.node: Example B: value rewards over time

steps.title: Evaluate a decision policy
steps.prose: A policy is a rule for choosing actions from available information. Logged outcomes depend on which actions an earlier policy selected, so ordinary prediction accuracy does not establish that a new policy would improve outcomes. A bandit observes feedback for chosen actions; reinforcement learning can model longer sequences of state changes.
steps.terms: Policy value is expected return under that policy. Estimating it needs explicit assumptions or a suitable experiment.
steps.next: The deeper notes compare recommendation, bandits and sequential learning without treating them as interchangeable trainers.

ML15.title: Generalization and distribution shift
ML15.definition: Generalization means performing well on new examples, not only examples used for fitting. A score may change because the new population contains a different mixture of easy and difficult cases. Distribution shift is the broader name for a change between the data used to develop a model and the data where it is evaluated or used.
ML15.example: Group A has average loss 0.1 and group B has average loss 0.4. The original population is 80% A and 20% B. Change their proportions while keeping these within-group losses fixed to see why the overall average changes.
ML15.connection: The direct weighted average is the simplest explanation. Importance weighting is an equivalent way to express it using the original population. Learning-theory and uncertainty notes discuss other questions; they are not later operations on this average.

steps.title: Original group proportions and errors
steps.prose: Average loss depends both on each group's difficulty and how common it is. Here group A is easier and much more common in the source population, so it dominates the original average. Nothing about this setup says the model will improve when the population changes.
steps.terms: Source means the development/reference population. Risk is a mathematical name for expected or average loss.
steps.next: State the new population mix before calculating its average error.

steps.title: New proportions and importance weights
steps.prose: Compare each group's new proportion with its original proportion. The ratio tells us how much more or less that group should count when using source cases to represent the new mix. Large ratios can make estimates unstable when based on few cases.
steps.terms: An importance weight is target proportion divided by source proportion. Source coverage is needed wherever the target has cases.
steps.next: Use the new proportions directly, or equivalent source-weighted losses, to calculate the new average.

steps.title: Average error in the new population
steps.prose: Multiply each group's unchanged average loss by its new proportion, then add. If the harder group becomes more common, the overall loss rises even though the model's within-group performance has not changed.
steps.terms: This example assumes the group losses stay fixed. More general covariate-shift correction assumes unchanged outcome relationships conditional on the inputs.
steps.next: Check this assumption before interpreting weighting as a remedy.
steps.node: Average error in the new population

steps.title: When reweighting is not enough
steps.prose: A different label definition or a changed relationship between inputs and outcomes can alter errors inside each group. Changing only group weights cannot fix that. The model, labels or training data may need revision, and target-domain evaluation is needed.
steps.terms: Aleatoric uncertainty concerns outcome variability; epistemic uncertainty concerns limited knowledge of the model or relationship. These are separate from the mixture calculation.
steps.next: The notes introduce uncertainty models and learning-theory assumptions as distinct extensions, not guarantees that weighting solves generalization.

ML16.title: Run and report an ML experiment
ML16.definition: A complete experiment compares models under a clear task, data split and metric. Fit a simple baseline, choose candidate pipelines using validation evidence, and evaluate the final choice on reserved test data. Save enough information for someone else to check how the result was produced.
ML16.example: The worked plan compares a baseline and two candidates. Their displayed scores are invented examples used to explain selection. They are not measured rankings of the model families taught in this course.
ML16.connection: The training/validation split lesson introduced the split boundaries. This capstone turns them into concrete outputs: data-split IDs, fitted preprocessing/model, chosen settings, per-example predictions and a result report.

steps.title: Write the experiment plan
steps.prose: State the target, available inputs, intended population and main metric. Reserve the final test cases before model development, using groups or time order where needed. Record the comparison budget so one candidate is not silently given far more tuning.
steps.terms: A protocol is the written procedure. A split ID identifies which original case belongs to which partition.
steps.next: Build baseline and candidate pipelines under this plan.

steps.title: Fit baseline and candidate pipelines
steps.prose: Fit preprocessing and each candidate using only the relevant training portion. Save the settings, software versions and random seeds. The baseline needs the same valid input and split rules as the more complex methods.
steps.terms: A fitted pipeline contains learned preprocessing and the model. A saved configuration lists the choices used to create it.
steps.next: Compare their validation scores to choose one final fitting procedure.

steps.title: Choose using validation results
steps.prose: Use the preselected metric and rule to choose among candidates. Validation includes decisions about hyperparameters, thresholds and checkpoints. The largest illustrative validation score here selects candidate B; it does not guarantee that B has the best population performance.
steps.terms: Selection is part of development. An untouched test set must remain outside these choices.
steps.next: Follow the declared final refitting procedure, then evaluate the frozen selected system.

steps.title: Evaluate and save the result
steps.prose: Score the selected system on the reserved test cases. Save predictions and labels, metric conventions, fitted artifacts and the data revision/split so the result can be checked. Report relevant errors and limits, not just the best-looking number.
steps.terms: A manifest is an optional structured record of files, settings and hashes. Hashes detect changed bytes, not whether an experiment was fair.
steps.next: Use the training lab for supported experiments; course-only methods are not silently executable because this plan mentions them.

P8.title: Evaluation metrics
P8.definition: A metric turns predictions and known answers into a number that summarizes one aspect of performance. Different metrics answer different questions: accuracy counts correct decisions, recall counts recovered positives, and a numerical error measures distance from a target value. Choose a metric to match the task and the consequences of mistakes, not because it gives the largest-looking score.
P8.example: Choose a task below to inspect its cases and calculations. For binary classification, 'positive' means the class we want to detect, such as spam; 'negative' means the other class.
P8.connection: The examples show what is counted and divided. Metrics on the same cases are not separate processing stages: precision does not become an input to recall. The calibration lesson separately studies whether probabilities are reliable and how decision costs affect a cutoff.

classification.example: Six labelled cases have fixed positive-class probabilities. The cutoff changes which cases are predicted positive. Compare the confusion counts and the highlighted denominators as you inspect each metric.

steps.title: Convert probabilities to class labels
steps.prose: A binary classifier can assign a probability to the class we want to detect. A threshold turns that probability into a positive or negative decision. Changing only the threshold can change precision and recall even when the underlying model is unchanged.
steps.terms: Positive and negative are class names, not judgements of whether the model is correct.
steps.next: Pair the class decisions with known labels to count correct predictions and errors.

steps.title: Count correct predictions and mistakes
steps.prose: A True Positive is a correctly detected positive; a False Positive is a false alarm. A False Negative is a missed positive; a True Negative correctly rejects a negative. The confusion matrix groups the six cases into these four categories.
steps.terms: TP, FP, FN and TN abbreviate these four full names. Rows here are actual labels; columns are predictions.
steps.next: Accuracy, precision and recall select different subsets of these same counts.

steps.title: Accuracy: fraction of all cases correct
steps.prose: Add correct positive and correct negative predictions, then divide by all cases. This is useful when overall correctness matters, but a common class can dominate it. An always-negative rule may look good while missing every rare positive.
steps.terms: N is the total number of evaluated examples.
steps.next: Precision changes the question to correctness among predicted positives.
steps.node: Accuracy: fraction of all cases correct

steps.title: Precision: correctness of positive predictions
steps.prose: Among all cases called positive, count how many really are positive. False alarms enlarge the denominator without helping the numerator. This answers 'When the system flags a case, how often is it right?' on this evaluation sample.
steps.terms: The denominator TP + FP counts predicted positives. It is zero when the model flags nothing.
steps.next: Recall uses actual positives as its denominator instead.

steps.title: Recall: fraction of positives found
steps.prose: Among cases that really are positive, count how many the system detected. Missed positives remain in the denominator. This answers 'Of the cases we needed to find, how many did we find?'
steps.terms: The denominator TP + FN counts actual positives, including missed ones.
steps.next: F1 summarizes the balance between finding positives and avoiding false alarms.

steps.title: F1: balance precision and recall
steps.prose: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It becomes small when either is small and does not count correctly rejected negatives. The count formula avoids taking two rounded ratios first; it is not an average of every kind of model quality.
steps.terms: In the formula, each True Positive counts twice, while each false alarm and missed positive counts once.
steps.next: Ranking metrics ask how scores order cases across thresholds, rather than judging one selected cutoff.

steps.title: ROC-AUC and average precision
steps.prose: Varying the threshold changes recall and false-positive rate. The ROC curve plots those rates; its area summarizes positive-versus-negative score ordering. A precision–recall view instead follows correctness among retrieved positives. Average precision summarizes precision at successive positive hits.
steps.terms: ROC means receiver operating characteristic. AUC is area under its curve; AP means average precision and is not generally trapezoidal PR area.
steps.next: Use the deeper curve note for averaging conventions and population effects. Choose an operating cutoff on validation data.

multiclass.example: The matrix contains three classes, A, B and C. Select one class to see how its row and column determine that class's errors, then compare different averaging rules.

steps.title: Read a multiclass confusion matrix
steps.prose: For each row, start from the actual class and see where the predictions landed. Correct cases are on the diagonal. To evaluate one class, temporarily treat it as positive and all the others as negative.
steps.terms: Class support means how many actual cases belong to that class. One-versus-rest is this class-against-all-others view.
steps.next: Use its diagonal and off-diagonal row/column counts to calculate class-level F1.

steps.title: Calculate F1 separately for each class
steps.prose: Take each class in turn as positive and calculate its own precision, recall and F1. A common class and a rare class can have very different detection quality even if overall accuracy looks strong.
steps.terms: False positives come from the selected column outside the diagonal; false negatives come from its row outside the diagonal.
steps.next: Choose how much influence each class should have in the overall summary.
steps.node: Calculate F1 separately for each class

steps.title: Macro-F1: equal weight per class
steps.prose: Average the already calculated class F1 values equally. This makes each included class equally influential regardless of how many examples it has. It is not F1 calculated after averaging class precision and recall.
steps.terms: Macro means equal class weighting, not a different per-class formula.
steps.next: Weighted and micro averages combine the same evaluation evidence in other ways.

steps.title: Weighted F1 and micro-F1
steps.prose: Weighted F1 averages class F1 values in proportion to their actual class counts. Micro-F1 first pools the class-level correct detections and errors, then calculates F1. These answer different aggregation questions.
steps.terms: Here micro-F1 equals accuracy because every example has exactly one class and all classes are included.
steps.next: Balanced accuracy uses equal class weights too, but averages recall rather than F1.

steps.title: Balanced accuracy: equal weight per recall
steps.prose: Calculate recall for each class, then take their mean. This measures whether each actual class is recovered well without letting a large class dominate. It is different from macro-F1 because false-positive effects enter the two metrics differently.
steps.terms: Averaging rules, included labels and zero-denominator conventions are part of the metric specification.
steps.next: Use the aggregation note when moving to multilabel tasks or excluded classes.
steps.node: Balanced accuracy: equal weight per recall

regression.example: Targets [1, 2, 3, 4] are compared with predictions [1, 3, 2, 5]. Each error is measured in the same units as the target; the metrics differ in how they combine those errors.

steps.title: Calculate signed prediction errors
steps.prose: Subtract each observed target from its prediction. Positive means an overprediction and negative means an underprediction. Simply averaging signed errors can hide mistakes when positive and negative misses cancel.
steps.terms: A residual is prediction minus target in this course's convention.
steps.next: MAE ignores the signs and averages error sizes.

steps.title: Mean absolute error (MAE)
steps.prose: Take the absolute size of each residual, then average. An error twice as large contributes twice as much. MAE keeps the target units, so it can be explained as an average miss in units such as euros or degrees.
steps.terms: Absolute value removes an error's sign, not its size.
steps.next: Squared-error metrics place more emphasis on large misses.

steps.title: Mean squared error and RMSE
steps.prose: Square every residual and average to get MSE. Taking its square root gives RMSE in the original target units. Squaring makes very large mistakes contribute more strongly than they do to MAE.
steps.terms: MSE has squared target units. RMSE means root mean squared error.
steps.next: R² instead compares squared error with the variation in the evaluation targets.

steps.title: R²: improvement over a mean reference
steps.prose: Compare the model's squared error with predicting the evaluation sample's mean for every case. R² is one minus their error ratio. It can be negative if the model does worse than that reference; it is not a percentage of correct predictions.
steps.terms: The denominator is variation around this evaluation sample's target mean. Constant targets need a stated convention.
steps.next: Choose the error measure that reflects the practical cost and target units of the application.
steps.node: R²: improvement over a mean reference

language.example: The probabilities assigned to three known next tokens are [0.5, 0.25, 0.1]. The scoring mask decides which targets count. These are prediction probabilities for an arithmetic example, not outputs measured from a trained checkpoint.

steps.title: Choose which token targets count
steps.prose: Some positions, such as padding or prompt tokens in response-only training, may be excluded from the loss. Mark scored targets before computing totals so the numerator and denominator refer to the same region.
steps.terms: A loss mask includes or excludes target positions. Valid count is the number included.
steps.next: Calculate the loss assigned to each observed target that is scored.

steps.title: Negative log-probability of each target
steps.prose: For each known target token, take minus the natural logarithm of the probability assigned to it. A smaller target probability produces a larger penalty. This judges next-token prediction, not whether a generated answer is factually correct.
steps.terms: Negative log-likelihood, or NLL, is measured in nats when using natural logarithms.
steps.next: Add losses for included targets, then divide by their valid count.

steps.title: Mean NLL and perplexity
steps.prose: Mean NLL is the total included loss divided by included targets. Perplexity is the exponential of that mean; it is derived from the same probabilities, not a second independent measure of usefulness.
steps.terms: Matched comparisons require the same scored text, tokenization, context handling and masks.
steps.next: Byte-normalized loss uses a different denominator and needs aligned text bytes.

steps.title: Bits per byte
steps.prose: Convert the summed loss from nats into bits, then divide by the number of raw-text bytes belonging to exactly the scored region. If that aligned byte count is unavailable, do not report a made-up value.
steps.terms: One bit is log(2) nats. Different token counts do not automatically imply different amounts of scored text.
steps.next: Keep text, context coverage and scoring boundaries explicit when comparing tokenizers or language models.

retrieval.example: Documents A and C are relevant; the ranked result list is B, A, C. Change k to inspect the first one, two or three results, while the full-list ranking remains fixed.

steps.title: Known relevance and ranked results
steps.prose: Retrieval returns an ordered list of candidates. Evaluation needs known relevance labels for the same query. The selected prefix means only the first k returned documents; it is not the full collection.
steps.terms: A relevant document meets the query's relevance definition. Gold relevance is the reference annotation, which may itself be incomplete.
steps.next: Count relevant items in the prefix to calculate precision@k and recall@k.

steps.title: Precision@k and recall@k
steps.prose: Precision@k asks what fraction of the k returned items are relevant. Recall@k asks what fraction of all known relevant items appear in that prefix. The numerator is the same number of hits; the denominators differ.
steps.terms: k is the number of top results inspected. Hits are relevant results found within that prefix.
steps.next: Reciprocal rank asks a different question about where the first relevant result appears.

steps.title: Reciprocal rank
steps.prose: Find the first relevant result and take one divided by its rank. A relevant first result gets 1; a first relevant result at position 2 gets 1/2. This emphasizes how soon a user encounters the first useful hit.
steps.terms: MRR is mean reciprocal rank across queries; one query gives a reciprocal rank, not a mean across many queries.
steps.next: AP and nDCG consider relevance at more than just the first useful position.

steps.title: Average precision and nDCG
steps.prose: Average precision rewards precision at each relevant hit. nDCG adds position-discounted relevance gains and compares them with an ideal ordering. Both displayed values use the full list here, so changing only the inspected prefix does not change them.
steps.terms: nDCG means normalized discounted cumulative gain. MAP averages average precision across queries.
steps.next: Relevance scores do not by themselves establish answer support or citation correctness for a downstream system.

DL01.title: Neural networks and multilayer perceptrons
DL01.definition: A neural network combines learned weighted sums with nonlinear functions. A multilayer perceptron, or MLP, uses dense layers: each output feature reads all features in the preceding layer. Hidden layers create intermediate representations that can support a more flexible prediction rule than one linear transformation.
DL01.example: Our network has two inputs, two hidden features and one numerical output. Its weights stay fixed while you switch between ReLU and tanh, so you can see how the nonlinear function changes the prediction before studying training.
DL01.connection: Linear regression combines inputs once. An MLP inserts intermediate features and nonlinearities; the prediction, loss and gradient-update principles from the foundations still apply.

steps.title: One example with two features
steps.prose: The vector [1,2] describes one observation, not two training examples. A dense layer will read both entries to calculate each hidden feature. Keeping the example axis separate from the feature axis prevents common shape mistakes.
steps.terms: A feature is an input measurement or representation. A batch groups several examples; this example's batch size is one.
steps.next: The first layer combines these inputs using its weight matrix.

steps.title: Hidden-layer weighted sums
steps.prose: Each hidden unit multiplies the two inputs by its own weights and adds the contributions. A bias could add a learned constant; the biases are zero here. The two results are new feature scores, not two separate class decisions.
steps.terms: An affine transformation is a weighted sum plus bias. Dense means every input is connected to each output in this layer.
steps.next: Apply a nonlinear function to each hidden score.

steps.title: ReLU or tanh
steps.prose: ReLU replaces negative values with zero and keeps positive ones. Tanh smoothly limits values to between −1 and 1. Applying a nonlinearity between layers matters: without it, a stack of affine layers is still equivalent to one affine transformation.
steps.terms: An activation function transforms a score. An activation value is the result of that computation, not a stored learned weight.
steps.next: The output layer combines the resulting hidden features.

steps.title: Output-layer prediction
steps.prose: The output layer takes a weighted sum of the hidden features. Here it subtracts the second from the first to produce one numerical prediction. A different task could require several class scores instead.
steps.terms: A prediction head is the final mapping to the required target type. This scalar output is not a class probability.
steps.next: Compare the prediction with a known target to calculate a training loss.

steps.title: Loss for a known target
steps.prose: The target is 1. Squared error measures how far the output is from this target and provides the scalar objective for differentiation. Full training would calculate gradients for both layers; changing the activation control here does not fit any weights.
steps.terms: A loss measures the training penalty. Architecture, fixed example weights and a trained model are different things.
steps.next: The backpropagation lesson traces how a loss supplies gradients to several weights.

links: Both input features contribute to each hidden unit's weighted sum.

DL02.title: Backpropagation and automatic differentiation
DL02.definition: Backpropagation calculates how each trainable weight affects a loss by following the model's operations backwards. It applies the chain rule and adds contributions when a weight affects the loss through several paths. Automatic differentiation records these operations for you; the optimizer, not backpropagation itself, changes the weights.
DL02.example: The calculation has two weights: a = w × 2, then prediction = 0.5 × a, with target 3. Change the first weight and inspect the prediction, loss and the separate gradients for both weights.
DL02.connection: The foundations introduced one gradient. This example shows why different weights receive different gradients, and why clearing or accumulating gradient buffers is a separate programming decision.

steps.title: First weighted calculation
steps.prose: Multiply input 2 by the first trainable weight. The intermediate result must remain connected to the loss if automatic differentiation is to compute that weight's gradient. Detaching it means deliberately breaking that dependency.
steps.terms: A computation graph records operations and the values they depend on. An intermediate value is computed, not independently learned.
steps.next: The second weight multiplies this intermediate result.

steps.title: Second weighted calculation
steps.prose: Multiply the intermediate value by the second coefficient, 0.5, to produce the prediction. Both coefficients influence the final answer, even though they occur at different points in the graph.
steps.terms: A parameter is a value training can learn. The letters w and v distinguish two separate weights.
steps.next: The prediction and target determine the scalar loss.

steps.title: Loss and output derivative
steps.prose: Calculate squared error against target 3. Differentiating that error with respect to the prediction gives the starting signal for the backward pass. No weight has changed yet.
steps.terms: An upstream gradient describes how a later result changes when an earlier value changes. Here the initial result is the scalar loss.
steps.next: Multiply the output derivative by the local derivatives for each weight.

steps.title: A gradient for each weight
steps.prose: The second weight multiplies the intermediate a, so its gradient includes a. The first weight affects the output through the second weight and input 2, so its gradient includes both. If a weight were used along several paths, their contributions would be added.
steps.terms: A partial derivative varies one weight while holding the others fixed. Gradients are sensitivities, not attention scores or weight updates.
steps.next: An optimizer can now use these gradients to choose updates.

steps.title: Gradient buffers and the optimizer step
steps.prose: In PyTorch, backward normally adds to existing parameter gradients. Clear them before an independent update, or deliberately accumulate correctly scaled contributions from several microbatches. The displayed SGD step illustrates a weight change; a real optimizer also updates every intended trainable parameter.
steps.terms: zero_grad clears gradient storage. Accumulation combines gradients before one optimizer step; it does not keep old predictions as new training data.
steps.next: A new iteration uses updated weights, an appropriate next batch and the intended gradient-clearing policy.

DL03.title: Optimizers, initialization and training stability
DL03.definition: An optimizer turns gradients into parameter updates. Plain stochastic gradient descent, or SGD, subtracts a learning-rate-scaled gradient. Adam keeps moving averages of gradients and squared gradients to adapt update sizes. Initialization chooses the starting weights; a schedule changes learning rate over time. These are related choices, not interchangeable methods.
DL03.example: We compare one SGD step with the first Adam step from weight 1 and gradient 2 at learning rate 0.1. The Adam-state sections explain Adam even when SGD is selected; the final update uses the selected rule. No weight decay is included in this arithmetic.
DL03.connection: Backpropagation supplies gradients. This lesson explains how optimizer rules use them, then the deeper notes cover initialization, clipping, normalization, schedules and failure diagnosis.

steps.title: The same starting gradient
steps.prose: Use the same weight, gradient and learning rate to isolate the update rule. SGD uses the current gradient directly. Adam's result also depends on its stored averages, which start at zero for this first-step example.
steps.terms: The learning rate scales the attempted update; it does not have an identical numerical effect under every optimizer.
steps.next: The next two sections explain the state used by Adam, not additional stages of plain SGD.

steps.title: Adam's moving averages
steps.prose: Adam retains a smoothed history of gradients and squared gradients. Beta values determine how strongly old history is retained. With zero starting state and this gradient, its first stored values are 0.2 and 0.004.
steps.terms: The first moment is a moving average of gradients; the second moment averages squared gradients. Plain SGD has neither state in this comparison.
steps.next: Adam corrects the initial shrinkage caused by starting those averages at zero.

steps.title: Adam's bias correction
steps.prose: Early moving averages are pulled towards their zero initialization. Dividing by the appropriate factors corrects that effect under the optimizer's definition. On this first step, corrected values are 2 and 4, producing a normalized direction close to 1.
steps.terms: This bias correction concerns optimizer-state initialization, not statistical fairness or an intercept term. Epsilon prevents a zero denominator.
steps.next: The chosen optimizer's direction is multiplied by the learning rate to update the parameter.

steps.title: Compare the actual parameter change
steps.prose: SGD subtracts 0.1 × 2. First-step Adam subtracts approximately 0.1 × 1 under these assumptions. Neither this one-step difference nor a common learning rate establishes which method will learn better on a real task.
steps.terms: AdamW additionally applies decoupled weight decay. That operation is intentionally absent here; later Adam steps depend on history.
steps.next: Use the initialization and stability notes to interpret real learning curves, rather than treating this first step as an optimizer ranking.

DL04.title: Regularization, dropout and training diagnostics
DL04.definition: Regularization changes training to discourage a model from relying too strongly on limited or accidental patterns. Dropout is one method: during training it randomly masks activation values, encouraging the network to cope without any particular selected feature. It does not permanently delete weights, and it is not a guaranteed improvement.
DL04.example: The features are [2,4]. Choose the probability of keeping a feature, q. A declared mask shows the arithmetic: retained values are divided by q. This fixed demonstration mask is not a randomly sampled training run.
DL04.connection: Regularization was introduced in ML. Here we distinguish a particular dropout sample, its expectation over many masks and evaluation-mode behaviour; those are three related explanations, not a serial architecture.

steps.title: Activations before dropout
steps.prose: Start with the computed feature values [2,4]. These are outputs of a layer, not the saved weights. Dropout will perturb these values during a training forward pass while leaving the model's parameter dimensions unchanged.
steps.terms: An activation is a computed feature value. Keep probability q is the chance a feature survives the random mask.
steps.next: Apply the mask and scaling rule to these activations.

steps.title: Training mask and scaling
steps.prose: For each feature, a sampled mask would choose keep or drop. Multiply by that mask, then divide retained values by q under inverted dropout. Here the mask is explicitly selected so the calculation can be inspected; changing q does not generate repeated random samples.
steps.terms: The drop probability is 1−q. PyTorch Dropout's p argument is the drop probability, not this control's keep probability.
steps.next: The expectation section explains the average over possible masks, not another operation applied to this particular output.

steps.title: Expected values across random masks
steps.prose: Under independent Bernoulli sampling with keep probability q, the mask's mean is q. Dividing surviving activations by q therefore preserves each activation's expected value over masks. A single masked vector can be very different from the original vector.
steps.terms: Expectation is an average over possible random outcomes. Mean preservation does not preserve every downstream nonlinear prediction.
steps.next: Evaluation uses the original activations without this dropout sampling or rescaling.

steps.title: Evaluation mode versus gradient tracking
steps.prose: With inverted dropout, evaluation returns [2,4] unchanged at this layer. model.eval() switches dropout and other mode-sensitive modules to evaluation behaviour. A no_grad context separately disables gradient recording; one does not replace the other.
steps.terms: Evaluation mode controls module behaviour. Gradient tracking controls whether operations are recorded for differentiation.
steps.next: The deeper notes connect these distinctions to train/validation curves, early stopping and small-data diagnostics.

DL05.title: Convolutional neural networks
DL05.definition: A convolutional neural network, or CNN, learns local pattern detectors and reuses their weights across image positions. Each filter produces a feature map. Stacking convolutions and nonlinearities lets later features combine earlier patterns; pooling can reduce spatial resolution, and a final head maps the remaining features to task outputs.
DL05.example: The walkthrough uses one 8×8 grayscale image, two convolution blocks with ReLU (zeroing negative values) and max pooling (keeping local maxima), and three illustrative classes. Kernel size sets filter width; stride sets its movement; padding supplies boundary zeros here. All weights are fixed teaching values, so the example explains computation rather than measuring image-recognition accuracy.
DL05.connection: A dense layer combines all input features at once; a convolution first combines local patches with shared weights. The final dense head still uses the weighted-sum and classification ideas introduced earlier.

steps.title: Image tensor and channels
steps.prose: The image is arranged by example, channel, row and column. One grayscale image has one channel; an RGB image usually has three. A channel is a plane of features, not another independent training example.
steps.terms: B is batch size, C is channels, H is height and W is width. This input has shape [1,1,8,8].
steps.next: The first convolution reads local patches of this image.

steps.title: First convolution: shared local filters
steps.prose: Place a small filter over an image patch, multiply matching entries, add the products and the filter's bias. Reuse that same filter at other positions. Inspecting another output cell changes the patch, not the shared weights.
steps.terms: Kernel size is patch width/height. Stride is movement between positions; padding adds specified boundary values. PyTorch uses cross-correlation without reversing the kernel.
steps.next: ReLU transforms the signed filter responses before pooling.

steps.title: ReLU: keep positive responses
steps.prose: A filter can produce positive or negative values. ReLU replaces a negative response with zero and keeps a positive response unchanged. Applying it between learned layers makes the overall network nonlinear.
steps.terms: ReLU means rectified linear unit. It changes values without changing their dimensions or adding learned parameters.
steps.next: Pooling summarizes small regions within each activated feature map.

steps.title: First pooling: reduce spatial size
steps.prose: For each channel separately, keep the maximum value in each non-overlapping 2×2 window. This reduces the number of spatial positions while retaining strong local responses. It can also discard small patterns or precise location information.
steps.terms: Pooling has no learned weights in this example. It changes spatial resolution, not the number of channels.
steps.next: The second convolution combines patterns across both pooled channels.

steps.title: Second convolution: combine channels
steps.prose: Each new output filter has a spatial kernel for every input channel. Add contributions across those channels and then add one output bias. This produces four new feature maps here; input-channel contributions are summed, not returned as separate predictions.
steps.terms: Input channels describe available feature planes; output channels count new filter banks. Shared weights still apply at all valid positions.
steps.next: A second ReLU transforms these new combinations.

steps.title: Second ReLU
steps.prose: Apply the same nonnegative activation rule to every entry in the four new maps. The feature values change but the four-channel structure remains. Later features depend on a wider region of the original image because earlier operations have already combined nearby inputs.
steps.terms: A receptive field is the part of the original input that can affect a particular computed feature.
steps.next: The second pooling layer reduces these maps before the final head.

steps.title: Second pooling
steps.prose: Keep a local maximum from each 2×2 region of each later feature map. All channels are retained while their height and width decrease. A different pooling scheme would change the retained representation and may change the required classifier dimensions.
steps.terms: Local max pooling differs from global average pooling, which averages a whole channel.
steps.next: Flatten arranges the retained values into the vector expected by the head.

steps.title: Flatten into a feature vector
steps.prose: List the channel and spatial values in a defined order. Flattening changes the arrangement, not the values or their count. If stride or pooling changes the retained map size, the head's input width must match that new feature count.
steps.terms: Flattening is a reshape, not feature selection, averaging or a learned layer.
steps.next: A dense classifier now combines this vector into three class scores.

steps.title: Class logits from the dense head
steps.prose: Calculate a weighted sum of the retained features for each class, then add its bias. The three logits can be any real values. Their ordering gives a score preference before normalization.
steps.terms: A logit is a raw class score. The head's weights and biases are learned parameters in a real trained CNN.
steps.next: Softmax converts these three scores into a class-probability vector.
steps.node: Class logits from the dense head

steps.title: Softmax over classes
steps.prose: Normalize the class logits into three probabilities that sum to one for this image. The largest probability gives the default predicted class. This normalization is across classes, not image positions or feature channels.
steps.terms: A predicted probability is the model's assigned probability, not automatically a calibrated confidence guarantee.
steps.next: A labelled training example additionally supplies a target for calculating loss.

steps.title: Cross-entropy for a known target
steps.prose: The teaching target is class B. Its cross-entropy loss is minus the natural logarithm of the probability assigned to B. This is a training objective for one image, not an accuracy measurement on a dataset.
steps.terms: Nats are natural-log loss units. A real batch loss needs an explicit sum or mean reduction across examples.
steps.next: Backpropagation can calculate how changing parameters would affect this loss.

steps.title: A limited head-only update
steps.prose: The displayed SGD calculation freezes the convolutional features and updates the classifier weights and biases only. It demonstrates an exact gradient update without pretending to train the full CNN. Full training also differentiates through convolution, activation and pooling layers.
steps.terms: Backpropagation calculates sensitivities; the optimizer changes parameters. Max-pool gradients follow the winning inputs under a defined tie rule.
steps.next: Use the actual training lab for supported trained CNN runs; no checkpoint is changed by this walkthrough.

DL05.legend: Solid arrows carry image features towards class predictions. The loss and dashed update path explain a separate, head-only training calculation. Selecting a component never trains or edits a checkpoint.

DL06.title: Residual networks and transfer learning
DL06.definition: A residual block adds its input to a transformed version of that input: output = input + correction. This shortcut lets information and gradients use a direct path around the transformation. Transfer learning is a separate choice: reuse a pretrained model and decide which parameters to freeze or adapt. Residual architectures can be trained from scratch or transferred.
DL06.example: The input is 2 and the transformed branch multiplies it by a chosen scale. We calculate the addition and its derivative. A separate section then compares a frozen 1,000-parameter backbone with a trainable 20-parameter head; it is not another operation on the scalar output.
DL06.connection: The CNN lesson stacks transformations. A residual connection changes how those transformations are connected; freezing changes which weights an optimizer may update. Keep these two decisions separate.

steps.title: Keep an unchanged shortcut
steps.prose: Carry the original input directly to the later addition. This is a forward path, not a repetition or a backwards training loop. Its values must have a compatible shape with the transformed branch when they meet.
steps.terms: An identity shortcut copies values without changing them. A projection shortcut can adjust dimensions when an identity is insufficient.
steps.next: In parallel, the transformation branch calculates a change to add to this input.

steps.title: Calculate the transformation branch
steps.prose: The branch applies a transformation to the same input. Our scalar example multiplies by a chosen scale; a real residual CNN branch can include convolutions, normalization and activations. A branch scale of zero leaves only the shortcut contribution.
steps.terms: F(x) names the branch's transformation. It need not be a complete replacement for the incoming representation.
steps.next: Add its output to the unchanged shortcut at the matching dimensions.

steps.title: Add the two paths
steps.prose: Add corresponding values from the shortcut and the transformed branch. This is elementwise addition, not concatenation. The structure lets a block produce a small change when that is useful, but does not guarantee every network will train well.
steps.terms: Concatenation joins feature lists; addition combines matching entries and keeps their compatible shape.
steps.next: The next section analyzes the derivative of this addition, not another forward layer.

steps.title: Why the shortcut helps gradients
steps.prose: For y = x + sx, the derivative with respect to x is 1+s. The identity term contributes a direct gradient route alongside the transformed branch. This can help optimization in deep networks, but gradients can still behave poorly elsewhere.
steps.terms: Different paths contribute terms that are added by the chain rule. A gradient route is not a separate stored copy of the model.
steps.next: Transfer learning is a distinct policy about parameters, explained next rather than connected as a forward operation.

steps.title: Separate choice: freeze or fine-tune
steps.prose: A pretrained backbone produces features; a task head maps them to the new target. Freezing the backbone prevents its parameter updates while the head can learn. Unfreezing selected layers permits adaptation but changes data and compute requirements.
steps.terms: A backbone is the main feature-producing network. A frozen module can still have mode-sensitive running statistics that need deliberate handling.
steps.next: The deeper notes compare freezing, partial fine-tuning and scratch training without assuming every residual network is pretrained.

DL07.title: Recurrent networks, GRUs and LSTMs
DL07.definition: A recurrent neural network (RNN) processes an ordered sequence by updating a state at each position. The same cell weights are reused over time, so the current output can depend on earlier inputs. A vanilla RNN has one hidden-state update; a gated recurrent unit (GRU) controls how new and old states are mixed, and long short-term memory (LSTM) additionally maintains a separate cell-memory state.
DL07.example: The inputs are [1,0,1]. We calculate three state updates with fixed teaching weights. The GRU and LSTM gates are held constant to expose the arithmetic; real gates are computed from learned transformations of inputs and previous states.
DL07.connection: This is the DL overview of shared weights and sequence history. The NLP course provides the detailed RNN/BiRNN, GRU/BiGRU and LSTM/BiLSTM gate/state walkthroughs, so their full architecture explanations are not duplicated here.

steps.title: Initial state and sequence boundary
steps.prose: Define the state before reading the first input. This example starts hidden state at zero and, for LSTM, cell memory at zero. Separate sequences need a deliberate reset or carry policy so one example's history does not leak into another.
steps.terms: A hidden state is a computed summary of earlier inputs. An LSTM cell state is a separate memory quantity.
steps.next: The chosen cell combines its initial state with the first input.

steps.title: First input and cell update
steps.prose: Use input 1 and the initial state in the selected recurrent equation. A vanilla RNN applies tanh to an input/state weighted sum. A GRU mixes a candidate with the old hidden state; an LSTM updates cell memory before exposing a hidden output.
steps.terms: Here GRU reset r=0.5 and update z=0.25; z weights the old state. LSTM input/forget/output gates are 0.5/0.8/0.7. These are fixed illustrative coefficients.
steps.next: Carry the resulting state, not newly fitted weights, into the next position.

steps.title: Second input with retained history
steps.prose: The next input is zero, but the previous state may be nonzero. Reusing the cell therefore still produces a history-dependent result. The picture's repeated cells are copies of the operation, not separate parameter sets.
steps.terms: Unrolling draws time positions separately while keeping their weights shared. Time index is different from network-layer depth.
steps.next: The third update uses this newly calculated state.

steps.title: Third input and sequence output
steps.prose: Process the final input 1 with the state from the second position. A final-state head could summarize the sequence, while a per-position head could use every hidden state. Neither choice turns the state into a loss without a target and objective.
steps.terms: A recurrent state is a finite representation and can lose information about long sequences. LSTM cell and hidden state remain different values.
steps.next: The separate training section explains gradient contributions through these reused operations.

steps.title: Training: backpropagation through time
steps.prose: Attach a loss to the appropriate sequence outputs, then differentiate through the unrolled operations. Because the same parameters were used repeatedly, their gradient contributions are added. Truncated backpropagation deliberately cuts how far that gradient history extends.
steps.terms: Forward state carry and backward gradient history are separate choices. This demo calculates forward states, not a complete recurrent training loss or gradient.
steps.next: Use the NLP gate diagrams for detailed state mechanics and the training-system lesson for a full optimizer loop.

DL08.title: Attention and Transformer building blocks
DL08.definition: Attention updates a representation by taking a weighted combination of value vectors. A query is compared with keys to calculate matching scores; after masking forbidden positions, softmax turns those scores into mixing weights. The values supply the content being combined. Attention weights are not automatically explanations of truth or model correctness.
DL08.example: We update one query using two candidate key/value pairs. Allow both positions or block the later one with a causal mask, then see how the allowed scores, weights and output change. The model weights and vectors are authored examples, not trained measurements.
DL08.connection: Recurrent cells carry information through a sequence state. Attention provides another way to combine information across positions. The LLM Transformer lesson shows how heads, projections, residuals and feed-forward layers surround this operation.

steps.title: Query, keys and values
steps.prose: Use one query vector and two key/value pairs. Comparing the query with a key determines how strongly the corresponding value contributes. In a real model these vectors usually come from learned projections; queries and keys are not text strings being searched literally.
steps.terms: Q contains queries, K keys and V values. Their matching-vector widths must agree; output width follows the value vectors.
steps.next: Compare the query with each key and apply the visibility mask.

steps.title: Matching scores and visibility
steps.prose: Take a dot product with each key and scale by the square root of key width. A causal mask blocks future positions before normalization. Its blocked entry receives zero mixing weight after softmax, rather than merely being ignored by the training metric.
steps.terms: The attention mask controls information access. A loss mask instead controls which target positions count in the objective.
steps.next: Normalize the allowed scores across keys for this query.

steps.title: Softmax over allowed positions
steps.prose: Exponentiate and normalize the score row so its weights sum to one across permitted keys. These numbers tell us how to mix input content for this query. They are not probabilities over output vocabulary words.
steps.terms: The normalization axis is key positions. With only one allowed key, its weight becomes one.
steps.next: Multiply each value vector by its mixing weight and add them.

steps.title: Weighted sum of the values
steps.prose: Use the weights to combine the two value vectors. The result keeps the value-feature width; it is usually a mixture, not a hard choice of one source. Changing visibility changes which information can contribute.
steps.terms: Multi-head attention repeats this calculation with separate projected features, then combines the head outputs.
steps.next: The full Transformer architecture is linked as further reading rather than repeated on this page.

DL09.title: Autoencoders and self-supervised representations
DL09.definition: An autoencoder learns to encode an input into a representation and decode it back into a reconstruction. A bottleneck can limit how much information passes through, but accurate copying alone does not prove the representation is useful for another task. Self-supervised learning is broader: its training targets are derived from the data rather than supplied as separate human labels.
DL09.example: For input [1,0], a one-feature code averages the coordinates and reconstructs [0.5,0.5]. A two-feature identity map copies it exactly. These are fixed maps, not trained encoders. A separate final section introduces contrastive learning as a different objective.
DL09.connection: PCA also compresses and reconstructs using a linear subspace. Autoencoders can learn nonlinear mappings; contrastive and masked-prediction methods ask them to preserve different information.

steps.title: Encode into a smaller representation
steps.prose: The encoder maps input features to a code, also called a latent representation. Here width one averages the two coordinates, while width two uses the identity map. In real training, the encoder's mapping is learned rather than fixed by this control.
steps.terms: Latent width is the number of retained code features. A latent code is not automatically interpretable or disentangled.
steps.next: The decoder uses this code to produce an approximation of the input.

steps.title: Decode a reconstruction
steps.prose: For the one-feature example, repeat the encoded mean to create two reconstructed values. The identity example instead returns its two coordinates. This makes the information loss visible without pretending that width alone determines every trained decoder's behaviour.
steps.terms: A reconstruction has the input's shape. It is an approximation, not necessarily a cleaned or more truthful observation.
steps.next: Compare this reconstruction with the original input.

steps.title: Squared reconstruction loss
steps.prose: Subtract reconstruction from input coordinate by coordinate, square the differences and add them. This demo reports a sum: [1,0] versus [0.5,0.5] gives 0.5. Averaging across its two features would instead give MSE 0.25.
steps.terms: SSE is summed squared error. MSE divides a sum by a stated count; reductions and coordinate units must match in comparisons.
steps.next: The next section changes objective; contrastive loss is not computed from this reconstruction-loss value.

steps.title: Different objective: contrastive learning
steps.prose: Contrastive learning encourages matched views or pairs to be more similar than selected alternatives. Its targets and negatives define what similarity is encouraged to mean. Masked prediction instead asks a model to recover withheld content; neither is a later operation in this autoencoder's forward path.
steps.terms: A positive pair is a declared match. Temperature rescales similarity scores in the displayed contrastive objective.
steps.next: Evaluate the learned representation on an independent downstream task rather than assuming any one pretext objective is best.

DL10.title: Generative models: VAEs, GANs and diffusion
DL10.definition: A generative model learns a way to produce new samples with patterns resembling its training data. The main families use different mechanisms: a variational autoencoder, or VAE, encodes a distribution over latent codes and decodes samples; a generative adversarial network (GAN) trains a generator against a real/fake discriminator; diffusion learns to remove controlled noise. Their objectives are not interchangeable quality scores.
DL10.example: The selected example shows one mechanism with authored numbers, not generated images or measured model quality. Choose a family to see its specific inputs, calculations and limitations; no generative model is trained by the selector.
DL10.connection: Autoencoders introduced a code and reconstruction. This lesson distinguishes probabilistic codes, adversarial learning and denoising, before comparing what each objective actually encourages.

steps.title: Clean data and noise level
steps.prose: Begin with a clean scalar value and a sampled noise value. The selected retention coefficient controls how much signal and noise are mixed. A real diffusion model must know the time or noise level to interpret its noisy input.
steps.terms: x₀ denotes clean data; epsilon denotes noise. Alpha-bar is a cumulative signal-retention coefficient, not a confidence score.
steps.next: Use the specified coefficients to construct a noisy training example.

steps.title: Construct the noisy observation
steps.prose: Mix clean signal and noise using their declared square-root coefficients. This forward corruption is defined by the noise process, not learned by the denoiser. During training the chosen noise is known because we generated it.
steps.terms: The noisy observation x_t and time/noise level are inputs to the learned denoising model.
steps.next: The denoiser predicts the noise; the original noisy value is also needed for a clean-value estimate.

steps.title: Predict noise and score it during training
steps.prose: The denoiser receives the noisy value and time level. We assume its prediction equals the true noise only to make the arithmetic transparent. Comparing predicted and known noise gives a training loss; that loss value is not the input to the next estimate.
steps.terms: A noise prediction and its squared-error loss are different objects. The zero loss here is an assumption, not evidence of a trained system.
steps.next: Use the predicted noise, original noisy observation and noise level to estimate the clean value.

steps.title: Estimate a clean value
steps.prose: Rearrange the corruption equation using the noise prediction. A perfect prediction in this example recovers the original scalar. This one algebraic estimate is not a complete reverse diffusion sampler, which uses a specified sequence of denoising steps.
steps.terms: Sampling schedules and prediction parameterizations change a real generative procedure. An estimated x₀ is not itself a quality metric.
steps.next: The family-specific notes compare objectives, sampling costs and evaluation limitations.

steps.title: Encode distribution parameters
steps.prose: A VAE encoder outputs parameters of a distribution over latent codes rather than just one deterministic code. Our example assumes mean 0.5 and standard deviation 0.5. Those parameters support both sampling and a comparison with a prior distribution.
steps.terms: A latent distribution describes possible codes. The mean is its location; variance is squared standard deviation.
steps.next: Sample a code for decoding; separately use these parameters to calculate the prior penalty.

steps.title: Sample a differentiable code
steps.prose: Write the sample as mean plus scale times standard-normal noise. This separates randomness from the learned parameters so gradients can pass through the mean and scale. The selected noise draw is 1 for this arithmetic example.
steps.terms: Reparameterization expresses a random sample using parameter-free noise and differentiable transformations.
steps.next: The decoder receives this sampled code.

steps.title: Decode into an observation model
steps.prose: The decoder specifies how observations depend on the code. An image model might produce distribution parameters for pixel values. No trained decoder is present here, so no reconstruction image or numerical reconstruction quality is invented.
steps.terms: A likelihood is a probability or density assigned to observed data under the specified decoder. It depends on the observation model.
steps.next: The prior penalty is a separate branch from encoder parameters, not a calculation consuming the decoder's output.

steps.title: KL penalty and the complete VAE objective
steps.prose: Compare the encoded Gaussian distribution with a unit-normal prior using the displayed analytic KL term. This is only one part of the VAE objective: the other is expected negative log-likelihood of the observation. A small KL alone does not establish good reconstructions or samples.
steps.terms: KL divergence measures a specified distribution mismatch and is not generally symmetric. It is calculated here from the encoder's mean and variance.
steps.next: Compare both objective terms and generated-sample evaluation under an explicit protocol.

steps.title: Two input streams: noise and real data
steps.prose: Supply a noise sample for the generator and independent real observations for discriminator training. A generated sample does not need a particular paired real reconstruction target. These streams are separate inputs, not one being calculated from the other.
steps.terms: A prior supplies latent noise. The training-data distribution supplies observed real examples.
steps.next: Noise enters the generator; real observations enter the discriminator branch.

steps.title: Generator produces a candidate
steps.prose: The generator maps latent noise to a candidate observation. Training adjusts its parameters using an objective supplied through the discriminator. The diagram explains this mechanism; it does not execute an image generator.
steps.terms: The generator G is a learned mapping from noise to candidate samples.
steps.next: The same discriminator evaluates this candidate and real observations.

steps.title: Discriminator sees real examples
steps.prose: The discriminator also evaluates genuine observations from training data. This real branch is necessary to learn a real/fake distinction; a generator trained only on its own ungrounded outputs would not supply the same training signal.
steps.terms: A discriminator D assigns a score under its current learned rule, not an objective truth certificate.
steps.next: Compare real and generated discriminator scores under the chosen objective.

steps.title: Real and generated scores
steps.prose: Use the same discriminator on both kinds of input. The probabilities 0.9 for real and 0.8 for generated are authored values for loss arithmetic. As the models learn, these values and the quality of that distinction can change.
steps.terms: A real/fake score is specific to this adversarial setup. It is not directly comparable with reconstruction MSE or diffusion noise MSE.
steps.next: Each parameter set uses its own objective, calculated from these scores.

steps.title: Separate generator and discriminator losses
steps.prose: The non-saturating generator objective rewards a larger discriminator score for generated data. The discriminator objective rewards separating real and generated examples. Their parameter sets are updated separately, so these are not one shared loss minimized by both models.
steps.terms: Adversarial learning couples two changing objectives. Instability and collapse require evaluation beyond one displayed loss pair.
steps.next: The notes explain how these objectives differ from VAE regularization and diffusion denoising.

DL11.title: Graph neural networks
DL11.definition: A graph represents objects as nodes and relationships as edges. A graph neural network, or GNN, updates node features by collecting messages from connected neighbours. Its calculation therefore depends on both the feature values and which connections are present; merely listing nodes in a table would omit important information.
DL11.example: The graph is A—B—C, with scalar features [1,2,4]. We calculate B's update using mean or sum neighbour messages and its own feature. A separate readout section applies the same rule to all nodes and shows a whole-graph sum.
DL11.connection: CNNs share local filters on a regular image grid. Message-passing GNNs generalize local information exchange to an explicit graph; neighbour order should not arbitrarily change an invariant aggregation.

steps.title: Graph connections and original features
steps.prose: Node B is connected to A and C. This declared neighbour set does not include B itself; its own feature is added separately. A directed edge or explicit self-loop convention would describe a different calculation.
steps.terms: Nodes are objects with features; edges specify relationships or permitted message routes. All updates here use original states synchronously.
steps.next: Read neighbour features for B while preserving its own original feature.

steps.title: Messages from neighbours
steps.prose: A sends feature 1 and C sends feature 4 to B. These are identity messages in the small example; a learned GNN may transform neighbour features first. Do not overwrite A before C's update if all nodes are meant to use the same previous layer.
steps.terms: Synchronous updating uses one common old-state snapshot for a layer. It prevents node iteration order from changing results.
steps.next: Aggregate the two incoming messages using the selected rule.

steps.title: Mean or sum aggregation
steps.prose: Summing gives 5; taking their mean gives 2.5. Mean reduces direct dependence on neighbour count, while sum can retain information related to that count. Neither choice is universally better; it changes the model's assumptions.
steps.terms: A permutation-invariant aggregation is unaffected by the order in which the same messages are listed.
steps.next: Combine this summary with B's original feature.

steps.title: Update node B
steps.prose: Add B's original feature 2 to its neighbour summary, multiply by 0.5, then apply ReLU. This is the declared layer, not a universal GNN formula. Other networks use learned projections, normalized neighbours, concatenation or attention.
steps.terms: ReLU keeps the positive value here. Self information and neighbour information are separate inputs to the update.
steps.next: The next section is a separate graph-readout example, not another learned update to B.

steps.title: Separate node updates from graph readout
steps.prose: A node-level task can predict from each updated node. For a whole-graph task, first update all nodes with the same synchronous rule, then pool their representations. The fixed sum shown here adds A', B' and C'; it is independent of whether neighbour messages used mean or sum.
steps.terms: A graph readout produces one representation from a set of node features. Edge-level tasks need another appropriate head.
steps.next: The deeper notes discuss normalization, multi-layer reach and limitations without implying that one pooled number solves a graph task.

DL12.title: Prediction heads, targets and losses
DL12.definition: A prediction head maps learned features to the outputs a task needs. One class for a whole example, one label for each token, a numerical value and a segmentation map need different shapes and objectives. The head, target alignment, loss reduction and evaluation metric must agree with one another.
DL12.example: The hidden representation has shape [B,T,D] = [1,3,4]: one example, three positions and four features per position. Choose a target type to inspect its output shape and a separate authored score/loss calculation; no trained head is loaded.
DL12.connection: Earlier architectures produce features. This lesson connects those features to an actual prediction task without treating softmax as the right operation for every output. The shared metrics lesson explains general evaluation; a deeper note adds segmentation-specific IoU and Dice.

steps.title: What receives a target?
steps.prose: Decide whether the label belongs to the whole example, each valid position or a numerical measurement. Example-level classification usually summarizes positions first; token labelling preserves them. A span or structured target can require additional alignment or constraints.
steps.terms: B counts examples, T positions and D feature dimensions. These axes are not interchangeable just because their sizes match.
steps.next: Choose a projection whose output axes match the target unit.

steps.title: Projection and output dimensions
steps.prose: A task head transforms hidden features into the necessary scores or numbers. Three mutually exclusive classes require three scores at the relevant unit. Regression may require one number; token classification requires a class-score vector for every labelled token.
steps.terms: A head is a learned mapping. Pooling summarizes positions for an example-level target; it is not appropriate when each position needs its own label.
steps.next: Interpret these outputs according to the task before calculating a loss.

steps.title: Class probabilities or numerical values
steps.prose: For exclusive classes, softmax normalizes each unit's class scores. For regression, keep the numerical prediction instead of forcing it into a class probability. Independent binary labels would use a different probability/objective setup.
steps.terms: Logits are unnormalized class scores. Token softmax works across classes separately at each position.
steps.next: Compare the prediction with the aligned observed target using a suitable loss.

steps.title: Loss, valid positions and reduction
steps.prose: Choose the objective for the target type, then score only valid labelled positions. Padding and unlabelled positions may be excluded. The displayed token-classification arithmetic concerns one token; a full sequence objective needs an explicit aggregation over valid positions.
steps.terms: A loss mask controls scored targets and is different from an attention mask. A sum and a mean use different denominators.
steps.next: The retained task notes compare regression, multilabel, span and segmentation conventions before evaluation.

DL13.title: The neural training loop and its system state
DL13.definition: Training is a repeated procedure: fetch a batch, calculate predictions and loss, compute gradients and update trainable parameters. The data loader, device, optimizer state and checkpoint rules are part of that procedure, not extra neural-network layers. Validation checks a model without fitting on those cases; saving state makes selected results or later resumption possible.
DL13.example: We have 32 examples with 16 float32 features each. Change batch size to see input-memory bytes and updates per epoch under one-update-per-batch training. These calculations exclude other memory costs and do not launch a job.
DL13.connection: The earlier lessons explain individual model operations. Here we connect them to data movement, training/evaluation modes, gradient clearing, periodic validation and recoverable state.

steps.title: Fetch the next training batch
steps.prose: A data loader selects a batch and applies the declared training-data transformations. Its size controls how many examples are processed together. Multiplying input entries by bytes per value estimates input-tensor storage only, not the total memory needed to train.
steps.terms: A batch is a group of examples. An epoch is one pass over this finite training set; float32 uses four bytes per value.
steps.next: Move the batch and model to compatible devices/types before their forward calculation.

steps.title: Forward calculation and loss
steps.prose: Use the current parameters to compute predictions and compare them with training targets. Training mode can affect dropout and running statistics. Retain the operations needed for differentiation, but do not keep every old computation graph unnecessarily.
steps.terms: Device and numeric type must be compatible. CUDA is an NVIDIA backend; Apple MPS is a different backend, not a CUDA setting.
steps.next: The scalar training objective supplies the backward pass and optimizer update.

steps.title: Backward pass and parameter update
steps.prose: Clear old gradients for an independent batch update, or deliberately accumulate appropriately weighted microbatch contributions. Backward computes derivatives; the optimizer changes parameters and updates its own stored state. The next iteration fetches the next batch without resetting learned weights.
steps.terms: Gradient accumulation changes the update schedule. It does not mean every microbatch should be averaged equally when valid-target counts differ.
steps.next: Continue with the next batch; at chosen intervals, separately evaluate current weights on validation data.

steps.title: Periodic validation and checkpoints
steps.prose: Switch mode appropriately and evaluate separate validation cases without optimizer updates. Use the declared validation rule to choose a checkpoint. For resumption, save optimizer/progress/random/sampler state as needed, not only model weights; then restore training mode before continuing.
steps.terms: A selected inference checkpoint and an exactly resumable training checkpoint have different state requirements.
steps.next: The system notes explain accumulation denominators, device limits, serving and which runtime features are actually implemented.
