DL14.title: Compare neural and classical models
DL14.definition: A useful neural-model experiment asks whether it improves a real outcome over a strong classical alternative. Both candidates need the same target definition and held-out evaluation cases. Their preprocessing and fitting procedures may differ, but each must use legitimate training information and a declared selection budget.
DL14.example: The worked comparison uses hypothetical final scores 0.82 and 0.80 to illustrate a difference of 0.02. They are not measured evidence that deep learning wins. The actual lab's saved results keep their own dataset, protocol and configuration information.
DL14.connection: The ML capstone defined a complete experiment. This DL capstone applies that plan to a cross-family comparison, including tuning effort, errors, uncertainty and compute cost rather than just architecture labels.

steps.title: Common task, split and metric
steps.prose: State what each candidate predicts, which inputs it may use and how its result is measured. Evaluate the final candidates on the same held-out row IDs or independent groups. Different target units or label definitions would answer different questions.
steps.terms: Matched evaluation means compatible task and test evidence, not identical internal architecture or preprocessing.
steps.next: Develop the classical and neural candidates under the same data boundaries.

steps.title: Fit a strong classical baseline
steps.prose: Give the classical pipeline suitable preprocessing and a reasonable validation search over its own settings. A poorly tuned baseline does not establish that a more complex model was necessary. Save the selected procedure, not just its best-looking score.
steps.terms: Relevant settings depend on the family: ridge strength, neighbour count and tree depth do not have interchangeable numeric meanings.
steps.next: Develop the neural candidate separately; one candidate is not a processing stage of the other.

steps.title: Fit and select the neural candidate
steps.prose: Architecture width, optimizer settings, training duration and checkpoint selection all use development evidence. Record the compute/search budget and respect the same held-out boundaries. Equal epochs are not automatically equal cost across architectures.
steps.terms: Selection includes a checkpoint chosen by validation performance. The test set must not choose architecture or stopping time.
steps.next: Compare the frozen selected candidates on shared held-out outcomes.
steps.node: Fit and select the neural candidate

steps.title: Paired errors, uncertainty and cost
steps.prose: Measure both systems on the same cases, inspect disagreements and report the score difference. Use appropriate independent-unit resampling for test uncertainty and separate repeated seeds for training variation. Include latency, memory or other costs relevant to the use case.
steps.terms: Paired comparison keeps the same sampled cases for both systems. A confidence interval does not undo test-based selection.
steps.next: A defensible result can favour the classical model or find no clear gain; useful evidence does not require a neural-model victory.

P6.title: Language, tokens and model inputs
P6.definition: Natural language processing, or NLP, builds systems that analyze or produce human language. A model first needs a numerical input: tokenization splits text into chosen units, and a vocabulary assigns each unit an integer ID. These units are not necessarily words, and the IDs do not represent meaning by their numerical size.
P6.example: We split the words 'low' and 'lower' into characters, then apply two supplied merge rules. The controls show how pieces, sequence length and IDs change. These rules are a small demonstration, not a tokenizer trained on a real corpus.
P6.connection: The shared foundations explained vectors and prediction targets. This lesson explains how text becomes the discrete inputs for those calculations; the following NLP lessons define what a system should predict from them.

steps.title: Text and initial pieces
steps.prose: Start from two separate words, low and lower. In this simplified example each character is a piece, giving eight pieces in total. Real tokenizers also specify how to handle spaces, bytes, normalization and special markers.
steps.terms: A token is a tokenizer-defined piece. A vocabulary lists permitted pieces; a word boundary and a document boundary are not the same thing.
steps.next: Apply the supplied ordered merge rules within each word.

steps.title: Combine adjacent pieces
steps.prose: The first rule joins l and o; the second can join lo and w. Applying more rules shortens this particular sequence. The rules are fixed before this demonstration; a real BPE training algorithm learns rules from corpus counts.
steps.terms: Byte-pair encoding, or BPE, learns ordered merges. Applying saved rules to new text is tokenization, not training the tokenizer again.
steps.next: Map the resulting pieces through a vocabulary to obtain integer IDs.

steps.title: Convert pieces to token IDs
steps.prose: Each piece is assigned an integer that selects its vocabulary entry. Here the mapping is rebuilt in first-occurrence order only to make the tiny example readable. A real model requires its saved mapping, unchanged between inputs.
steps.terms: An ID is a name for a row, not an ordered semantic feature. The embedding layer later looks up a vector using this ID.
steps.next: Use the ID sequence to illustrate how next-token targets are constructed.

steps.title: Shift the sequence to make prediction targets
steps.prose: For a causal next-token task, each input position is paired with the following token as its target. The last item is therefore a target without a following input in this slice. This is one possible NLP objective, not the target for every text task.
steps.terms: Causal prediction uses earlier tokens to predict a successor. Source boundaries, special tokens and target masks must be defined for a real corpus.
steps.next: The next lesson defines task outputs; the deeper notes explain templates, truncation and tokenizer comparisons.

links: Apply saved merge rules to the initial character sequences.

P7.title: Embeddings, similarity and retrieval
P7.definition: An embedding represents an object, such as a token, sentence or document, as a numerical vector. A retrieval system compares a query with candidate documents and returns a ranked list. Vector similarity can help find related text, but it does not establish that the text answers the question or supports a claim.
P7.example: The query vector is [1,0]. Document A is [0.8,0.6] and document B is [0,1]. All have length one, so their dot products give cosine similarities of 0.8 and 0. Selecting top one or top two changes the returned list, not the scores.
P7.connection: Token IDs identify discrete pieces; embeddings supply numerical representations on which models and search systems can operate. This lesson introduces retrieval geometry before later lessons compare how lexical and neural encoders learn their representations.

steps.title: Use compatible query and document vectors
steps.prose: The three supplied vectors share two coordinates and the same representation space. Each has Euclidean length one. Real query and document encoders must be designed to produce comparable vectors; equal dimension alone does not ensure compatibility.
steps.terms: A vector norm measures its length. Unit normalization rescales a nonzero vector to length one without changing its direction.
steps.next: Compare the query with each eligible document using a stated similarity rule.

steps.title: Calculate cosine similarity
steps.prose: Multiply matching coordinates, add the products and divide by both vector lengths. Since the supplied vectors are already normalized, the denominator is one. A receives score 0.8 and B receives score zero.
steps.terms: Cosine measures direction alignment. It can be negative and is not a probability that a document is relevant, true or supportive.
steps.next: Order the eligible documents by these scores and select the requested number.

steps.title: Return the top eligible documents
steps.prose: The control changes how many candidates are kept. It does not improve their representations or recompute the similarity rule. Apply permissions before exposing results; a highly similar document is not automatically an authorized one.
steps.terms: Top-k means the k highest-ranked eligible items. Retrieval candidates are proposed evidence, not verified answers.
steps.next: Read the candidates to determine whether they actually address the question.

steps.title: Check relevance and source support
steps.prose: Finding nearby text and checking its meaning are different tasks. A passage can share topic words while denying the proposed answer. Inspect the claim, negation, quantities and qualifications instead of treating the similarity score as a truth check.
steps.terms: Relevance concerns usefulness for a question; source support concerns whether a particular claim follows from the passage.
steps.next: The later encoder comparison explains caching and reranking; the shared metrics lesson defines retrieval evaluation.

links: Use the shared vector coordinates to compute query–document similarity.
Rank eligible documents by their scores, then keep the selected top-k.

N01.title: NLP tasks and annotation guidelines
N01.definition: An NLP task specifies what a system must predict from language: a document label, a token tag, an answer span, a relation or a generated sequence. Annotation guidelines explain what each label means and which context may be used. A task name such as sentiment or argument identification is not enough to define the correct answer.
N01.example: For 'not good', sentence sentiment asks for one negative label; token tagging asks for labels aligned to individual words. We also compare four binary annotations from two people to see how agreement depends on their label usage.
N01.connection: After deciding how text is represented, decide what counts as a correct output. The same text can support different tasks or guidelines, so this choice must come before classifier architecture and score comparisons.

steps.title: Define the prediction unit and allowed context
steps.prose: Write down what one answer refers to and what evidence the system may read. One sentiment label for a sentence is not one tag per word. Including a preceding conversation can change the available evidence without changing the sentence itself.
steps.terms: A prediction unit is the object receiving an output. A guideline operationalizes a label by defining positive, negative and uncertain cases.
steps.next: Have annotators apply the written policy independently before resolving disagreements.
steps.node: Define the prediction unit and allowed context

steps.title: Measure observed annotation agreement
steps.prose: Annotator A assigns [1,1,0,0] and B assigns [1,1,1,0], so they agree on three of four cases. This describes consistency, not whether the task captures the intended meaning. Discussing answers first would hide the independent disagreement.
steps.terms: Observed agreement is matching labels divided by compared cases. Adjudication chooses a final label after independent annotation.
steps.next: Account for how often each annotator uses each class before interpreting adjusted agreement.

steps.title: Interpret chance-adjusted agreement
steps.prose: A uses each class twice; B uses class 1 three times and class 0 once. Cohen's kappa compares their observed agreement with an expectation from those frequencies, yielding 0.5 here. Prevalence and annotation design affect its interpretation; it is not a universal quality grade.
steps.terms: Marginals are each annotator's class frequencies. Kappa adjusts against their expected agreement, not against a known perfect annotation.
steps.next: Keep the original labels and policy alongside the resolved dataset, rather than saving only one agreement score.

steps.title: Record the policy and independent sources
steps.prose: Save source identifiers, permitted context, policy version and labels separately. Related sentences from one document may share wording or author clues, so splitting them independently can exaggerate generalization. Use the true source grouping when appropriate.
steps.terms: A source group collects examples that must remain together for the intended evaluation. Policy changes alter the target, not merely model settings.
steps.next: The next lesson examines text transformations that can accidentally remove the evidence required by this policy.
steps.node: Record the policy and independent sources

N02.title: Text processing, morphology and source offsets
N02.definition: Text processing changes how language is represented before a model uses it. Normalization, stemming, lemmatization and subword tokenization perform different jobs and may discard different information. Extraction tasks also need a reliable map back to the original text so that a predicted name or answer can be located exactly.
N02.example: The original string is 'not good'. Its word spans are [0,3) and [4,8), using zero-based character positions and an exclusive end. Removing 'not' changes the sentiment; it is not harmless cleanup even though the remaining string is shorter.
N02.connection: An annotation policy defines which distinctions matter. Preprocessing must preserve those distinctions and the required source anchors before feature extraction, token tagging or span evaluation can be trusted.

steps.title: Keep original text and offset conventions
steps.prose: Keep the original string as the reference for extracted spans. In this example slicing positions zero up to but excluding three returns not. The separator space belongs to neither word. Record which indexing convention an implementation uses.
steps.terms: An offset locates a position in a particular string. Character/code-point, byte, UTF-16 and subword positions are different coordinate systems.
steps.next: Decide which transformations are permitted while retaining a mapping to the source.
steps.node: Keep original text and offset conventions

steps.title: Check whether a transformation changes meaning
steps.prose: Compare the two control settings on the same phrase. Keeping not preserves the negative statement; deleting it leaves good and removes the relevant evidence. A transformation is useful only relative to a task and its invariances.
steps.terms: Normalization changes form under a chosen policy. A label-preserving transformation must retain the meaning that determines the task label.
steps.next: Distinguish linguistic word analysis from the model's encoding units before applying either.
steps.node: Check whether a transformation changes meaning

steps.title: Distinguish lemmas, stems and subword pieces
steps.prose: A lemma aims to identify a dictionary form, often using grammatical context. A stemmer uses simpler stripping rules. A tokenizer might instead split running into pieces to fit its vocabulary; those pieces are not necessarily a linguistic analysis.
steps.terms: Morphology concerns word formation and grammatical features. Subword segmentation is an encoding choice, not proof of morphological structure.
steps.next: When one labelled word becomes several model pieces, choose how supervision and evaluation stay aligned.
steps.node: Distinguish lemmas, stems and subword pieces

steps.title: Align word labels and model pieces
steps.prose: If a word becomes three pieces, do not count three independently correct entities. One policy scores the first piece and ignores the rest in the loss; another propagates tags under a specified scheme. Recover original words or spans before task evaluation.
steps.terms: An ignored loss position contributes no target to the objective. BIO tags encode entity boundaries and require a declared propagation rule.
steps.next: The next lesson builds lexical features from processed text while keeping their vocabulary and fitting boundary explicit.
steps.node: Align word labels and model pieces

N03.title: Word counts, TF-IDF and lexical retrieval
N03.definition: A bag-of-words representation gives each vocabulary term a feature column and counts its occurrences in a document. TF-IDF weights those counts using term frequency and inverse document frequency, reducing the relative influence of terms that occur across many documents. This supplies sparse features for classification or lexical search without learning contextual word meaning.
N03.example: Our corpus contains 'cat sat', 'cat slept' and 'dog sat'. The vocabulary has four columns. Cat occurs in two documents and dog in one, so dog receives a larger rarity weight under the displayed smoothed IDF rule.
N03.connection: Once text has been processed consistently, counts provide a transparent first representation. These features can feed the text classifiers in the next lesson or support lexical retrieval, offering a baseline before neural encoders.

steps.title: Create a fixed vocabulary and count columns
steps.prose: Each document becomes a row with one column per known term. The first document has counts [1,0,1,0] in the stated vocabulary order. Fit the vocabulary on training data for a held-out classification study, then reuse it unchanged.
steps.terms: Sparse means most entries are zero. A vocabulary column must keep the same term meaning across training and evaluation rows.
steps.next: Count how many training documents contain each term to obtain its rarity statistic.

steps.title: Count documents containing the term
steps.prose: Document frequency counts containing documents, not the total number of token repetitions. The term control selects which column to inspect; it does not change the corpus. Cat appears in two documents, while dog appears in one.
steps.terms: Document frequency, written df, counts documents containing a term. Repeating a word ten times in one document still contributes one to df.
steps.next: Combine raw term counts with inverse document frequency and the chosen normalization.

steps.title: Calculate TF-IDF and normalize each row
steps.prose: The displayed rule uses a smoothed logarithmic rarity weight, multiplies it by raw counts and rescales each nonzero row to unit length. Read the matrix as documents by terms. Other TF-IDF conventions can produce different values.
steps.terms: TF is term frequency; IDF is inverse document frequency. N counts training documents and df counts containing documents. L2 normalization divides a vector by its Euclidean length.
steps.next: Use the resulting feature rows in a declared classifier or similarity computation.

steps.title: Choose a downstream scoring method
steps.prose: TF-IDF is a representation, not a complete prediction system. A classifier learns how its columns relate to labels; retrieval uses a matching rule. BM25 is another lexical scoring family with frequency saturation and document-length adjustment.
steps.terms: A retrieval score ranks matching evidence; it is not a calibrated relevance probability. BM25 and TF-IDF are different formulas.
steps.next: The next lesson compares how Naive Bayes and logistic regression turn lexical features into class scores.

links: Count which training document rows contain each vocabulary term.

N04.title: Naive Bayes and linear text classifiers
N04.definition: A text classifier turns a feature representation into a task label. Multinomial Naive Bayes combines class-specific word probabilities; logistic regression combines learned feature weights into a conditional class score. Both can use simple lexical features, but they estimate different quantities and should be evaluated rather than ranked by their complexity.
N04.example: The phrase 'good good bad' becomes the count vector [2,1]. We compare supplied positive/negative token counts with a fixed logistic weight vector. Switching models demonstrates their arithmetic; it does not train them or establish which is more accurate.
N04.connection: The previous lesson constructed sparse document features. This lesson attaches a class-prediction rule and shows why a baseline includes fitted parameters, preprocessing and independent evaluation—not simply a small architecture.

steps.title: Represent the sentence with counts
steps.prose: Count two occurrences of good and one of bad in the fixed vocabulary. The resulting feature vector has two coordinates. It preserves repetition but loses word order, so it cannot directly distinguish all phrases that contain the same words.
steps.terms: Bag-of-words counts describe token occurrences. A feature vector is not yet a prediction or a normalized probability distribution.
steps.next: Combine the sentence features with the selected model's supplied parameters.

steps.title: Specify the model parameters
steps.prose: Naive Bayes uses class priors and smoothed token probabilities. The logistic alternative uses coefficients [1,−1] and zero bias. These quantities are supplied for transparency; fitting them from data is a separate operation.
steps.terms: A prior describes class frequency before reading features. In the NB equation, c is a class, w a token, V vocabulary size and alpha a pseudocount strength.
steps.next: Calculate the selected model's class evidence from the sentence counts and parameters.

steps.title: Calculate class scores and probabilities
steps.prose: Naive Bayes adds count-weighted log probabilities to the class prior, then normalizes across classes. Logistic regression applies a sigmoid to its weighted feature sum. Keep these mechanisms distinct rather than treating their coefficients as interchangeable.
steps.terms: Conditional independence is the Naive Bayes modelling assumption given the class. A sigmoid maps a scalar score to a value between zero and one.
steps.next: Test the fitted pipeline on independent texts before interpreting it as a useful baseline.

steps.title: Evaluate the complete baseline
steps.prose: A lexical model should be compared with a majority predictor and justified alternatives on the same held-out cases. Examine negation, boilerplate and author markers. Good-looking supplied probabilities do not provide evidence of generalization.
steps.terms: Macro-F1, calibration and error slices answer different evaluation questions. Use their shared definitions rather than training accuracy alone.
steps.next: The next lesson uses counts for a different target: predicting the next token instead of a class label.

links: Sentence feature counts weight the selected model's class-evidence calculation.

N05.title: N-gram language models and smoothing
N05.definition: A language model assigns probabilities to text sequences, often by predicting each token from an earlier history. An n-gram model restricts that history to the previous n−1 tokens. Smoothing adjusts count estimates so that unseen continuations can receive probability rather than making an entire held-out sequence impossible.
N05.example: After 'like', the training counts are cats twice and dogs once. There are seven permitted next-token items, including an unknown token. Change the continuation and smoothing strength to see both its probability and negative log-likelihood change.
N05.connection: Text classification predicts labels; this lesson predicts the next token from counts. It introduces the same conditional-probability target that later recurrent and large language models learn with richer representations.

steps.title: Fix the history and next-token vocabulary
steps.prose: This bigram example conditions only on like. Its vocabulary has seven possible continuations, so every probability must be normalized over those same seven items. A truly new token maps to the saved unknown entry before scoring.
steps.terms: A bigram uses one preceding token. An unknown-token symbol collects inputs outside a saved vocabulary under its mapping policy.
steps.next: Use the selected continuation's count and the common vocabulary size in the probability estimate.

steps.title: Estimate a smoothed continuation probability
steps.prose: Add alpha to the selected token's observed count and add seven alpha to the history total. Probability is redistributed over all vocabulary items, not only unseen ones. Setting alpha to zero returns the unsmoothed count estimate.
steps.terms: Alpha is a pseudocount strength. Increasing it moves this distribution toward uniformity over the fixed vocabulary.
steps.next: Score the observed continuation using its negative log-probability.

steps.title: Calculate the prediction loss
steps.prose: A high assigned probability gives a smaller penalty for the observed token. A zero probability gives infinite negative log-likelihood, not zero loss. The display reports that boundary explicitly when an unseen continuation has no smoothing.
steps.terms: Negative log-likelihood is the prediction penalty in nats when natural logs are used. Sequence evaluation combines declared token events.
steps.next: Compare alternative count-model estimators only after fixing their histories and evaluation units.

steps.title: Compare backoff, interpolation and discounting
steps.prose: Longer histories may be more informative but have fewer observations. Backoff consults shorter contexts, interpolation mixes estimates, and Kneser–Ney uses discounted counts with continuation evidence. None is just a renamed add-alpha formula.
steps.terms: A smoothing family defines a full estimation procedure. Document boundaries, unknown handling and score reduction are part of the language model.
steps.next: Static word vectors next learn representations from context pairs rather than directly estimating this count table.

links: Use the selected history count and fixed vocabulary to estimate a normalized distribution.
Take the negative logarithm of the probability assigned to the observed token.

N06.title: Static word vectors: Word2vec, GloVe and fastText
N06.definition: A static word embedding assigns a reusable numerical vector to a word or lexical unit. Word2vec, GloVe and fastText learn these vectors from different forms of corpus evidence. Nearby vectors can capture useful regularities, but the same static lookup does not change meaning according to the sentence in which a word appears.
N06.example: The worked example uses one centre word, one observed context word and one sampled negative. It calculates their compatibility scores and a negative-sampling loss from supplied vectors. No word vectors are trained when you select the explanation.
N06.connection: Lexical counts keep explicit vocabulary columns. Word embeddings instead learn a compact shared feature space, preparing the transition to text CNNs and recurrent models that operate on sequences of vectors.

steps.title: Form observed and sampled word pairs
steps.prose: Skip-gram treats a centre word and nearby context word as a positive training pair. It also samples alternatives as negative pairs. The two embedding tables can represent centre and context roles separately; the chosen sampling distribution matters.
steps.terms: A positive pair is observed under the context-window rule. A sampled negative is a training contrast, not a claim that two words can never be related.
steps.next: Calculate a compatibility score for each pair using the supplied vectors.

steps.title: Score the positive and negative pairs
steps.prose: A dot product adds the coordinate-wise products of the centre and context vectors. The positive score here is 0.5 and the sampled-negative score is zero. These are compatibility scores, not similarities already calibrated for an external task.
steps.terms: A dot product is an unnormalized vector comparison. Negative sampling uses its score in a binary training objective.
steps.next: Penalize low positive compatibility and high sampled-negative compatibility.

steps.title: Calculate the negative-sampling loss
steps.prose: The positive term rewards a high sigmoid score for the observed pair; the negative term rewards a low score for the sampled pair. Their negative log terms add into one loss. Training would differentiate that objective to change the vectors.
steps.terms: SGNS means skip-gram with negative sampling. Sigmoid maps a compatibility score to a value between zero and one; the displayed log-loss uses natural logarithms.
steps.next: Compare other lexical-vector objectives without presenting them as additional operations on this loss.

steps.title: Compare lexical-vector families
steps.prose: CBOW predicts a centre from surrounding words, GloVe fits weighted co-occurrence relations, and fastText includes character n-gram information. Static bank still has one lookup representation here whether the sentence concerns a river or finance.
steps.terms: A contextual representation changes with the occurrence's surrounding text. A static representation is reused under a fixed lexical lookup policy.
steps.next: The next lesson learns local sequence patterns from these kinds of token features.

links: Read the centre/context vectors for each observed or sampled training pair.
Apply the positive and negative sigmoid log-loss terms to the pair scores.

N07.title: Convolutional networks for text
N07.definition: A text convolutional neural network applies shared filters to nearby positions in a sequence. A filter can detect local patterns across token embeddings or characters, and pooling summarizes responses for a larger unit such as a sentence. Local feature extraction and sentence-level aggregation are separate operations with different information losses.
N07.example: Three scalar token features [1,−1,2] pass through the same width-two filter [0.5,−0.5]. Two responses are produced, then ReLU removes negative responses. Switch max and mean pooling to see how the sentence feature changes while the filter stays fixed.
N07.connection: Static embeddings represent individual tokens; a text CNN combines neighbouring tokens into learned local patterns. The shared DL convolution lesson explains spatial mechanics, while this lesson focuses on language sequence axes and pooling.

steps.title: Arrange token features in sequence order
steps.prose: Each sequence position has an embedding feature vector. Our tiny example uses just one feature per token so the arithmetic is visible. A width-two filter reads two adjacent positions, giving two valid windows from three tokens without padding.
steps.terms: The token axis records order; the feature axis records coordinates per token. A real temporal filter spans its input feature channels.
steps.next: Apply the same filter weights to both local windows.

steps.title: Reuse one filter across local windows
steps.prose: Multiply each window's features by [0.5,−0.5] and add. The resulting signed responses differ because the inputs differ, not because each location has separate filter parameters. Real text CNNs can use many filters and widths.
steps.terms: Weight sharing reuses one parameter set across positions. In the equation, x is the input feature, k the filter weight and z the response at position t; valid convolution adds no padding.
steps.next: Apply the nonlinearity, then summarize the valid response locations.

steps.title: Apply ReLU and sentence pooling
steps.prose: ReLU keeps positive responses and replaces negative ones with zero. Max pooling keeps the strongest surviving response; mean pooling averages them. Both compress the position axis, so neither retained scalar specifies where the pattern occurred.
steps.terms: Pooling aggregates locations rather than learning a new token order. Invalid padded windows need deliberate masking in a real model.
steps.next: A task head can use the pooled features to learn a label-prediction rule.

steps.title: Choose where the convolution belongs
steps.prose: A word-level CNN can supply sentence features; a character CNN can instead build word features before another token encoder. These are different architectures. The displayed filter is fixed, so its response is not a trained classification result.
steps.terms: A prediction head maps representations to task outputs. Local receptive field size limits which interactions one convolution can directly combine.
steps.next: Recurrent models next provide a different sequence mechanism by carrying state between positions.

links: Slide the same width-two filter over both valid token windows.
Transform local responses with ReLU, then aggregate over valid positions.

N08.title: Recurrent and bidirectional recurrent networks
N08.definition: A recurrent neural network, or RNN, processes a sequence by updating a hidden state at each position. The state combines the current token with information carried from earlier positions. A bidirectional RNN adds a separate right-to-left pass, allowing each aligned token representation to use both sides of an already available input.
N08.example: We use three scalar inputs [1,0,−1] and one hidden feature per direction. The forward and reverse passes have different supplied weights. Select a token to inspect its aligned states, or switch to forward-only mode to remove future-context access.
N08.connection: A text CNN reads local windows. An RNN reuses a transition along the sequence instead; bidirectionality changes which input context is available, not how backpropagation computes gradients during training.

steps.title: Set sequence order and directional parameters
steps.prose: The forward pass reads left to right. The optional backward pass reads the same inputs in reverse using another parameter set, then realigns outputs to the original positions. Both begin from a zero boundary state in this example.
steps.terms: Bidirectional refers to two forward computations through input order. It is not the backward differentiation pass used for learning.
steps.next: Compute the forward and optional reverse states as independent branches.

steps.title: Update the forward hidden state
steps.prose: At the selected position, multiply the current input and preceding hidden state by their weights, add and apply tanh. The same weights are reused at each time step. This state alone cannot read later input positions.
steps.terms: A hidden state is a fixed-width carried representation. Parameter sharing across time differs from having a different layer's weights at every token.
steps.next: If the whole sentence is available, compare the reverse-direction state for the same original token.

steps.title: Update the reverse-direction state
steps.prose: The reverse pass summarizes suffix context using its own parameters. Its state at original position t comes from processing positions to the right first. Forward-only mode omits this branch; its formula is not an additional operation then executed.
steps.terms: A reverse state must be aligned back to the original token index. It would expose forbidden future information in causal next-token prediction.
steps.next: Combine only the directional states that belong to the same original position.

steps.title: Concatenate aligned token states
steps.prose: Joining the forward and reverse states creates two feature channels per token, not two tokens. In forward-only mode there is just one channel. Concatenation preserves both values; it is not an average or an agreement vote.
steps.terms: Output width is hidden width times the number of directions. Sequence length remains unchanged by bidirectionality.
steps.next: Choose separately whether a downstream task needs token outputs or terminal sentence states.

steps.title: Choose token outputs or terminal summaries
steps.prose: The last aligned token output is generally not the complete bidirectional terminal summary. This example combines forward-last with backward-first for that summary. Padding and valid lengths must be respected before selecting either state.
steps.terms: The terminal reverse state is aligned with the first valid original token. Pooling and terminal selection are different representation choices.
steps.next: LSTMs next change the state-update mechanism while retaining this distinction between time direction and output alignment.

N09.title: LSTMs and bidirectional LSTMs
N09.definition: A long short-term memory network, or LSTM, is a recurrent model with a cell state for carried memory and a hidden state exposed to other layers. Gates determine how much old memory to retain, new information to write and memory to expose. A bidirectional LSTM uses two independent such recurrences when both input directions are available.
N09.example: The scalar cell uses inputs [1,0,−1], fixed input/output gates and a selectable forget gate. Inspect one position to see its previous memory, candidate, new cell and hidden output. A second direction changes the representation width, not the sequence length.
N09.connection: An ordinary RNN repeatedly transforms its carried state. LSTM adds an additive gated memory path to address some training difficulties; the earlier rules for bidirectional alignment, padding and terminal summaries still apply.

steps.title: Read the token and both previous states
steps.prose: An LSTM receives the current input plus the preceding hidden state h and memory cell c. These states have different roles, even when they have the same width. The selected position shows their actual values from the fixed forward trace.
steps.terms: The cell carries memory; the hidden state is its gated exposed output. State variables are activations, not the model's learned weights.
steps.next: Use the input and previous hidden state to determine gates and candidate information.

steps.title: Calculate gates and a candidate
steps.prose: Forget, input and output gates control different routes. Here their values are deliberately fixed by biases so the effect is easy to follow; a general trained cell makes them depend on input and previous hidden features. The candidate uses tanh.
steps.terms: A gate scales a contribution, usually elementwise between zero and one. A candidate is proposed content before the write gate is applied.
steps.next: Combine retained old cell content with the gated candidate to form the new memory.

steps.title: Retain and write memory
steps.prose: The new cell adds two contributions: forget-gated old memory and input-gated candidate. Increasing the forget value retains more of this old cell, but does not guarantee that it contains useful long-distance information or that training succeeds.
steps.terms: The additive memory path differs from simply replacing the whole state. Elementwise multiplication gates each feature in a wider cell.
steps.next: Expose a gated transform of the new cell as the current hidden output.

steps.title: Produce the hidden output
steps.prose: Apply tanh to the new cell and multiply by the output gate. This does not replace or erase the cell. Both h and c continue to the next position, while h can also feed a token-level task head or another layer.
steps.terms: The cell itself is not restricted to the tanh output range. Hidden output and stored cell therefore need not have equal numerical values.
steps.next: For a complete sentence, optionally align a second directional hidden stream.

steps.title: Align directions for the downstream task
steps.prose: A BiLSTM concatenates forward and reverse hidden features at matching original positions. Its terminal sentence summary is selected differently from the last aligned token output. A streaming system cannot use an unseen sentence suffix this way.
steps.terms: Bidirectional LSTM has separate parameters and boundary states per direction. Token outputs and terminal states are distinct tensors.
steps.next: The next lesson compares a simpler gated recurrence with one carried hidden state and no separate cell.

links: Use current input and previous hidden state to calculate candidate/gates.
Carry the previous memory cell along the retention path.

Combine forget-gated old memory with input-gated candidate information.
The output gate controls how much transformed new memory is exposed.

N10.title: GRUs and recurrent training
N10.definition: A gated recurrent unit, or GRU, controls a recurrent hidden state without a separate LSTM memory cell. The reset gate controls old-state information used in the candidate; the update gate mixes the candidate with the old state. The exact gate convention and reset placement must be read from the equation, because implementations can differ.
N10.example: The inputs are [1,0,−1]. We hold the old-state mixture weight z at 0.25 and change the reset value. The example uses PyTorch's reset-after-projection convention; a separate matrix-and-bias check demonstrates why placement matters.
N10.connection: LSTM introduced gated memory and exposed hidden state. GRU merges these into one carried state, while the same choices about directions, padding, gradient history and sequence summaries remain separate training decisions.

steps.title: Read the token and previous hidden state
steps.prose: The GRU carries h but no separate cell c. In the displayed convention, update gate z weights the old hidden state; one minus z weights the candidate. The reset gate affects how the old state contributes to that candidate.
steps.terms: Reset and update are distinct gates. A gate name alone is insufficient when two sources use opposite update-mixture conventions.
steps.next: Form a candidate from the current input and reset-controlled recurrent contribution.

steps.title: Calculate the reset-controlled candidate
steps.prose: Project the old hidden state, multiply that recurrent contribution by reset, add the input contribution and apply tanh. Reset zero removes the recurrent candidate contribution here, but does not remove the old-state bypass into the final mixture.
steps.terms: PyTorch applies reset after the recurrent affine transformation. With matrices and biases this need not equal resetting the raw state before projection.
steps.next: Mix the proposed candidate with the preserved old state under the displayed update equation.

steps.title: Mix the candidate and old state
steps.prose: Use 0.75 times the candidate plus 0.25 times the old state. Changing reset affects the candidate and therefore this new state; z remains fixed. A larger z would retain more old state under this convention, not write more candidate.
steps.terms: A complementary mixture uses weights z and one minus z. Both routes remain differentiable under the stated cell computation.
steps.next: Repeat the recurrence along the input; choose directions and gradient-history boundaries separately.

steps.title: Choose directions and gradient history
steps.prose: A second GRU direction supplies suffix context using another parameter set. Detaching carried state instead cuts how far a training gradient reaches into earlier steps; it does not create a reverse input pass. Resetting state between independent documents is another choice.
steps.terms: Backpropagation through time, or BPTT, differentiates through repeated state updates. Truncation limits its history; clipping limits gradient magnitude.
steps.next: Encoder–decoder models next use sequence representations to condition generation of another sequence.

links: Use input and the reset-controlled recurrent projection to propose a candidate.
Preserve the old hidden state for its update-gated mixture contribution.
bypass
Weight the candidate by one minus z and add the old-state contribution.

N11.title: Encoder–decoder models, attention and beam search
N11.definition: An encoder–decoder model represents an input sequence and generates a separate output sequence. Attention lets a decoder read different source positions while producing each target token. Beam search is a decoding procedure that keeps several candidate target prefixes; it changes the search, not the learned model weights or the definition of attention.
N11.example: First we mix source values [1,2,4] using supplied attention weights to obtain context value 2. Separately, a two-token search tree shows greedy choosing a x with probability 0.30 while beam width two can keep b y with probability 0.38.
N11.connection: Recurrent encoders supply sequence states; an encoder–decoder uses source states to support another sequence's predictions. Distinguish source conditioning from candidate search before considering translation and other generation tasks.

steps.title: Separate source and target-prefix streams
steps.prose: The source contains information to condition on; the target prefix contains only permitted earlier generated or supplied target tokens. A source length of three and target-prefix length of two therefore create different attention axes.
steps.terms: Cross-attention uses target queries and source keys/values. Causal target visibility prevents future target answers from entering a prediction.
steps.next: Encode the source and keep the decoder's permitted target prefix as a separate input.

steps.title: Encode the source sequence
steps.prose: The encoder can read the complete supplied source while retaining its valid-position mask. Its states can remain available while target generation grows. The numerical example supplies three scalar source values rather than executing a trained encoder.
steps.terms: Source memory means representations available to the decoder, not persistent memory across unrelated user sessions.
steps.next: Let a decoder query read a weighted combination of these source values.

steps.title: Read source memory with attention
steps.prose: The supplied weights sum to one and mix the three source values into context value 2. A learned decoder normally obtains weights from query–key scores. The example isolates the mixing step without pretending to run complete translation.
steps.terms: In the equation a_tj is the attention weight on source position j for target step t, and v_j is its value. The weighted sum supplies one context feature.
steps.next: The next two sections separately demonstrate how a search procedure selects target sequences.

steps.title: Keep candidate output prefixes
steps.prose: At the first output step the fixed tree assigns a probability of 0.6 to a and 0.4 to b. Greedy keeps only a; beam width two keeps both. These probabilities are supplied independently of the attention-mixing example above.
steps.terms: A hypothesis is a candidate output prefix. Beam width caps the retained set; it does not modify parameters or make outputs truthful.
steps.next: Extend only the retained prefixes and compare their full equal-length probabilities.

steps.title: Extend and compare complete candidates
steps.prose: Multiply each retained prefix probability by its continuation probability. Greedy resolves its a x/a y tie in favor of x, scoring 0.30; beam two can find b y at 0.38. There is no end-of-sequence rule or length penalty in this fixed-length fixture.
steps.terms: Search score and usefulness are different concepts. Real beam search must specify stopping, length normalization and pruning choices.
steps.next: The sequence-labelling lesson next scores complete tag paths rather than generated token strings.

links: Encode the supplied source sequence while preserving its valid positions.
The permitted decoder target prefix supplies the query side of attention.
bypass
Source representations supply the keys and values read by the decoder.
