N12.title: Sequence labelling with HMMs, CRFs and Viterbi
N12.definition: Sequence labelling assigns a tag to each position while allowing neighboring tags to influence one another. A hidden Markov model, or HMM, uses probabilities for hidden transitions and observed emissions; a conditional random field, or CRF, uses scores to model tag sequences given an input. Viterbi finds a best path, while summing paths supplies a different normalization calculation.
N12.example: Three positions each permit tags A or B, creating eight possible sequences. The displayed emission, start and transition values determine all path scores. We compute the best sequence and, independently, the sum needed to normalize path probabilities.
N12.connection: An encoder can produce per-token evidence without deciding a complete output structure. This lesson adds dependencies between adjacent output tags and separates structured decoding from training and task-specific span evaluation.

steps.title: Specify emissions, transitions and starts
steps.prose: Emissions describe the evidence at each position for each tag. Transitions connect a previous tag to a next tag, and start values score the first tag. The tables expose all inputs used by this fixed three-position calculation.
steps.terms: HMM emissions are P(observed token | tag), so a displayed row need not sum to one over tags. Recurrence uses log probabilities; CRF emissions/transitions are scores, not row-normalized probabilities.
steps.next: Use the same path evidence for either best-path decoding or path-sum normalization.

steps.title: Keep the best prefix for each ending tag
steps.prose: For each possible current tag, compare predecessor prefix scores plus transition scores, keep the maximum and add this position's emission. Remember the winning predecessor. This dynamic program avoids enumerating all sequences in larger problems.
steps.terms: Viterbi keeps delta_t(j), the best prefix score ending in tag j. e_t(j) is that position's emission and A_ij the previous-i to next-j transition score.
steps.next: Follow the stored predecessor choices to reconstruct the best full sequence.

steps.title: Recover the best tag sequence
steps.prose: Choose the best ending tag and follow the stored pointers back through the sentence. Reversing those recovered indices yields the forward-order tag path. A best final score without these pointers does not identify the whole prediction.
steps.terms: A backpointer records which previous tag gave a stored prefix maximum. Independent token argmax can ignore valuable transition evidence.
steps.next: Span reconstruction and evaluation can now use this decoded path; normalization is a separate branch.

steps.title: Sum paths to obtain a normalizer
steps.prose: Independently combine all path scores with log-sum-exp rather than max. For a CRF this normalizes conditional sequence scores; for an HMM it gives the observation likelihood. The displayed conditional best-path probability uses the normalizer, but Viterbi itself does not require it.
steps.terms: Z sums exp(score) over paths and logZ is its natural logarithm. CRF loss is logZ minus the gold path score, not necessarily minus the best-path score.
steps.next: The deeper notes distinguish supervised CRF learning and HMM forward–backward from best-path decoding.

steps.title: Turn word tags into the required outputs
steps.prose: The example uses tags A/B, not a complete entity scheme. A real entity tagger must align word or subword predictions, apply any declared boundary constraints and reconstruct source spans before scoring them. A CRF is not automatically BIO-valid.
steps.terms: BIO tags distinguish beginning, inside and outside positions. An exact entity match needs the required boundaries and entity type.
steps.next: The next lesson predicts grammatical trees, a different structure from a chain of output tags.

links: Maximize predecessor path scores using the supplied starts, emissions and transitions.
Follow stored predecessor indices from the winning ending tag.
Separately sum exp(path score) over paths to normalize probabilities.

N13.title: Syntax: dependency and constituency parsing
N13.definition: Syntactic parsing predicts how words form a grammatical structure. A dependency parse connects words through head–dependent links; a constituency parse groups spans into nested phrases. These are alternative representations of a sentence, not successive processing stages or the same object as a list of word-class tags.
N13.example: In 'cats chase mice', the example dependency tree makes chase the root, with cats as subject and mice as object. The deeper constituency example instead groups chase mice as a verb phrase and calculates a small grammar derivation.
N13.connection: Sequence labelling assigns tags along input order. Parsing adds a tree structure between or around those positions. Its constraints and evaluation must therefore match the chosen grammatical representation.

steps.title: Choose a grammatical representation
steps.prose: Number the tokens before assigning links or phrase boundaries. Part-of-speech tags can describe word classes, but do not determine which word depends on which or which spans form phrases. A treebank's annotation scheme defines the desired structure.
steps.terms: A dependency head governs another word under a scheme. A constituent is a span grouped as a grammatical phrase.
steps.next: Inspect the authored dependency example while keeping constituency as an alternative representation.

steps.title: Read the example dependency tree
steps.prose: The artificial ROOT points to chase; chase points to cats and mice as subject and object. These arcs describe one simple grammatical analysis. They do not by themselves establish who supports an argument or whether the proposition is true.
steps.terms: An arc connects a head to a dependent. The root convention and relation inventory must come from the chosen annotation scheme.
steps.next: A real parser must choose a legal structure rather than simply maximize every independent arc.

steps.title: Decode under structural constraints
steps.prose: Independent highest-scoring heads can create cycles or invalid roots. Graph-based parsers optimize a tree under constraints; transition-based parsers construct one through actions. Constituency instead combines spans, illustrated by the grammar/chart notes.
steps.terms: Projectivity concerns whether dependency links cross in surface order. Grammatical constraints and semantic correctness are different requirements.
steps.next: Evaluate the chosen tree representation using its own matching convention.

steps.title: Measure the right structural errors
steps.prose: Unlabelled attachment checks heads; labelled attachment also requires the relation type. Tokenization, punctuation and root conventions affect these scores. A high average attachment score can still hide errors important for an extraction application.
steps.terms: UAS means unlabelled attachment score; LAS means labelled attachment score. Neither is a sentence classification accuracy.
steps.next: Contextual encoders next change how token evidence is represented without making any particular output tree automatic.

N14.title: Contextual token encoders: ELMo and BERT
N14.definition: A contextual encoder gives a token a representation that depends on its occurrence, not just its word identity. ELMo combines directional recurrent language-model features; BERT uses bidirectional Transformer context and masked-token pretraining. These methods produce token-level features that still need an appropriate head or pooling rule for a downstream task.
N14.example: The illustration supplies a three-position input with a masked target and hidden width four. A target probability of 0.8 gives negative log-likelihood about 0.2231. The shapes and probability are supplied examples, not an actual downloaded BERT run.
N14.connection: Static word vectors reuse one lexical lookup, while recurrent and attention mechanisms can incorporate context. This lesson connects those mechanisms to pretraining objectives and explains why token encodings are not automatically good sentence-similarity embeddings.

steps.title: Construct a masked-token training example
steps.prose: Withhold selected original tokens under a declared corruption policy, then ask the model to predict those originals from the available input. The simplified view masks its selected target; original BERT's corruption recipe also included other cases.
steps.terms: Masked-language modelling, or MLM, supplies targets from observed text. It differs from predicting a successor using only a causal prefix.
steps.next: Encode the permitted input context while keeping padding visibility separate from target selection.

steps.title: Produce one contextual vector per position
steps.prose: An encoder transforms the input into a batch-by-token-by-feature tensor. Here [1,3,4] means one example, three positions and four features at each position. Context changes these features, but does not change which original position each row represents.
steps.terms: An attention mask restricts visible positions; a loss mask selects scored targets. Neither operation substitutes for the other.
steps.next: Project selected target-position states to vocabulary scores for the pretraining objective.

steps.title: Score the selected original token
steps.prose: The supplied gold-token probability is 0.8, so one target's loss is minus log 0.8. Unselected positions do not contribute MLM targets in this calculation. This objective measures prediction of withheld text, not sentence similarity or factual reliability.
steps.terms: A vocabulary head maps hidden features to scores over token IDs. A per-target negative log-probability is not a downstream task score.
steps.next: For downstream use, choose a head and representation suited to the required prediction unit.

steps.title: Choose a downstream representation and head
steps.prose: A token head can label each position; a pooled head can classify the whole input. Sentence similarity may require different training and pooling. The first special-token vector is not automatically optimized so that cosine distance reflects semantic similarity.
steps.terms: ELMo, BERT, RoBERTa and ELECTRA use distinct pretraining designs. A bidirectional encoder is not automatically a causal generator.
steps.next: The next lesson compares encoders trained or arranged for sentence and query–document comparison.

links: Encode the corrupted visible input, preserving token alignment and validity masks.
Score selected original token targets through a vocabulary head.

N15.title: Sentence encoders and query–document interaction
N15.definition: A sentence encoder represents a larger text unit for comparison rather than assigning one static vector to each word. A bi-encoder computes query and document representations separately; a cross-encoder reads the pair jointly; late interaction keeps token vectors and compares them later. Where the texts first interact determines caching, computation and what information can be compared.
N15.example: Compare a query with two documents using one of three architectures. Bi-encoder mode shows masked pooling and cosine scores; cross-encoder mode shows a joint pair structure without inventing a relevance score; late interaction calculates each query token's best document match.
N15.connection: A contextual token encoder supplies per-position vectors. Turning those into retrieval scores requires a deliberate pooling, training and interaction design, extending the earlier embedding geometry rather than treating every encoder as an interchangeable search model.

steps.title: Choose separate query and document encoding
steps.prose: In a bi-encoder the two texts meet only after each has been encoded. The towers may share weights or use distinct parameters and instructions. Independent document computation makes a reusable vector index possible.
steps.terms: A bi-encoder's document representation is query-independent under its saved encoding contract. Shared weights do not mean the inputs are jointly encoded.
steps.next: Pool the query's valid token states and prepare independent document vectors in parallel.

steps.title: Pool valid query states and normalize
steps.prose: Average only the two real token rows, then rescale to unit length. Including the nonzero padding row intentionally demonstrates a wrong pooling rule that changes the query. Validity masking and normalization perform different operations.
steps.terms: Masked mean pooling divides the sum of valid rows by their count. L2 normalization then changes vector length, not which rows were included.
steps.next: Use this exact pooled query in the downstream document comparison.

steps.title: Prepare reusable document vectors
steps.prose: The two supplied unit vectors represent independently encoded documents. They can be reused across queries only while model revision, instructions, pooling and normalization remain compatible. A changed encoder may require rebuilding the stored vectors.
steps.terms: Caching saves a reusable result. A compatible index must preserve the representation and score conventions used for the query side.
steps.next: Compare the query vector against each independently prepared document vector.

steps.title: Compare vectors and calculate a training loss
steps.prose: With unit vectors the dot product equals cosine. The fixed scores determine ranking; temperature rescales them only inside the displayed contrastive loss. A positive document competes with the supplied negative in that training objective.
steps.terms: In the contrastive equation s is a similarity, the positive is the designated matching document and tau>0 is temperature. Negatives are training contrasts, not guaranteed irrelevant text.
steps.next: Audit actual relevance judgements and candidate retrieval separately from this fixed-vector loss.

steps.title: Evaluate retrieval, negatives and reranking
steps.prose: Relevant items can be mistakenly used as negatives during training. At use time, a reranker can reorder only the candidates it receives. Check candidate recall, final ranking and resource cost instead of assuming a more interactive architecture wins.
steps.terms: A false negative is a relevant candidate treated as a negative label. Candidate recall and reranked quality describe different stages.
steps.next: The following task lessons attach encoders to classification and extraction with explicit output definitions.

links: Encode and pool the query independently, with the declared valid-token mask.
Encode documents independently so their representations can be cached.
The actual pooled query vector supplies one side of the score.
Compare each saved document vector with that same query vector.

steps.title: Prepare one joint query–document input
steps.prose: A cross-encoder reads the pair together before producing its relevance score. It cannot reuse one final query-independent document vector for every query, because each joint representation depends on the other input.
steps.terms: A joint encoder permits token interactions between both segments. Pair formatting and special tokens belong to the selected model.
steps.next: Prepare query and document segments under a shared pair-length budget.

steps.title: Supply the query segment
steps.prose: The query contributes two content tokens before the format's special markers. These are input tokens, not separately pooled query vectors. The joint encoding happens later when both segments are supplied together.
steps.terms: A segment identifies part of a paired input. The tokenizer/model contract determines separators and any segment IDs.
steps.next: Combine this segment with the candidate document in the joint encoder.

steps.title: Supply the document segment
steps.prose: The candidate contributes three content tokens. Its accessible text depends on the shared pair budget, so truncation can remove important evidence. Changing the query requires re-evaluating the pair rather than reusing a final document vector.
steps.terms: Content-token count excludes special markers. Pair-level truncation and independent document embedding are different operations.
steps.next: Encode both segments jointly before applying the relevance head.

steps.title: Jointly encode and score the pair
steps.prose: With the illustrative three special tokens, the pair has eight positions and 64 potential attention pairs per head. A task head would score its joint features. No trained relevance value is supplied here, and pair counts are not measured runtime.
steps.terms: Joint contextual features depend on both texts. A relevance score needs its training and calibration contract before being called a probability.
steps.next: Use joint scoring as a reranking stage and evaluate it on the candidate set it actually receives.

steps.title: Evaluate the reranked candidate set
steps.prose: A joint model can examine each candidate more closely, but cannot recover a relevant document missing from its input set. Measure the first-stage retrieval recall separately from reranking quality and the extra computation per pair.
steps.terms: Reranking reorders existing candidates. End-to-end retrieval can fail before the expensive scoring stage is reached.
steps.next: Compare caching and interaction trade-offs across the three architectures under a matched task.

links: Prepare the query segment without making an independent pooled query embedding.
Prepare the candidate segment under the joint input budget.
Both token streams enter the same encoder before relevance scoring.
Joint attention can connect document and query positions.

steps.title: Retain token vectors on both sides
steps.prose: Late interaction encodes query and documents independently but keeps several token vectors instead of immediately pooling each text to one vector. This permits document-side caching while preserving more local matching choices.
steps.terms: A multivector representation contains several feature vectors for one text. It is not the same as one vector with extra dimensions.
steps.next: Prepare query-token and document-token vectors independently before their late comparison.

steps.title: Keep query token vectors separate
steps.prose: The query has two supplied unit vectors, [1,0] and [0,1]. Each will select its own strongest document-token match. Averaging them first would change the scoring method and can change ranking behaviour.
steps.terms: Each valid query token contributes its own matching term. Padding positions must be excluded from the scoring contract.
steps.next: Keep document token vectors available for each query token's comparison.

steps.title: Cache document token vectors
steps.prose: Document A has vectors [1,0] and [0,1]; B has two copies of [0.8,0.6]. Each document can be encoded independently of the query. Multiple stored vectors cost more space than one pooled document vector.
steps.terms: A token index stores several features per document. Compression and approximate search introduce separate quality/cost trade-offs.
steps.next: For each query vector, find its strongest document-token match and then sum.

steps.title: Calculate best token matches and sum
steps.prose: For A the two query tokens each find a perfect dot-product match, giving 2. For B they contribute 0.8 and 0.6, giving 1.4. These MaxSim scores are neither probabilities nor interchangeable with single-vector cosine.
steps.terms: MaxSim sums the maximum token similarity for each query token. It differs from averaging all matches or using joint cross-attention.
steps.next: Evaluate a complete trained retrieval/indexing system separately from this supplied-vector example.

steps.title: Compare storage, ranking and latency
steps.prose: The point of interaction changes which representations can be cached and how much matching computation remains. The example demonstrates a scoring mechanism, not a leaderboard of trained models or a full ColBERT indexing implementation.
steps.terms: Recall, final ranking, index size and latency are different measured outcomes. A toy score cannot establish their trade-off.
steps.next: Use this distinction when selecting an architecture for the classification, extraction and retrieval tasks that follow.

links: Encode the query independently while retaining its valid token vectors.
Encode documents independently and cache their token vectors.
Each query token selects its best matching document token.
Document token vectors supply alternatives for the MaxSim comparisons.

N16.title: Text classification and paired-input inference
N16.definition: Text classification maps a document, token sequence or input pair to a defined label structure. Single-label classification chooses one mutually exclusive class; multilabel classification can assign several labels at once. The target structure determines the loss and decoding rule, not merely how many label names appear in a dataset.
N16.example: The three supplied logits are [1,−1,0.2] for sports, politics and finance. Switch between one exclusive class and multiple allowed labels to compare softmax with independent sigmoids, then inspect the corresponding prediction rule.
N16.connection: Encoders and lexical pipelines create representations; a classifier turns them into task outputs. This lesson connects the output head to label semantics before the course moves to richer span and relation structures.

steps.title: Define exclusive or overlapping labels
steps.prose: A single-label example needs one class index; a multilabel example needs a binary decision for each label. A document can concern both sports and finance even when a different dataset forces one choice. Specify the task before choosing the activation.
steps.terms: A logit is an unnormalized score. Labels can be mutually exclusive, overlapping, ordered or hierarchical; these relations affect modelling.
steps.next: Transform the fixed score vector using the rule appropriate to the chosen label structure.

steps.title: Convert logits to task-compatible scores
steps.prose: Softmax creates one distribution summing to one across exclusive classes. Independent sigmoids give one score per label, without imposing that sum. Their numerical outputs alone do not show that probabilities are calibrated on real texts.
steps.terms: Cross-entropy suits an exclusive class target; binary cross-entropy can score per-label binary targets. Activation and training objective must agree.
steps.next: Decode one class or apply declared per-label thresholds to the resulting scores.

steps.title: Decode labels with a declared decision rule
steps.prose: Argmax returns one highest-scoring class in single-label mode. The illustrative 0.5 threshold returns sports and finance in multilabel mode. Threshold tuning uses development evidence, not the test labels later used to report performance.
steps.terms: Argmax chooses an index; thresholding chooses a subset. Class weighting changes fitting, whereas thresholding changes the final action rule.
steps.next: The final section separately explains how token, document and input-pair heads use representations.

steps.title: Match the head to the input and output unit
steps.prose: A token head keeps position-level outputs; a document head summarizes input evidence. A paired-input classifier may decide whether a premise entails a hypothesis. Swapping that pair can change the answer, unlike a symmetric similarity calculation.
steps.terms: Natural-language inference, or NLI, concerns entailment, contradiction or unresolved relations under a premise. Paraphrase and similarity are different targets.
steps.next: Information extraction next predicts anchored mentions and relationships rather than one generic class.

links: Choose softmax or independent sigmoid outputs to match the declared target structure.
Apply argmax or declared thresholds to produce the allowed label object.

N17.title: Information extraction: entities, relations and events
N17.definition: Information extraction converts text into structured records about mentions, entities, relations and events. A mention is a source span; coreference links mentions intended to refer to the same entity. Relation and event extraction add typed connections or roles. A valid output format does not by itself make these records supported by the text.
N17.example: In 'Maya founded Acme. She leads it.', the intended reading links She to Maya and it to Acme. Founder and leader are different relations. Keeping these links and original mentions visible helps locate errors instead of hiding them inside a fluent generated record.
N17.connection: Classification assigns a label to a chosen unit. Extraction adds boundaries and links between units, so reliable source offsets and task-specific validation become essential in addition to a good encoder.

steps.title: Identify mentions in the source
steps.prose: Find the spans Maya, Acme, She and it before linking them. A mention is an occurrence in this text; it need not already have a database identifier. Nested or discontinuous spans may need more structure than one flat tag per word.
steps.terms: Named-entity recognition detects typed mentions. Entity linking maps a mention to an external record; coreference groups mentions within a discourse.
steps.next: Resolve references while keeping the original span and any ambiguous alternatives available.

steps.title: Group mentions that share a referent
steps.prose: Under the supplied reading, She and Maya refer to one entity, while it and Acme refer to another. Matching strings alone would miss the pronouns. Another context might make a link ambiguous, so the example's intended reading is not a universal rule.
steps.terms: A coreference cluster groups mentions of the same intended entity. An entity type does not establish a particular referential link.
steps.next: Use grounded mentions and, where needed, resolved references to interpret relations and event arguments.

steps.title: Extract typed relations and event roles
steps.prose: Founded connects Maya and Acme in one proposition; leads expresses another. Keep the event identity, arguments and source evidence explicit. A correct entity link does not automatically tell which relation holds between those entities.
steps.terms: A relation schema names permitted connection types. An event schema can also specify a trigger and several typed participant roles.
steps.next: Validate the references and the source support of the resulting records separately.

steps.title: Check structure, references and meaning
steps.prose: First reject malformed fields, illegal types or references to missing spans. Then inspect whether the text supports the proposed relation. A well-formed record can still be semantically wrong; gold-mention evaluation is also easier than full end-to-end extraction.
steps.terms: Schema validation checks form; source-reference checks locate evidence; semantic checks assess meaning. These tests are complementary.
steps.next: Generation lessons next evaluate whole text outputs, where fluent wording can still omit or reverse source content.

links: Use the anchored mentions to propose intended reference clusters.
Mention spans identify candidate participants and source predicates.
bypass
Resolved references help interpret pronoun arguments when the relation needs them.
Check the candidate records' form, source references and semantic support.

N18.title: Machine translation and BLEU evaluation
N18.definition: Machine translation produces a target-language sequence intended to preserve a source's meaning. Automatic reference-based metrics compare a candidate with permitted reference translations, but they test different kinds of agreement. BLEU combines clipped n-gram precision with a brevity penalty; the simple example here isolates unigram BLEU-1 rather than implementing standard corpus BLEU.
N18.example: The reference is 'the cat sat down'. Choose a short candidate, a repeated word or the exact reference. Clipping stops a repeated sat from gaining unlimited credit, and the brevity penalty reduces the score of an otherwise matching short fragment.
N18.connection: Encoder–decoder attention and search explain how a translation may be produced. This lesson asks how to evaluate the resulting text without confusing lexical overlap with preserved meaning or full translation quality.

steps.title: Fix the candidate, reference and token units
steps.prose: Use the same tokenizer to count both texts. The worked example uses whitespace-separated words and one reference. A real evaluation must specify tokenization, references and aggregation before comparing scores across systems or language pairs.
steps.terms: A reference is an accepted target wording, not necessarily the only valid translation. BLEU-1 uses unigrams rather than the standard multi-order recipe.
steps.next: Count allowed word matches using reference occurrence limits.

steps.title: Clip repeated word matches
steps.prose: Each candidate occurrence can match only an available occurrence in the reference. Repeating sat therefore cannot create another reference match. Divide the clipped count by candidate length to obtain this unigram precision.
steps.terms: Clipping caps a candidate word's matched count at its reference count. Higher-order n-grams additionally check local word order.
steps.next: Use candidate and reference lengths to penalize omission by an overly short output.

steps.title: Apply the brevity penalty
steps.prose: A short fragment could otherwise obtain precision one by avoiding difficult words. Multiply the unigram precision by the displayed length penalty. Standard corpus BLEU aggregates counts across sentences before scoring rather than averaging these toy sentence values.
steps.terms: In the length penalty c is candidate length and r reference length. BP is at most one; scoring also needs its n-gram, smoothing and aggregation conventions.
steps.next: Check meaning preservation separately and document the real scorer used for any reported benchmark.

steps.title: Audit meaning and report scorer settings
steps.prose: Inspect names, numbers, negation, omissions and added claims. Character-overlap chrF and learned COMET contribute different evidence from BLEU. Neither a fluent output nor one high score guarantees suitability for every translation use.
steps.terms: A scorer signature records configuration. Learned metric versions/checkpoints must also be pinned to interpret a comparison.
steps.next: Question answering next uses span and answer-token matching rather than translation n-gram precision.

links: Count candidate/reference tokens under the fixed tokenizer and clip matches.
Their lengths supply the brevity-penalty calculation.
bypass
Multiply clipped unigram precision by the stated brevity factor.

N19.title: Question answering, answer spans and abstention
N19.definition: Question answering predicts an answer to a question under a defined information-access setting. An extractive reader chooses a span in supplied context; a generative system may produce new wording. Answer correctness, source support and deciding when no answer is available are separate requirements, with different evaluation rules.
N19.example: The context tokens are 'The red car stopped .', and the gold answer is red car. Select car, red car or The red car to compare exact answer matching with partial token credit. All span coordinates here use inclusive token ends.
N19.connection: Translation metrics compare generated wording with references. Question answering additionally needs a question, a permissible evidence source and an answerability decision; it must not reuse an unrelated classification or entity-matching score.

steps.title: Identify the supplied context and gold answer
steps.prose: Locate red car at token indices one through two, including both ends. This coordinate convention differs from the exclusive character-end offsets used in preprocessing. The reader sees a passage; it is not being tested on unaided factual recall.
steps.terms: Extractive QA selects source positions. Gold means the reference answer for this fixture, not every possible acceptable answer formulation.
steps.next: Choose a permitted answer span before comparing it with the reference.

steps.title: Decode a valid context span
steps.prose: The control chooses one of three supplied spans rather than running a trained start/end head. A real decoder must enforce start no later than end, valid context positions and any length restriction. Independent highest-scoring endpoints can violate these constraints.
steps.terms: Span decoding converts position scores into an allowed answer region. Padding and question tokens are not answer positions merely because they occupy the same tensor.
steps.next: Evaluate the selected span with the declared exact and partial matching rules.

steps.title: Compare exact match and answer-token F1
steps.prose: Exact match requires the whole selected answer to match this reference. Token precision and recall give partial overlap credit for car alone, while the wider span adds an extra predicted token. This is answer-token F1, not exact entity F1 or classification macro-F1.
steps.terms: Precision divides overlap by predicted answer tokens; recall divides by reference tokens. Real scorers add specific normalization and multiple-reference rules.
steps.next: Handle questions without supported answers as a separate decision, rather than always forcing a span.

steps.title: Decide when to abstain and localize failures
steps.prose: A plausible nearby span may not answer the question. A no-answer rule should be selected on development examples, while retrieval coverage, reader accuracy and source support are evaluated separately. Generative answers need support checks even when wording is correct.
steps.terms: Abstention is an explicit choice not to answer under a rule. A retrieved passage being on-topic is not sufficient evidence for a specific answer.
steps.next: Summarization next requires preserving several relevant source claims rather than selecting one answer region.

links: Select an allowed span using the available context positions.
The gold answer supplies the reference tokens and exact target.
bypass
Compare the selected answer with that reference under the declared matcher.

N20.title: Summarization, dialogue and source faithfulness
N20.definition: Summarization selects and compresses source content, either by extracting passages or generating new wording. Source faithfulness asks whether the output preserves what the source supports; external truth asks a different question. Dialogue adds an interaction goal: helping a user may require clarification, correction or abstention rather than simply producing agreeable text.
N20.example: The supplied source says 'trial improved symptoms'. Replacing improved with worsened leaves two of three reference words unchanged while reversing the main claim. The control reveals why lexical overlap alone cannot certify a faithful summary.
N20.connection: Generation scores and QA matching test limited forms of agreement. This lesson examines their blind spots and connects language-model outputs to source claims and actual interaction usefulness, without treating style as correctness.

steps.title: Identify the source claim and its scope
steps.prose: The example source asserts improvement, not worsening. In a real report, participants, quantities, uncertainty and conditions can be just as important as the verb. A source-faithful summary preserves the relevant assertion without automatically verifying it externally.
steps.terms: Faithfulness concerns consistency with supplied source content. Truthfulness concerns the world; a false source can be summarized faithfully.
steps.next: Compare the candidate's predicate and participants before relying on an overlap score.
steps.node: Identify the source claim and its scope

steps.title: Check whether the candidate changes meaning
steps.prose: The improved candidate matches the supplied direction; the worsened candidate reverses it. This meaning judgement is authored for the example, not computed by a factuality model. Longer summaries may contain many independently checkable claims.
steps.terms: A proposition expresses an asserted relation. A fluent sentence can preserve most words while changing that relation's polarity or scope.
steps.next: Calculate word overlap to see which aspect of the error that metric misses.
steps.node: Check whether the candidate changes meaning

steps.title: Interpret lexical overlap as limited evidence
steps.prose: The reversed statement still matches trial and symptoms, yielding recall two thirds under this three-word unigram rule. That score says nothing about whether the remaining verb contradicts the source. Full ROUGE variants use their own matching conventions.
steps.terms: Unigram recall counts matched reference words divided by reference length. It is neither a complete ROUGE implementation nor a semantic support test.
steps.next: For summaries and dialogue, evaluate the goal and support beyond superficial wording.
steps.node: Interpret lexical overlap as limited evidence

steps.title: Evaluate useful interaction, not automatic agreement
steps.prose: A helpful system may ask a question, challenge a false premise or state uncertainty. Test task completion and grounded responses alongside preference ratings. Judge models can favor verbosity or agreement, so audit their decisions on meaningful failures.
steps.terms: Grounding links output to available evidence. User preference and task success can disagree, especially when a pleasing answer repeats a false assumption.
steps.next: The next lesson examines inference and argument structures where context and target definitions also change the correct interpretation.
steps.node: Evaluate useful interaction, not automatic agreement

N21.title: Inference, discourse and argument mining
N21.definition: Language understanding involves more than classifying a sentence in isolation. Natural-language inference compares a premise with a hypothesis; discourse analysis relates text units; argument mining identifies claims, reasons and support or attack relations under a specified scheme. These tasks share language evidence but do not define the same output or universal argument label.
N21.example: Three authored units have roles claim, premise and other. One toy guideline counts only claims as positive; another counts claims and premises. The same premise therefore changes binary label when the policy changes, even though its text and supplied role stay fixed.
N21.connection: Source faithfulness asks whether a statement is supported; this lesson distinguishes semantic inference, discourse roles and argumentative structure. It also shows why a successful intermediate representation must be tested against the actual target guideline.

steps.title: Separate text, context and argumentative role
steps.prose: Fund transit is treated as a claim, It reduces traffic as a premise and Hello as other under the intended example reading. These roles are supplied annotations. A model-generated role would itself require validation rather than becoming gold because it is structured.
steps.terms: A claim expresses a standpoint; a premise supplies a reason under a scheme. Context and speaker intent can affect how a unit functions.
steps.next: Map the supplied roles into the selected task's binary labels rather than assuming the mapping is universal.

steps.title: Apply the declared binary-label guideline
steps.prose: Claims-only returns positive for the claim but not the premise. Claims-or-premises marks both as positive. This is a deliberate difference in what counts as the target, not a failure by one classifier to recognize identical language.
steps.terms: An annotation policy maps evidence into task labels. A role can stay fixed while a downstream binary definition changes.
steps.next: The next section separately considers relations between units rather than treating binary labels as a complete argument.

steps.title: Distinguish argumentative units from relations
steps.prose: Identifying a claim and a premise does not prove how they relate. Under the supplied reading, reduced traffic can support funding transit, but a support/attack link is another target to predict. Conversational and implicit arguments may require more context.
steps.terms: Argument mining can include unit identification, role classification and relation extraction. Their errors and matching units should be evaluated separately.
steps.next: Test whether an intermediate record helps the actual task rather than looking persuasive on its own.

steps.title: Test intermediate representations and their scope
steps.prose: Compare direct text with context, guidelines and generated fields under matched information and selection rules. A role-only rule can help claim-oriented labels yet fail with other definitions. Keep that useful diagnostic without turning it into a universal theory.
steps.terms: An ablation removes or isolates a stated field to test its contribution. Improved task score need not imply every generated field is accurate.
steps.next: The transfer lesson next asks how such findings behave when language, domain or annotation policy changes.

links: Apply the chosen annotation guideline to the supplied roles to obtain binary labels.

N22.title: Cross-lingual and cross-domain transfer
N22.definition: Transfer evaluation tests whether a system developed under one condition works under another. Cross-lingual transfer changes language; cross-domain transfer changes the source or content distribution; annotation-policy changes can alter the label meaning itself. These shifts can coexist, so a score drop alone does not explain its own cause.
N22.example: A two-by-two authored table uses fine-tuning sources as rows and evaluation targets as columns. Selecting source A or B changes the highlighted row. The scores are invented for interpretation practice, not measurements of real languages or named models.
N22.connection: Earlier lessons fixed targets, representations and evaluation units. Transfer now asks which parts remain compatible across conditions, including whether a base multilingual model had already encountered target-language text during pretraining.

steps.title: Name the source and target conditions
steps.prose: State what was used for fine-tuning and what changes at evaluation. Cross-lingual transfer may omit target-language task labels while still using a base model pretrained on that language. It is therefore not necessarily zero target-language exposure.
steps.terms: Source and target describe experimental conditions. Language, domain and label-policy shifts are separate variables even when datasets differ on all three.
steps.next: Read the table's row and column meaning before averaging its values.
steps.node: Name the source and target conditions

steps.title: Read within-source and transferred scores
steps.prose: Diagonal entries evaluate a model on its source condition; off-diagonal entries test another target. Compare per-target values before the row mean. The A-to-B and B-to-A differences need not be symmetric, and a grand average hides that pattern.
steps.terms: A source–target matrix keeps fitting and evaluation axes distinct. The displayed row mean is a summary, not evidence that all targets behave alike.
steps.next: Inspect competing causes of the observed pattern rather than assigning the gap to one factor automatically.

steps.title: Separate representation and target-definition shifts
steps.prose: A different script or terminology can affect representation coverage. A different label guideline can instead require another correct answer for the same text. Use documentation, prediction slices and controlled cases to distinguish these explanations where possible.
steps.terms: Label-policy shift changes target semantics. Covariate or content differences concern what inputs occur; neither alone identifies every cause of transfer failure.
steps.next: Declare which target information can be used for adaptation and selection.

steps.title: Keep target adaptation boundaries explicit
steps.prose: Translation, multilingual fitting and target-label tuning use different information. Group translated or near-duplicate versions of one example when splitting. A rule chosen using target test labels is target-adapted rather than untouched transfer.
steps.terms: Low-resource settings also involve script, morphology, dialect, community meaning and annotation availability, not only a smaller row count.
steps.next: The long-document lesson next changes evidence access through windows and information paths rather than language alone.

N23.title: Long-document encoding and evidence coverage
N23.definition: A long-document system must specify how distant text can influence a prediction. Chunking encodes local windows and combines their representations; a hierarchical encoder adds a second level; sparse attention changes token-to-token connections within a sequence. These are different information paths, not interchangeable ways of increasing a context-length setting.
N23.example: Eight token positions are processed in four-token windows. An answer needs positions 3 and 4 together. Overlap two makes that boundary jointly visible while increasing processed positions from eight to twelve; a separate control illustrates local versus global sparse-attention connections.
N23.connection: The earlier sequence encoders assumed the relevant input was accessible. Long documents expose a new failure: evidence can be lost at truncation or window boundaries before an otherwise capable model can combine it.

steps.title: Locate the evidence the task requires
steps.prose: The example needs positions three and four together. A model that sees only the first four positions cannot recover that relationship from this truncated input. Decide whether the task needs a local span, several distant facts or a whole-document summary.
steps.terms: Evidence coverage means the required text is accessible through the chosen input path. It does not establish that a model understands that evidence.
steps.next: For a chunking design, construct windows and account for repeated processing.
steps.node: Locate the evidence the task requires

steps.title: Build windows and count repeated exposure
steps.prose: Window stride is width minus overlap. With width four, overlap two creates three windows over eight unique positions. Twelve processed positions count repeated appearances, not twelve distinct tokens or additional training examples.
steps.terms: Overlap repeats positions across adjacent windows. Independent encodings do not share hidden state unless a separate mechanism connects them.
steps.next: Check whether any valid window contains all positions required by the example.
steps.node: Build windows and count repeated exposure

steps.title: Check span coverage across boundaries
steps.prose: Without overlap, no window contains both positions three and four. With overlap two, the middle window does. This repairs this particular accessibility problem at extra computation, but says nothing yet about prediction quality.
steps.terms: A coverage test is a structural check before model evaluation. A longer answer or distant relation may require more than this local repair.
steps.next: Sparse attention offers a separate alternative; compare its connectivity rather than placing it after chunking as another step.

steps.title: Compare local and global attention paths
steps.prose: The mask selects allowed query–key pairs in one sequence. Local connections limit direct access; a global token connects to all positions in this illustration. This differs from encoding separate chunks, and pair counts are not measured runtime or quality.
steps.terms: Sparse attention changes the computation graph. A_ij indicates whether query position i may read key position j; a global token adds permitted connections.
steps.next: Choose an aggregation method explicitly if the design instead produces several chunk or sentence vectors.
steps.node: Compare local and global attention paths

steps.title: Combine representations for the required output
steps.prose: A hierarchical design can encode tokens into sentence or chunk vectors and then combine them. Mean pooling discards order; ordered or attention-based second levels add other assumptions. Record truncation, overlap and aggregation before comparing systems.
steps.terms: A hierarchical encoder adds representation levels. Increasing a configured input limit does not prove trained long-context capability.
steps.next: The final NLP lesson assembles task definitions, matched metrics and reproducible artifacts into a complete study.
steps.node: Combine representations for the required output

N24.title: NLP evaluation and a complete study
N24.definition: An NLP evaluation counts matches between predicted and reference objects under a declared task rule. Token tags, complete entity spans, answer tokens and generated sequences are different objects, even when some metrics share a familiar name. A complete study also records preprocessing, model selection, source groups and failures so the result can be interpreted and reproduced.
N24.example: Two gold entities and two predicted entities have one exact span-and-type match, giving one correct match, one false positive and one false negative. A separate six-token example has five correct tags. The scores differ because the evaluated objects differ.
N24.connection: The task lessons introduced distinct outputs and error sources. This final lesson connects them to the shared metric formulas and an executable research workflow without inventing one universal NLP accuracy.

steps.title: Define what counts as one match
steps.prose: For exact named-entity evaluation, both the source boundary and type must agree. Matching only part of a name can leave one missed gold entity and one incorrect predicted entity. Start with the objects and matcher before choosing an aggregation formula.
steps.terms: A true positive is a matched prediction; a false positive is an unmatched prediction; a false negative is an unmatched reference object.
steps.next: Apply the shared precision, recall and F1 definitions to these entity-level counts.
steps.node: Define what counts as one match

steps.title: Calculate exact entity precision, recall and F1
steps.prose: One of two predictions matches one of two references, so precision and recall are both one half and their F1 is one half. Report entity types, strict or permissive boundary-tag handling and scorer version with a real result.
steps.terms: The count formula can be reused across tasks, but the matching objects determine its interpretation. Entity F1 is not automatically macro classification F1.
steps.next: Compare this with a separate token-level example without treating it as a replacement score.
steps.node: Calculate exact entity precision, recall and F1

steps.title: Keep token accuracy and answer matching distinct
steps.prose: The separate six-token fixture has five correct labels, or accuracy five sixths. It does not reconstruct the entity example or contradict its F1. Answer-token F1 and generated-text overlap introduce yet other match and normalization rules.
steps.terms: A denominator defines what each score averages over. Identical names such as F1 can hide different match units and reductions.
steps.next: Build a controlled pipeline that saves enough intermediate evidence to locate these errors.
steps.node: Keep token accuracy and answer matching distinct

steps.title: Run and report a controlled NLP experiment
steps.prose: Begin with a justified lexical baseline, compare a neural representation under the same source-grouped split, and save per-case predictions. Record label policy, preprocessing, model/scorer revisions, selection budget and resource use. Optional real-data exercises require separate access and setup.
steps.terms: A complete pipeline includes source processing, representation, prediction or decoding and evaluation. Reading a fixture is not a benchmark result.
steps.next: Use the linked implementation exercise and data routes to test understanding on permitted real tasks, with held-out evaluation.
steps.node: Run and report a controlled NLP experiment
